name: Ancient Egypt
blurb: Three thousand years of pharaohs, from Narmer to Alexander
dateConvention: All dates are BC, counting down with no year zero. Egyptian dates before about 690 BC are reconstructions and can be out by decades or more; the deck follows the chronology of Ian Shaw's Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) throughout and marks every date before 690 BC as approximate. Hatshepsut's card starts when she became regent for the young Thutmose III, and his card covers his sole rule after her death.
epilogue: Alexander was welcomed as pharaoh, visited the oracle at Siwa and founded Alexandria in 331 BC. After his death his general Ptolemy took Egypt, and the Ptolemaic Egypt deck continues the story.

reigns.tagline: The southern king who wore both crowns
reigns.previously: The Nile is split between rival kingdoms in the south and the Delta.
paragraphs: Before Narmer, the Nile valley was a patchwork. In the south, Upper Egypt, rival kingdoms grew up around Nekhen (Hierakonpolis), Naqada and This, near Abydos. In the north lay the marshy Delta, Lower Egypt. Around 3100 BC a southern king called Narmer ruled both halves. Historians start the Early Dynastic Period and the 1st Dynasty with him. Nobody knows how long he reigned, or quite how he pulled it off.

His calling card is the Narmer Palette, a carved siltstone slab found at Hierakonpolis by James Quibell and Frederick Green in their 1897–98 dig, and now in Cairo. On one side he wears the tall white crown of the south and raises a mace over a kneeling enemy. On the other he wears the red crown of the north and marches out to inspect rows of beheaded bodies.

His name, written with a catfish and a chisel, turns up on pots and seals all over Egypt and even in southern Canaan. Later Egyptians said their first king was Menes, founder of Memphis. Narmer may be that man. He was buried in the desert cemetery of Umm el-Qa'ab at Abydos, and the kings who came after him chose the same ground.

claims.text: Narmer is Menes, the legendary first king of Egypt.
claims.note: Menes appears only in king lists written over a thousand years later and in Manetho. Some scholars match him with Narmer, others with his successor Aha.

claims.text: The Narmer Palette records a real war of conquest.
claims.note: It may show a real victory, or a ceremonial picture of what a king was supposed to do. It was a temple offering, not a news report.

claims.text: Menes founded Memphis by damming the Nile, and was later carried off by a hippopotamus.
claims.note: Herodotus tells the dam story; the hippo comes from Manetho as quoted by the chronicler Africanus. Both wrote thousands of years later.

reigns.hook: Narmer's son Aha inherits a brand-new kind of country: one king, two crowns, and a court learning to write. Aha and his heirs will not go to their graves alone.

images.caption: Both faces of the Narmer Palette, carved in Narmer's own time and now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo; a ceremonial object, not a true likeness.
images.alt: Both sides of a carved stone palette showing a king in the white crown striking a kneeling captive, and the same king in the red crown with rows of figures and two long-necked beasts

reigns.tagline: The fighter king whose tomb came with lions
reigns.previously: Narmer rules north and south. Egypt is one kingdom.
paragraphs: His name means "the fighter", and he was probably Narmer's son. Aha took over a kingdom barely a generation old, in about 3000 BC by the dates used here, and nobody knows how long he held it. He is the first king of the Early Dynastic Period we can really picture, thanks to small wooden and ivory labels once tied to jars and boxes of goods for the royal stores.

One label from Naqada shows his name beside a shrine marked with the sign "mn", and scholars have argued ever since that Aha, not Narmer, was the Menes of legend. A giant mudbrick tomb at Naqada, full of seals with Aha's name, may belong to his mother, Neithhotep. And the first grand tombs for officials at Saqqara, above the new capital of Memphis, date from his reign.

At Abydos his own tomb was a new, grander design, with rows of smaller graves beside it for more than thirty people, most of them young men. German excavators also found the bones of at least seven young lions buried in the complex. Whether he hunted them or kept them, Aha wanted his lions with him for ever.

claims.text: Aha, not Narmer, was Menes, the legendary first king of Egypt.
claims.note: The Naqada label puts the sign "mn" next to Aha's name, but it may name a shrine or a person. Menes himself only appears in much later king lists.

claims.text: The young men in the graves beside Aha's tomb were killed to serve him after death.
claims.note: The graves were laid out and roofed together with the king's tomb, which points to sacrifice. No written source says so.

claims.text: Lions were buried in Aha's tomb complex.
claims.note: The German Archaeological Institute's excavations at Umm el-Qa'ab found the bones of at least seven young lions there.

reigns.hook: Aha is laid to rest among his lions and his servants. The next king, Djer, will rule far longer, and take far more people into the dark with him.

images.caption: An ebony label of Aha from Abydos, now in the British Museum; a record from his reign, not a portrait.
images.alt: Broken dark wooden label carved in rows with the king's name in a palace frame, shrines, figures and hieroglyphs

reigns.tagline: The king whose tomb became the grave of a god
reigns.previously: Aha is buried at Abydos, with servants and lions around him.
paragraphs: Djer seems to have reigned a long time, perhaps forty years or so, though the figure comes from a badly worn royal annal. The same annal names his mother as Khenthap. Labels from his reign mention festivals, new buildings and raids abroad, and objects with his name turn up all along the Nile. The young state was settling into a routine of scribes, storehouses and taxes.

His tomb at Abydos is the biggest of its day, and the most chilling. Around it lie more than 300 small graves for servants, officials and women of the household, laid out as if they were all filled at once. In 1900 Flinders Petrie's team found a mummified arm hidden in a hole in the tomb wall, still wearing four bracelets of gold, turquoise, amethyst and lapis lazuli.

About a thousand years later, in the Middle Kingdom, Egyptians decided this was the grave of the god Osiris. Pilgrims came for centuries and left so many pots that the cemetery's modern Arabic name, Umm el-Qa'ab, means "mother of pots". A stone figure of the dead god lying on his bier was even placed in the tomb.

claims.text: Over 300 people were killed and buried with Djer.
claims.note: The graves surround the tomb in neat rows and seem to have been closed together. Nothing written explains how their occupants died.

claims.text: The arm found in the tomb belonged to Djer's queen.
claims.note: Petrie guessed so. By his own account, museum staff in Cairo kept the bracelets and threw the arm away, so it can never be tested.

claims.text: Djer's tomb was the tomb of Osiris.
claims.note: Middle Kingdom pilgrims believed it. The tomb is a 1st Dynasty king's, built long before the Osiris cult took root there.

reigns.hook: Djer is buried with his household around him. His successor takes the cobra as his sign and leaves behind one of the finest carvings of the age.

images.credit: Unknown Egyptian goldsmith; photo vivafox/Francois Galuccio
images.caption: A bracelet from the arm Petrie's team found in Djer's tomb, now in Cairo; a royal jewel, not a portrait.
images.alt: Bracelet of small gold and turquoise plaques, each shaped like a falcon on a palace-front frame, strung in a row

reigns.tagline: The Serpent King and his perfect stone
reigns.previously: Djer dies after a long reign and is buried with hundreds.
paragraphs: Djet's name was written with a cobra, so he is often called the Serpent King. His reign seems to have been short, perhaps ten years, and few records of it survive. But he left one of the masterpieces of early Egyptian art: the tall limestone stela that stood at his tomb at Abydos, found by the Frenchman Émile Amélineau in the 1890s and now in the Louvre.

On it a falcon stands on top of a box, and inside the box is the snake. The falcon is the god Horus, and the box is a serekh, the front of a royal palace seen from above. Every king's Horus name was framed this way, because the king was Horus on earth. An ivory comb from his reign shows a falcon in a boat sailing across a pair of wings, one of the oldest pictures of the sky.

His tomb at Abydos had its ring of servant graves like those before it. At Saqqara a great mastaba from his reign, built for a top official, was edged with rows of clay bulls' heads fitted with real horns. When Djet died, his heir Den was still a boy, and his widow stepped forward.

claims.text: Djet was Merneith's husband and Den's father.
claims.note: A seal names Merneith as Den's mother. That Djet was her husband is worked out from the order of the kings and their tombs.

claims.text: Djet reigned only about ten years.
claims.note: No annal entry for his reign survives. The guess rests on how few objects and labels carry his name.

reigns.hook: Djet is dead, and the heir is a child. For a few years Egypt may be run by a woman: the boy's mother, Merneith.

images.caption: Djet's tomb stela from Abydos, now in the Louvre: his royal name, not a portrait.
images.alt: Tall limestone stela with a falcon standing on a rectangular palace frame that encloses a snake

reigns.tagline: Buried like a king, and maybe the first woman to rule
reigns.cameToPower: Regent for her young son Den
reigns.previously: Djet dies, and his heir Den is still a child.
paragraphs: When Flinders Petrie cleared her tomb at Abydos in 1900, he took Merneith for a king. Her tomb lay among the kings' at Umm el-Qa'ab, built on the same scale, with rows of servant graves around it, and two tall stone stelae carried her name. Only later did it sink in that the name honoured the goddess Neith and belonged to a woman. Queen Merneith had been buried like a pharaoh.

In the 1980s German excavators found seal impressions in Den's tomb listing the kings of the dynasty from Narmer to Den. Merneith is on the list, the only woman, called "king's mother". The simplest story is that Djet died with their son still a boy, and she ran the country until he was old enough. If so, she is the first woman known to have ruled Egypt.

claims.text: Merneith ruled Egypt as regent for the boy Den.
claims.note: Her royal-scale tomb and her place on the seal list point that way, but no text says outright that she governed.

claims.text: Merneith's tomb was surrounded by servant graves like a king's.
claims.note: Petrie found the rows of subsidiary graves around her tomb at Abydos, and later German work confirmed them.

claims.text: Petrie first thought Merneith was a male king.
claims.note: He published her as a king in his 1900 report; her identity as a royal woman was recognised later.

reigns.hook: Den grows up and takes the throne in his own right. He will wear both crowns at once, and his reign will be the high point of the dynasty.

images.credit: Unknown Egyptian sculptor; photo Juan R. Lazaro
images.caption: Detail of one of the two stelae that stood at Merneith's tomb at Abydos, now in Cairo; her name, not a portrait.
images.alt: Detail of a weathered stone stela carved with hieroglyphs of a name, including the crossed-arrows emblem of the goddess Neith

reigns.tagline: The first king to wear both crowns at once
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Merneith, probably of Djet
reigns.previously: Merneith steers Egypt while her son Den grows up.
paragraphs: Den reigned for decades and left more records than any king before him. Annal entries and dozens of ivory and wooden labels mention festivals, new statues of the gods, building and war. He is the first king shown wearing the double crown, the white crown of the south and the red crown of the north worn as one, and the first known to use the title later read as "king of Upper and Lower Egypt".

A small ivory label in the British Museum, once tied to a pair of his sandals, shows him clubbing a man from the eastern desert, with the words "first time of smiting the east". He held a sed festival, the jubilee where an ageing king ran a ritual course to show he was still fit to rule. His chancellor Hemaka was buried at Saqqara with a wooden box holding a blank papyrus roll, the oldest known.

Den's tomb at Abydos was the most advanced yet: the first with a long staircase running down into it, and the first floored with granite, brought down the Nile from Aswan. Around it lay more rows of servant graves. When he died, Egypt was richer and better run than ever before. The next reigns would not be so smooth.

claims.text: Den was the first king to wear the double crown.
claims.note: He is the earliest king shown in it. Earlier kings may have worn it in pictures that are lost.

claims.text: The sandal label records a real campaign into Sinai.
claims.note: The smiting pose is a set royal image. It may mark a real raid on the eastern desert, or simply show the king doing what kings were meant to do.

claims.text: Den celebrated a sed festival.
claims.note: Labels from his reign show him in the jubilee pavilion and running the ritual course.

reigns.hook: Den's long reign ends. His successor Anedjib inherits a golden age, and seems to have struggled to hold on to it.

images.caption: The ivory sandal label of Den in the British Museum; a set royal image, not a true likeness.
images.alt: Small ivory label showing a king raising a club over a kneeling man, with hieroglyphs above

reigns.tagline: Small tomb, short reign, and a name scraped away
reigns.previously: Den dies after decades on the throne, the dynasty at its peak.
paragraphs: After Den, Anedjib looks like a step down. He seems to have reigned only about seven years, and his tomb at Abydos is the smallest and most cheaply built of all the 1st Dynasty kings' tombs, with a modest ring of servant graves. Few labels or objects carry his name, and the later king lists call him Merbiapen.

Near the capital, though, something interesting was happening. At Saqqara the mastaba of a high official of his reign, Nebitka, turned out to hide a stepped mound of brick inside its outer walls. Some see it as an early hint of the idea Djoser's architects would one day build in stone.

After his death, stone vessels with Anedjib's name had it ground off and his successor Semerkhet's carved in. That looks like more than tidying up. Some historians think the throne was seized, perhaps after a rival had already taken the north.

claims.text: Semerkhet had Anedjib's name erased.
claims.note: Several stone vessels show Anedjib's name scraped off and Semerkhet's added. Whether it was spite or just reuse is guesswork.

claims.text: The stepped mound inside Nebitka's mastaba inspired the Step Pyramid.
claims.note: Walter Emery, who dug it, thought so. It was hidden inside the tomb and built some 250 years before Djoser, so the link is uncertain.

reigns.hook: Anedjib dies after a short reign. The next king, Semerkhet, scrubs out his name, and the later king lists will try to forget Semerkhet in turn.

images.caption: A stone vase fragment from Saqqara with Anedjib's name and a carving of a royal statue, now in Cairo; not a true likeness.
images.alt: Fragment of a dark stone vessel engraved with a royal name in a palace frame and a small striding figure of a king

reigns.tagline: The king the record keepers tried to forget
reigns.previously: Anedjib dies after a short, shaky reign.
paragraphs: Semerkhet's reign is one of the best measured of the dynasty: the royal annals carved on the Palermo Stone give him about nine years. Yet over 1,500 years later, when a priest named Tjuneroy had a list of past kings carved in his tomb at Saqqara under Ramesses II, Semerkhet was left out. It looks as if the official memory did not want him.

He had Anedjib's name ground off stone vessels and his own put in its place. Unlike the kings before him, he left almost nothing at Saqqara, where the court of Memphis buried its great men. Put together, that makes some historians think he took the throne by force, or ruled a kingdom that was not entirely his.

His tomb at Abydos was big, with a large ring of servant burials built in one go with the king's own grave. Manetho, the priest who wrote a history of Egypt under the Ptolemies, says that in the reign of a king he calls Semempses there were many strange omens and a great plague.

claims.text: Semerkhet seized the throne as a usurper.
claims.note: The erased names, the gap at Saqqara and his absence from the Saqqara king list all point that way, but none of it is proof.

claims.text: A great plague struck Egypt in his reign.
claims.note: Only Manetho says so, writing about 2,600 years later, and his Semempses is matched with Semerkhet by guesswork.

claims.text: The annals give Semerkhet about nine years.
claims.note: The Palermo Stone annals, carved in the 5th Dynasty, record his reign; the count is read as about eight and a half or nine years.

reigns.hook: Semerkhet dies. Qaa, the last king of the line, takes over, and his funeral will be the last of its terrible kind.

images.caption: An ivory label from an oil jar of Semerkhet's reign, now in the British Museum; a record, not a portrait.
images.alt: Small ivory label carved with rows of hieroglyphs and signs, including a royal name in a palace frame

reigns.tagline: Last of the line, and the last with company in the grave
reigns.previously: Semerkhet dies, a king the later lists will try to forget.
paragraphs: Qaa was the last king of the 1st Dynasty, and his name means something like "his arm is raised". Labels and stone vessels from his reign mention festivals, and his officials went back to building big mastabas at Saqqara, like the one of the noble Merka. After the upsets of the last two reigns, things looked settled again.

His tomb at Abydos, like every royal tomb since Aha's, came with graves for servants around it. It was the last. After Qaa, no Egyptian king is known to have taken people into the tomb with him. The custom died with the dynasty.

What happened next is murky. A few shadowy names, such as Sneferka, may belong to rivals who held power briefly. But German excavators found seal impressions of Hetepsekhemwy, first king of the 2nd Dynasty, at the entrance to Qaa's tomb. The new king, it seems, was the man who buried him.

claims.text: Qaa's funeral was the last with sacrificed retainers.
claims.note: His is the last royal tomb with subsidiary graves. Whether the people in them were sacrificed is debated for the whole dynasty.

claims.text: Short-lived rival kings fought over the throne after Qaa.
claims.note: Names like Sneferka appear on a few stone vessels from Saqqara and may belong to this moment. Their place in the story is guesswork.

claims.text: Hetepsekhemwy oversaw Qaa's burial.
claims.note: Seal impressions with his name lay at the tomb entrance, which suggests he closed it. It does not prove the handover was peaceful.

reigns.hook: Qaa is buried. A new family takes the throne, and its first king picks a name that sounds like a peace treaty.

images.caption: Qaa's tomb stela from Abydos, now in the Penn Museum, Philadelphia; his royal name, not a portrait.
images.alt: Rounded stone stela carved with a falcon above a palace-front frame holding the king's name

reigns.tagline: His name means "the two powers are at peace"
reigns.cameToPower: Buried Qaa, then took the throne
reigns.previously: Qaa dies and the 1st Dynasty comes to an end.
paragraphs: Manetho starts a new dynasty here, the 2nd, but the change may have been smoother than it sounds. Seal impressions of Hetepsekhemwy turned up at the door of Qaa's tomb, so he probably saw the old king into his grave. His name means "the two powers are at peace". Many read the two powers as Horus and Seth, gods of the two halves of the land, made friends again after trouble.

He broke with tradition in one big way. Instead of Abydos, he chose Saqqara, above Memphis, and had long corridors and rooms cut deep into the rock. The galleries were found under the causeway of King Unas, built about 500 years later right on top of them. Later kings of his family were buried nearby.

A granite statue of a kneeling priest named Hotepdief, now in Cairo, carries his name on its shoulder together with the next two kings'. Manetho says that under the first king of this dynasty a chasm opened in the earth at Bubastis, in the Delta, and many people died.

claims.text: Hetepsekhemwy buried Qaa, so the 2nd Dynasty began peacefully.
claims.note: His seals at Qaa's tomb show he was in charge of the burial. A peaceful takeover is a reasonable reading, not a fact.

claims.text: The galleries under the Unas causeway were Hetepsekhemwy's tomb.
claims.note: Seal impressions with his name were found there. Some scholars give the tomb to his successor Raneb.

claims.text: A chasm opened at Bubastis and swallowed many people.
claims.note: Only Manetho tells this, writing well over 2,000 years later.

reigns.hook: Hetepsekhemwy dies after a long reign. His successor will be the first king to put the sun god Ra into his name.

images.caption: The entrance to the rock-cut galleries at Saqqara credited to Hetepsekhemwy; his tomb, not a portrait.
images.alt: Entrance to an underground passage cut into pale rock at Saqqara

reigns.tagline: The first king to put the sun god in his name
reigns.previously: Hetepsekhemwy dies, buried in vast galleries under Saqqara.
paragraphs: Almost everything we know about Raneb fits on a few stones and seal impressions. Even his name is a puzzle: it can be read Raneb, "Ra is my lord", or Nebra, "lord of the sun". Either way, it marks something new. He seems to be the first king to put the sun god Ra into his royal name, centuries before Ra became the star of Egyptian religion.

His dates here are only a rough share of the 2nd Dynasty, since nobody knows how long he really reigned; about 20 years is a guess. His name turns up on seal impressions in the great underground galleries at Saqqara, near those of Hetepsekhemwy. A granite stela carved with his name, once set up at a royal tomb or shrine, is now in the Metropolitan Museum in New York.

claims.text: Raneb was the first king to include the sun god Ra in his name.
claims.note: It depends on reading his name with Ra in it, which most scholars accept. Earlier kings may simply have left no trace of the habit.

claims.text: Under Kaiechos, the 2nd Dynasty's second king, the Apis bull of Memphis and other sacred animals were first worshipped as gods.
claims.note: Manetho says so about 2,500 years later. Kaiechos is often matched with Raneb, but the match is a guess.

reigns.hook: Raneb's successor will reign far longer, and for once the records keep pace: festivals, a running of the sacred bull and a war in the north, all set down year by year.

images.caption: Raneb's granite stela, carved with his name in a royal frame under the falcon Horus; now in the Metropolitan Museum. Not a portrait.
images.alt: Tall rough granite slab carved near the top with a rectangular royal name frame topped by a falcon

reigns.tagline: Forty years of festivals, written down year by year
reigns.previously: Raneb, the king named for the sun, dies after a murky reign.
paragraphs: Nynetjer is the best-recorded king of the 2nd Dynasty, thanks to the Palermo Stone. This slab of black stone, carved centuries later, lists the kings' years one by one. For Nynetjer it records festivals, a census of the land's wealth every second year, a ceremonial "running of the Apis" bull and the height of each year's Nile flood.

One entry seems to say he "hacked up" two places in the north. If that is right, Egypt was already pulling apart. He reigned a long time, about 40 years or more, and was buried in another set of galleries cut deep into the rock at Saqqara. His name, with those of the two kings before him, is carved on the shoulder of a small kneeling statue of a priest named Hotepdief, now in Cairo.

claims.text: Nynetjer fought a war against towns in the north.
claims.note: The Palermo Stone entry for one of his years is usually read as "hacking up" two northern places. The signs are damaged and the meaning is argued over.

claims.text: He reigned for about 40 years or more.
claims.note: The Palermo Stone gives him many year-entries, and Manetho a long reign, but the total cannot be checked.

reigns.hook: After Nynetjer the year-by-year record breaks off. A string of kings follows whose names survive on jars and lists, and little else.

reigns.title: The Lost Kings of the Second Dynasty
reigns.tagline: Kings known by little more than their names
reigns.previously: Nynetjer dies after some 40 years. The records go dark.
paragraphs: After Nynetjer the year-by-year annals break off, and the 2nd Dynasty slips into one of the darkest corners of Egyptian history. The kings of the next few generations are known from scraps: names on stone jars, seal impressions, and king lists drawn up more than a thousand years later. Nobody knows how many there were, in what order they came, or how long any of them ruled.

Weneg's name turns up on stone vessels stored under Djoser's Step Pyramid. Sened was remembered long after: in the 4th Dynasty a priest named Shery still served his cult at Saqqara. Nubnefer is known from just two vessel inscriptions. The later lists add Neferkara, Neferkasokar and a "Hudjefa", which simply means "erased": the scribe copying the list had found a gap.

The scraps hint that the kingdom may have split, with some of these kings ruling at the same time in different halves of the country. Seals from Abydos name a king Sekhemib, who may be the next king under another name. When the fog lifts, a king is buried at Abydos under a royal name no ruler had dared to use before.

claims.text: Egypt split between rival kings after Nynetjer.
claims.note: Some read the scattered finds, Nynetjer's war in the north and Peribsen's Seth name that way. The evidence is thin, and others see a single line of kings.

claims.text: Weneg is the king Wadjenes of the later king lists.
claims.note: Weneg is known only from stone vessels. Matching him with the Wadjenes who follows Nynetjer in the lists is a common but unproven guess.

claims.text: "Hudjefa" was never a real king's name.
claims.note: Egyptologists read the word in the Turin and Saqqara lists as the copyist's note that a name in his older source was damaged or missing.

reigns.hook: Out of the dark steps a king who does something no pharaoh has done before. Peribsen takes the falcon god Horus off his royal name and puts Seth there instead.

images.caption: A seated statue of Khasekhem from Hierakonpolis, the king who would end this dark age; nothing survives that shows the lost kings themselves.

reigns.tagline: The king who swapped Horus for Seth
reigns.previously: Kings come and go in the dark; Egypt may be splitting in two.
paragraphs: Every king before him had written his main name in a frame topped by the falcon Horus, the god of kingship. Peribsen put the god Seth there instead, shown as a strange beast with a curved snout and tall square ears. Seth was the rival and murderer of Osiris in later myth. For an Egyptian king, it was an astonishing choice.

He was buried at Abydos, in the old royal cemetery, among the 1st Dynasty kings. Two granite stelae with his Seth name stood at his tomb, and one is now in the British Museum. Some scholars think he is the same man as King Sekhemib, who used Horus. Nobody knows how he came to power or how long he reigned; about 16 years is a guess.

He was not remembered as a villain. In the 4th Dynasty, about a century later, a priest named Shery was still serving the cult of Peribsen at Saqqara, as he says in his tomb. Whatever Peribsen's Seth name meant, his successor would find a way to put both gods on top of his name at once.

claims.text: Peribsen's Seth name shows Egypt was split by civil war.
claims.note: The Seth name is certain. What it meant is guesswork: a rival king in the south, a religious change, or a peaceful local choice.

claims.text: Peribsen and Sekhemib were the same king.
claims.note: Their names turn up in similar places and their seals look alike. Some think one man changed his name; others think they were rivals.

reigns.hook: The next king starts out under Horus alone and ends with Horus and Seth sitting side by side above his name. Something has been settled, and probably by force.

images.caption: Granite stela from Peribsen's tomb at Abydos, now in the British Museum; the Seth animal once above his name was chiselled away in antiquity. Not a portrait.
images.alt: Tall rounded granite stela carved with a royal name frame whose top figure has been erased

reigns.tagline: Horus and Seth side by side, and Egypt one again
reigns.cameToPower: Unclear; perhaps by winning a war
reigns.previously: Peribsen dies, buried at Abydos under his strange Seth name.
paragraphs: His name means "the two powers appear", and above it sat both Horus and Seth, the two gods facing each other. The message was hard to miss: the quarrel was over and the two halves of Egypt were one again. He may have begun his reign as a king called Khasekhem, "the power appears", who used Horus alone and changed his name once the fighting was won.

From Hierakonpolis, the old royal town in the far south, come two seated statues of Khasekhem. On their bases lie the twisted bodies of slain northerners, with huge numbers of enemy dead carved beside them. His tomb at Abydos is the largest in the old royal cemetery, with a burial chamber lined with cut limestone, and on the desert edge near the town his giant mudbrick enclosure, the Shunet el-Zebib, still stands.

He reigned about 17 or 18 years. Seal impressions from his tomb name a royal woman, Nimaathap, whom later Egyptians honoured as the ancestress of the next dynasty. With Khasekhemwy the 2nd Dynasty and the Early Dynastic Period end.

claims.text: Khasekhem and Khasekhemwy were one king who renamed himself.
claims.note: The two names never appear together and their monuments are similar. Many scholars think it was one man; some think two.

claims.text: Khasekhemwy killed huge numbers of northerners.
claims.note: The figures come from royal statue bases, boasts carved to impress, which cannot be checked.

claims.text: Nimaathap was Djoser's mother.
claims.note: Seals in Khasekhemwy's tomb call her mother of the king's children, and a seal of Djoser's time calls her king's mother. Which king is not said.

reigns.hook: Khasekhemwy is dead, and a new dynasty begins with a king later Egyptians called Nebka. Soon one of his successors and a clever official will build a mountain out of cut stone.

reigns.tagline: A king from the lists, and maybe the giant Sanakht
reigns.previously: Khasekhemwy dies, the last king of the 2nd Dynasty.
paragraphs: Nebka is the king that the dates in this deck put at the start of the 3rd Dynasty and the Old Kingdom. The catch is that his name comes from lists and stories written down centuries later. In one of them, the Westcar Papyrus, a priest in Nebka's day makes a little wax crocodile that comes to life and drags his wife's lover into a lake, and the king lets it keep its prey.

Many Egyptologists think Nebka was the later name for a king who appears on his own monuments as Sanakht. Two rock carvings from the turquoise mines of the Sinai show Sanakht striking down an enemy, and clay seals with his Horus name were found in a great mudbrick tomb at Beit Khallaf, north of Abydos. A skeleton from a tomb there belonged to a man about 1.87 metres tall.

Where he belongs is still argued over. Seals naming Djoser turned up in Khasekhemwy's tomb, which suggests Djoser buried him and came next, so many scholars now push Sanakht later in the dynasty. Shaw keeps Nebka first, with about 19 years, and this deck follows Shaw.

claims.text: Nebka and Sanakht were the same king.
claims.note: Rests on a damaged seal from Beit Khallaf that may show a cartouche ending in -ka beside Sanakht's name. Many accept it; others reject it.

claims.text: In Nebka's reign a magician's wax crocodile came alive and seized his wife's lover.
claims.note: A tale in the Westcar Papyrus, copied over a thousand years after Nebka's time. It is a story told at court, not a record.

claims.text: The tall skeleton from Beit Khallaf is the king himself.
claims.note: It came from a tomb with Sanakht's seals, but such tombs may belong to high officials, and nothing names the body.

reigns.hook: Nebka is gone. His successor has a clever official named Imhotep, and together they are about to build something nobody has ever seen: a mountain made of cut stone.

reigns.tagline: The first pyramid, and the genius who designed it
reigns.reignEnded: Died; buried at the Step Pyramid
reigns.previously: Nebka dies after about 19 years. Djoser takes the throne.
paragraphs: In his own day he was called Netjerikhet. The name Djoser only turns up in records written long afterwards. The dates used here put a king called Nebka just before him, though many Egyptologists now think Djoser came first. Either way, his reign belongs to the start of the Old Kingdom, the age of the pyramids, and he kicked it off with something nobody had ever seen.

At Saqqara, high above Memphis, rose the Step Pyramid: six stacked stages of stone, over 60 metres tall, at the heart of a vast walled complex of courts, shrines and dummy buildings. It is often called the first monumental building made entirely of cut stone. The designer was his official Imhotep, whose name and titles are carved on the base of a statue of the king.

Imhotep's fame outlived his master's. About 2,000 years later Egyptians worshipped him as a god of healing and wisdom, and the Greeks matched him with their medicine god, Asclepius. Djoser still keeps watch too. His painted limestone statue was found sealed in a tiny room beside the pyramid, peering out through two eye-holes. The original is in Cairo; a copy sits in its place.

claims.text: The Step Pyramid is the first monumental building made entirely of cut stone.
claims.note: Earlier kings used some stone, including in Khasekhemwy's tomb, but nothing on this scale is known before it.

claims.text: Djoser ended a seven-year famine by honouring the god Khnum.
claims.note: The Famine Stela on Sehel Island tells the story, but it was carved under the Ptolemies, over 2,000 years later, probably to back the claims of Khnum's priests.

claims.text: Djoser came before Nebka, not after him.
claims.note: Shaw puts Nebka first. Seal impressions naming Netjerikhet in Khasekhemwy's tomb lead many scholars to put Djoser right after Khasekhemwy.

reigns.hook: Djoser has shown what stone can do. His successor Sekhemkhet sets out to build an even bigger step pyramid, and it will vanish under the sand.

reigns.tagline: The lost pyramid, and a sealed coffin with nothing inside
reigns.reignEnded: Died with his pyramid barely begun
reigns.previously: Djoser dies, buried under the world's first pyramid.
paragraphs: Sekhemkhet wanted a pyramid like Djoser's, only bigger. He chose a site at Saqqara just south-west of it and planned a step pyramid that might have reached seven steps. Then he died. He reigned only about six or seven years, his pyramid never rose much above its first step, and in time the sand drifted over it and it was forgotten.

In the early 1950s the Egyptian archaeologist Zakaria Goneim found it again: the Buried Pyramid. Deep inside lay a sealed alabaster sarcophagus, its sliding door still shut. The world's press gathered for the opening in 1954. The lid came up and the coffin was empty. There was treasure in the corridors, though, including gold bracelets and a little gold box shaped like a shell.

Jar stoppers stamped with the king's name told Goneim whose pyramid it was. Far away in the Sinai, rock carvings show Sekhemkhet at the turquoise and copper mines, wearing the crowns of Egypt. After him, the last kings of the 3rd Dynasty are little more than names.

claims.text: The sarcophagus was empty because the king was never buried in it.
claims.note: It was still sealed when opened, so robbers are unlikely. He may have been buried elsewhere, or it may have been a ritual burial.

claims.text: Djoser's architect Imhotep also worked on this pyramid.
claims.note: Goneim found the name Imhotep in a graffito on the enclosure wall. It is probably the same man, but the name was common enough to leave doubt.

reigns.hook: Sekhemkhet's pyramid lies half-built under the sand. The next king, Khaba, will start a pyramid too, and it is far from certain that he finished it.

reigns.tagline: A name on stone bowls, and a pyramid in leaning layers
reigns.previously: Sekhemkhet dies, his pyramid stuck at its first step.
paragraphs: Khaba is a king we know almost only from his Horus name, which means 'the soul appears'. It is carved on a handful of fine stone bowls and stamped on clay seals, and that is about all. The style of the bowls looks like the very end of the 3rd Dynasty, close to the time of Sneferu, which is where this deck places him.

At Zawyet el-Aryan, between Giza and Saqqara, stands a ruined step pyramid built in leaning layers of stone, the Layer Pyramid. It carries no king's name. But bowls inscribed for Khaba were found in a big tomb beside it, so most scholars think it was his. It seems never to have been finished, which fits a king Shaw gives just three years.

claims.text: Khaba built the Layer Pyramid at Zawyet el-Aryan.
claims.note: No name was found in the pyramid itself; the link rests on his bowls from the tomb next door, Mastaba Z500.

claims.text: Khaba and Huni were the same king.
claims.note: Khaba is known only by a Horus name and Huni only by a cartouche name, so some scholars have wondered if they are one man. Nothing proves it.

reigns.hook: After Khaba comes Huni, who reigns for about 24 years yet leaves less behind than almost any long-lived king. His great legacy will be the man who comes next.

reigns.tagline: A long reign, a lost tomb, and a famous successor
reigns.previously: Khaba's short reign ends, his pyramid unfinished.
paragraphs: Huni closed the 3rd Dynasty, and later Egyptians remembered him. A wisdom text, the Instruction of Kagemni, ends by saying that King Huni died and King Sneferu was raised up in his place. The Turin king list gives him 24 years. Yet only two objects with his name survive from his own time: a red granite cone from the island of Elephantine and a stone bowl.

The cone probably comes from one of a set of small step pyramids dotted along the Nile, from Elephantine northwards. They had no burials inside and may have marked royal power in the provinces. Many scholars credit them to Huni. Some think he also began the pyramid at Meidum that Sneferu later finished. Where Huni himself was buried is a mystery.

A royal woman called Meresankh was remembered as Sneferu's mother, and she may have been one of Huni's wives. But no text calls Sneferu Huni's son. A granite royal head in the Brooklyn Museum has been given to Huni on its style alone.

claims.text: Sneferu was Huni's son.
claims.note: Often assumed, because Sneferu followed him and Meresankh may have been Huni's wife. No ancient text says so.

claims.text: Huni began the pyramid at Meidum.
claims.note: An old theory; visitors' graffiti of the New Kingdom at Meidum name Sneferu, and many scholars now give the whole pyramid to him.

claims.text: The Instruction of Kagemni names Huni as Sneferu's predecessor.
claims.note: The text survives in the Prisse Papyrus, copied in the Middle Kingdom, centuries after both kings.

reigns.hook: Huni is dead. His successor Sneferu will found the 4th Dynasty and move more stone than any king before or since.

reigns.tagline: Three pyramids, one wobble, and a king people liked
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Successor of Huni; perhaps his son
reigns.previously: Huni dies after 24 years, the last king of the 3rd Dynasty.
paragraphs: Sneferu founded the 4th Dynasty and probably shifted more stone than any other pharaoh. First came Meidum, a step pyramid that his predecessor Huni may have begun. Then, at Dahshur, the Bent Pyramid, which starts steep and switches to a gentler slope halfway up. Maybe the builders saw cracks and lost their nerve. Maybe they were in a hurry. Nobody knows for sure.

His third attempt worked. The Red Pyramid, also at Dahshur, was the first true pyramid with smooth, straight sides, and he was probably buried in it. Egypt's armies were busy too. The Palermo Stone, a slab of royal annals, records raids into Nubia and Libya that brought home captives and herds of cattle.

Later Egyptians remembered Sneferu as a kind, easy-going king who chatted with his courtiers as friends. With his queen, Hetepheres I, he had a son: Khufu. In 1925 George Reisner's team found her reburied tomb goods at Giza, gilded furniture and all, at the bottom of a deep shaft beside her son's pyramid.

claims.text: Bored at court, Sneferu was rowed round his lake by twenty girls dressed in fishing nets; when one dropped her turquoise pendant, a magician folded back the water to fetch it.
claims.note: From the Westcar Papyrus, a collection of tales written down centuries after Sneferu's death.

claims.text: The Bent Pyramid changed angle because it started to crack.
claims.note: Cracks and repairs inside are real. Whether they caused the change, or the builders just wanted to finish faster, is argued.

claims.text: Sneferu moved more stone than any other pharaoh.
claims.note: Add up Meidum, the Bent and the Red Pyramids and he beats even Khufu, but the totals are estimates and Meidum may be partly Huni's.

reigns.hook: Sneferu dies remembered for his kindness. His son Khufu will be remembered very differently, and he wants the biggest pyramid of all.

reigns.tagline: The biggest pyramid ever, and a statue you could hide
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Sneferu and Hetepheres I
reigns.reignEnded: Died; buried in the Great Pyramid
reigns.previously: Sneferu builds three pyramids and dies a much-loved king.
paragraphs: The Greeks called him Cheops. His Great Pyramid at Giza is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing. It took more than two million blocks of stone and roughly two decades of work by skilled crews, labourers and boatmen. When finished it stood about 146 metres high.

We even know a few of the workers. In 2013 Pierre Tallet's team found papyri at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast: the logbook of an inspector named Merer. His crew shipped fine limestone from the quarries at Tura, across the river, to Giza for the pyramid's casing. They are the oldest inscribed papyri ever found. In 1954 a full-size cedar boat turned up, taken apart and sealed in a pit beside the pyramid.

For all that, the only certain statue of Khufu is a little ivory figure about 7.5 cm tall, found by Flinders Petrie's team at Abydos in 1903. Greek visitors 2,000 years later heard dark stories about him. Herodotus was told that Cheops was a tyrant who shut the temples and worked his people to exhaustion. Two of his sons would wear the crown after him.

claims.text: Cheops was so short of money that he put his own daughter to work in a brothel.
claims.note: Herodotus heard it from guides about 2,000 years after Khufu. Nothing from Khufu's own time hints at it.

claims.text: The Great Pyramid was the tallest man-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years.
claims.note: It is usually said to have been overtaken by Lincoln Cathedral's spire in the early 14th century, but both heights are estimates.

claims.text: Merer's diary records stone being shipped for the Great Pyramid.
claims.note: The papyri date to late in Khufu's reign and were published by Tallet. They are the earliest eyewitness account of pyramid building.

reigns.hook: Khufu lies in the biggest tomb on Earth. His son Djedefre buries him, then heads for a hilltop north of Giza to build a pyramid of his own.

reigns.tagline: The first 'son of Ra', and a pyramid on a hilltop
reigns.previously: Khufu dies, buried in the Great Pyramid.
paragraphs: Djedefre was a son of Khufu, and one of his first jobs as king was burying his father. Some of the huge blocks that sealed the pits for Khufu's cedar boats carry Djedefre's name, painted by the work gangs. He was also the first king to call himself 'son of Ra', after the sun god. Every pharaoh after him would use the title.

He did not build at Giza. For his own pyramid he picked a hill at Abu Rawash, about eight kilometres to the north. It is now a ruin, so it was long thought he died before it was done. Digs since 1995 suggest it was finished and later stripped for its stone. Pieces of many statues were found there, among them a fine head of the king in red quartzite, now in the Louvre.
He married Hetepheres II, his own sister. His reign was short, about eight years in the dates used here. When he died, the crown went not to one of his sons but to his brother Khafre.

claims.text: Djedefre murdered his brother Kawab to seize the throne.
claims.note: A modern theory built on smashed statues at Abu Rawash. The damage is now put down to later stone robbers, and few scholars still hold it.

claims.text: He reigned for at least 11 years.
claims.note: The Turin king list gives him eight, but painted marks on the blocks over Khufu's boat pit have been read as a later year of his reign.

reigns.hook: Djedefre lies on his hilltop. His brother Khafre heads back to Giza, to build right next to their father.

reigns.tagline: The pyramid that looks taller, and maybe the Sphinx
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Khufu; brother of Djedefre
reigns.previously: Djedefre dies after about eight years, buried at Abu Rawash.
paragraphs: After Djedefre's short reign, another son of Khufu took over: Khafre, whom the Greeks called Chephren. He turned his back on his brother's hilltop at Abu Rawash, went back to Giza and built right next to his father.

His pyramid is a little smaller than Khufu's but looks taller, because it stands on higher ground. Near the top it still wears a cap of the smooth casing stones that once covered the whole thing. Below it crouches the Great Sphinx, a lion with a king's head, carved out of the bedrock. It is usually credited to Khafre.

His finest portrait is a seated statue in dark gneiss. The falcon god Horus perches behind the king's head and spreads its wings around it, as if on guard. Auguste Mariette found it in 1860 in a pit in Khafre's valley temple. It is now one of the great treasures of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

claims.text: Khafre had the Great Sphinx carved.
claims.note: It lines up with his valley temple and causeway, and the face may be his, but no ancient inscription names its maker.

claims.text: The Egyptians hated Cheops and Chephren so much they would not speak their names, and called the pyramids after a shepherd.
claims.note: Herodotus heard this from his guides about 2,000 years later. Both kings were honoured by cults for centuries.

reigns.hook: Khafre's pyramid towers over Giza. The next king will build a much smaller one, and the Greeks will remember him as the good man among tyrants.

reigns.tagline: The smallest Giza pyramid, the finest statues
reigns.previously: Khafre builds the second pyramid at Giza, and maybe the Sphinx.
paragraphs: The Greeks called him Mycerinus. His pyramid is the smallest of the big three at Giza, less than half the height of Khufu's. What his reign lacked in size it made up for in style. Between 1908 and 1910 George Reisner's Harvard–Boston team dug out his valley temple and found some of the finest statues Egypt ever produced.

There were triads, each showing the king with the goddess Hathor and a local god, and a pair statue of the king standing beside a queen with her arm around his waist. They are carved in greywacke, a hard dark stone, and are now in Boston and Cairo. Herodotus heard that Mycerinus was a fair-minded king who reopened the temples his father and uncle had shut.

Menkaure seems to have died before his monuments were finished, and his successor completed his temples in mudbrick. His pyramid was later entered by robbers and treasure hunters; a coffin from it was lost at sea in 1838 on its way to England. The age of the great Giza pyramids was nearly over.

claims.text: An oracle gave Mycerinus six years to live, so he lit lamps every night to turn night into day and live twelve.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, about 2,000 years later, from what priests told him.

claims.text: The queen in the pair statue is Khamerernebty II.
claims.note: No name is carved on the statue. She is the most likely candidate, but it is an educated guess.

claims.text: Menkaure's sarcophagus sank with the ship Beatrice off Spain.
claims.note: Howard Vyse's men removed it from the pyramid in 1837 and sent it to England. The merchant ship Beatrice was lost in 1838 after leaving Malta; where it sank is uncertain and the wreck has never been found.

reigns.hook: Menkaure dies before his temples are done. His successor will finish them in mudbrick, then build himself a tomb that is not a pyramid at all.

reigns.tagline: He broke the pyramid habit and built a giant stone coffin
reigns.previously: Menkaure dies with his pyramid temples unfinished.
paragraphs: Shepseskaf was probably Menkaure's son, and his first task was finishing his father's monuments at Giza. He did it fast and cheap, in mudbrick instead of stone. In Menkaure's temple he set up a royal decree protecting the dead king's offerings, the oldest decree of its kind to survive from the Old Kingdom.

For his own tomb he did something unexpected. At South Saqqara he built no pyramid at all, but a huge stone tomb shaped like a sarcophagus with a rounded lid, now called the Mastabat Faraun, the 'bench of Pharaoh'. Why he turned his back on pyramids nobody knows.

The Turin king list gives him only four years. Manetho names one more king, Thamphthis, after him, but no monument of such a king has been found. A powerful royal woman, Khentkaus I, appears around this time and was honoured as the mother of two kings. A new dynasty was on its way.

claims.text: Shepseskaf rejected the pyramid because he fell out with the priests of the sun god.
claims.note: A popular modern idea. There is no ancient evidence; a short reign or a change in royal ideas may explain it.

claims.text: A king named Thamphthis reigned after him.
claims.note: Only Manetho, writing over 2,000 years later, says so. No object of his reign is known.

reigns.hook: The Giza dynasty is over. The next king, Userkaf, will build a smaller pyramid and pour his energy into a new obsession: the sun god Ra.

reigns.tagline: A new dynasty, and the first temple to the sun
reigns.previously: Shepseskaf, last of the Giza dynasty, is buried in a giant stone tomb.
paragraphs: Userkaf founded the 5th Dynasty, and nobody is quite sure how. He may have been a grandson of Khufu's son Djedefre through his mother, or he may have married into the old royal family. Either way, he took Egypt in a new direction. His pyramid at Saqqara, tucked beside Djoser's enclosure, is small and was cheaply built, with a rubble core inside its fine stone casing.

His real passion went elsewhere. At Abusir, north of Saqqara, he built the first sun temple, a court open to the sky around a great raised platform, dedicated to the sun god Ra. Five of his successors would build their own. From his pyramid temple at Saqqara comes a huge pink granite head of the king, now in Cairo. He reigned only about seven years.

claims.text: Userkaf, Sahure and Neferirkare were triplets, fathered by Ra on a priest's wife named Rudjedet.
claims.note: From the Westcar Papyrus, a set of tales written down centuries later. In real life the three kings were not triplets, and Sahure was probably Userkaf's son.

claims.text: Userkaf's mother was Neferhetepes, a daughter of Djedefre.
claims.note: A Neferhetepes is linked to his pyramid area and to Djedefre's family, but the link to Userkaf rests on inference.

reigns.hook: Userkaf's successor will move the royal cemetery to Abusir, beside the new sun temple, and fill his pyramid temple with ships, wild animals and his own sons.

reigns.tagline: Seagoing ships, myrrh from Punt and a pyramid at Abusir
reigns.previously: Userkaf dies, having raised the first temple to the sun god Ra.
paragraphs: Sahure was the first king to build his pyramid at Abusir, close to Userkaf's sun temple. The pyramid itself was small, but its temple was lavish, with black basalt floors and long walls of painted reliefs. Only fragments survive, but they are superb: the king hunting in the desert, rows of captives and gods leading foreign prisoners.

One scene shows big seagoing ships coming home with Asiatic passengers, perhaps from the Levant coast. The Palermo Stone records that in his reign goods arrived from Punt, the far-off land of incense, including a large amount of myrrh. Reliefs from his temple show his sons too, among them a prince named Ranefer.

claims.text: Sahure sent an expedition to Punt.
claims.note: The Palermo Stone lists goods from Punt in his reign. Whether his own ships made the trip is less certain.

claims.text: The ships in his temple reliefs had sailed to Byblos in Lebanon.
claims.note: The reliefs show seagoing ships and Asiatic people, but no destination is named. Byblos is a guess based on later trade.

reigns.hook: Sahure dies after about 12 years. The crown goes to Neferirkare: his brother according to a later fairy tale, but very likely the prince Ranefer, his son.

reigns.tagline: A grand pyramid left unfinished, and a pile of paperwork
reigns.previously: Sahure dies, his Abusir temple glowing with painted reliefs.
paragraphs: Neferirkare Kakai is one of the first kings known to have used two names in cartouches, a throne name and a personal name. He planned the biggest pyramid at Abusir, begun as a step pyramid, but it never got its smooth outer casing. His pyramid temple was finished in a hurry, partly in mudbrick, after his death.

That cheap temple gave us a treasure. In 1893 villagers digging there found papyri, one of the biggest archives to survive from the Old Kingdom. These Abusir papyri are the temple accounts: duty rosters for the priests, lists of offerings, notes on damaged pots and an inventory of the temple's furniture. They show the daily running of a dead king's cult.
His queen, Khentkaus II, was buried in her own small pyramid beside his and was the mother of the next two kings. He reigned about 20 years.

claims.text: Neferirkare was Sahure's son.
claims.note: The Westcar tale makes them brothers. A relief from Sahure's temple shows his son Prince Ranefer, with Neferirkare's royal name added later, which suggests they were one man.

claims.text: The Palermo Stone was carved during or soon after his reign.
claims.note: Its record seems to stop in the 5th Dynasty, about his time. But it may be a later copy, and the end of the stone is lost.

reigns.hook: Neferirkare dies with his pyramid unfinished. After him, the record goes thin: a shadowy king who barely leaves a trace, and a young prince who will not live long.

reigns.tagline: A king known from a few seals and a hole in the ground
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Unclear; perhaps a son of Neferirkare
reigns.previously: Neferirkare dies, his great pyramid unfinished at Abusir.
paragraphs: Shepseskare is one of the most obscure kings of the Old Kingdom. His name survives on a few seal impressions from Abusir and in later king lists, and almost nothing else. Even his place in the line is argued over. The dates here follow one scheme that puts him straight after Neferirkare; the Czech excavators of Abusir think he came after Raneferef instead.

North of Sahure's pyramid, the Czech team found the start of a pyramid that was never built: a square cut into the bedrock, the first step in levelling the ground. It may have been his. If so, work stopped almost at once, which suggests his reign was short, perhaps only months. How it ended is unknown.

claims.text: Shepseskare reigned after Raneferef, not before him.
claims.note: Miroslav Verner's team argues this from the seals found at Abusir. Shaw's dates, used here, put him before Raneferef.

claims.text: The unfinished pyramid base north of Sahure's was Shepseskare's.
claims.note: No inscription names its owner. It is credited to him because he is the only king of the time with no known pyramid.

reigns.hook: Next comes the son of Neferirkare and Khentkaus II. He will die young too, but he leaves behind a temple full of statues and his own bones.

reigns.tagline: The young king whose pyramid became a flat-topped tomb
reigns.previously: Shepseskare's reign ends almost before it starts.
paragraphs: Raneferef, also called Neferefre, was the son of Neferirkare and Queen Khentkaus II. He began a pyramid at Abusir but died after only a couple of years. The builders had got no further than the first step, so they squared off the stump and capped it, turning it into a flat-topped tomb. The Czech excavators call it the Unfinished Pyramid.

His hastily built temple turned out to be a treasure house. In the 1980s the Czech team found another archive of papyri there, and a set of statues of the king, including one with the falcon Horus spreading its wings behind his head. They even found a slaughterhouse for the temple's offerings and, in the burial chamber, parts of a mummy that may be the king's own.

claims.text: The remains in his burial chamber are Raneferef's, and he died aged about 20 to 23.
claims.note: The Czech team's study fits a young man of the right period. The remains are fragmentary and nothing names them.

claims.text: He reigned only about two years.
claims.note: Based on how little of his pyramid was built and the dates in his temple papyri. Later king lists are damaged here.

reigns.hook: Raneferef dies young, and his younger brother takes the throne. He will finish his family's tombs and build the finest sun temple of them all.

reigns.tagline: The sun king who finished his family's tombs
reigns.previously: Raneferef dies young, buried in a pyramid squared off at its base.
paragraphs: Nyuserre Ini came to the throne with a family mess to tidy up: his father's pyramid temple unfinished, his mother's pyramid unfinished, his brother's tomb barely begun. He finished them, and squeezed his own pyramid in between them at Abusir, taking over part of his father's causeway.

His great work was his sun temple at Abu Ghurab, the best preserved of them all. A huge squat obelisk on a platform rose above a courtyard with an alabaster altar. One room was carved with scenes of the seasons, birds nesting, fish spawning and animals giving birth, now mostly in Berlin. He reigned about 24 years, long enough for a sed jubilee, and was still worshipped at Abusir centuries later.

claims.text: Nyuserre celebrated a sed festival, the royal jubilee.
claims.note: Reliefs from his sun temple show the festival in detail, but such scenes were sometimes carved in advance, before the king reached his jubilee.

claims.text: His reign lasted over 30 years.
claims.note: The Turin king list is damaged here and Manetho's figure looks too high. Estimates run from about a dozen years to over 30; Shaw allows about 24.

reigns.hook: Nyuserre's successor will be the last king to build a temple to the sun. Nobody has ever found it, and his pyramid was lost under the sand until 2008.

reigns.tagline: The last sun temple, and a pyramid that lost its head
reigns.previously: Nyuserre dies after some 24 years, his sun temple the finest of all.
paragraphs: Menkauhor Kaiu reigned about seven years and left little trace. He built the last of the sun temples, called the Horizon of Ra, but we know it only from the titles of its priests. It has never been found. His expedition left an inscription at the turquoise mines of Wadi Maghara in Sinai, and a small alabaster seated statue of him is in Cairo.

His pyramid was lost for a long time. In 2008 Zahi Hawass's team cleared the sand from a ruined pyramid at Saqqara, known as the Headless Pyramid because only its base survives, and argued it was Menkauhor's. His memory outlasted his monuments: over a thousand years later, he was still worshipped as a god in the Memphis area.

claims.text: The Headless Pyramid at Saqqara is Menkauhor's.
claims.note: Hawass's team argued so in 2008 from its date and setting. Others think it may belong to Merikare, a much later king; no inscription settles it.

claims.text: His sun temple, the Horizon of Ra, really was built.
claims.note: Its name appears in the titles of officials and priests who served it, though the building itself has never been found.

reigns.hook: Menkauhor dies. The next king, Djedkare Isesi, will turn his back on sun temples altogether and shake up the whole running of the state.

reigns.tagline: The king who stopped building temples to the sun
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Unknown; not known to be kin
reigns.previously: Menkauhor dies, the last king known to build a sun temple.
paragraphs: Djedkare Isesi broke the habit of his dynasty. For generations the 5th Dynasty kings had built sun temples to Ra beside their pyramids. Isesi built none. He moved his own pyramid away from Abusir to south Saqqara, and he spent his long reign, about 39 years in Shaw's scheme, reshaping the government: new ranks for officials, more posts out in the provinces, and viziers with real clout.

His men went far. Expeditions cut stone in Wadi Hammamat and mined turquoise in Sinai. One of his officials, Baurdjed, brought a pygmy home from Punt, and about a century later the boy king Pepi II still remembered it as the treasure to beat. Isesi held a sed jubilee, the festival meant to renew an ageing king, and a Louvre vase celebrates it.

Later Egyptians liked to set wise sayings in his court. The Teaching of Ptahhotep, a book of advice from an old vizier to his son, says it was spoken in the reign of King Isesi. Bones found in his pyramid in the 1940s may be his own. When he died, Unas took the throne.

claims.text: The Teaching of Ptahhotep was written by Isesi's vizier.
claims.note: The text names Isesi's reign, but the copies we have are Middle Kingdom, and setting advice in a famous old court was a literary habit.

claims.text: An official of Isesi brought a pygmy back from Punt.
claims.note: Pepi II's letter, carved on Harkhuf's tomb at Aswan, says the treasurer Baurdjed did so in Isesi's time.

claims.text: The remains found in his pyramid are his, and show a man in his fifties.
claims.note: Found in the burial chamber in the 1940s; there is no inscription on the body, and the age is a later estimate.

reigns.hook: Isesi is dead after nearly 40 years. The next king, Unas, will do something no king has done before: cover the walls of his tomb with magic spells.

reigns.tagline: The first king to take a spellbook into his tomb
reigns.reignEnded: Died with no son to follow
reigns.previously: Djedkare Isesi dies after a reign of nearly 40 years.
paragraphs: Unas built the smallest pyramid of the Old Kingdom, at Saqqara, but inside it he changed everything. The walls of his burial rooms are covered top to bottom with the Pyramid Texts, the first time anyone carved them in a tomb. Hundreds of spells were meant to haul the dead king up to the stars. In the Cannibal Hymn he hunts the gods, cooks them and eats them to swallow their power.

His causeway, the long covered road up to the pyramid, was carved with scenes from his reign. Barges haul granite columns down from Aswan. Elsewhere sit people so thin their ribs show, starving in the desert. Over a thousand years later, Ramesses II's son Khaemwaset restored the pyramid and carved his own note on its face, saying so.
He reigned about 30 years. He had daughters, and one of them, Iput, may have married the next king, but no son of his took the throne. With Unas the 5th Dynasty ends.

claims.text: Unas's pyramid has the first Pyramid Texts, including the Cannibal Hymn.
claims.note: The spells are carved in his burial chambers and are the oldest set known; the same hymn reappears in Teti's pyramid.

claims.text: The starving people on his causeway record a real famine.
claims.note: The relief is real. Some see a famine, others desert nomads shown to flatter the king who feeds Egypt.

claims.text: Queen Iput, Teti's wife, was a daughter of Unas.
claims.note: It would explain how Teti took over smoothly, but no text clearly calls her Unas's daughter.

reigns.hook: Unas leaves no son. A man named Teti takes the crown and starts a new dynasty, but some of the men guarding him have other plans.

reigns.tagline: The peacemaker king killed by his own guards
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No known blood tie to Unas
reigns.previously: Unas dies, his pyramid covered in spells, with no son to follow him.
paragraphs: Nobody knows where Teti came from. He may have won the throne by marrying Iput, perhaps Unas's daughter. His Horus name, Seheteptawy, means 'he who pacifies the Two Lands', which sounds like a man calming trouble. He built his pyramid at Saqqara with the spells inside, like Unas, and married a daughter to his vizier Mereruka.

Around his pyramid the great men built superb tombs. Mereruka's tomb has over 30 rooms. But Manetho, writing two thousand years later, says Teti was murdered by his own bodyguards. In the cemetery round his pyramid some officials' names and faces were hacked out, perhaps the guilty men damned after the event.
He reigned about 22 years. After him came not his son Pepi but a shadowy king named Userkare.

claims.text: Teti was murdered by his own bodyguards.
claims.note: Only Manetho says so, about 2,000 years later. No Old Kingdom text mentions it.

claims.text: Erased tombs near his pyramid show a palace conspiracy.
claims.note: Naguib Kanawati argues the defaced officials were plotters punished under Pepi I. Others think the damage could have other causes.

reigns.hook: Teti is dead, maybe murdered. His son Pepi is next in line, but first a stranger called Userkare sits on the throne.

reigns.tagline: A king who slipped in between father and son
reigns.previously: Teti dies, perhaps murdered by his own guards.
paragraphs: Userkare is a name with almost no story attached. The king list at Abydos puts him between Teti and Teti's son Pepi I. A few objects carry his name, and a damaged stone with the royal annals of this dynasty, found at south Saqqara, seems to leave room for a short reign. He had no pyramid that anyone has found.

That silence is suspicious. If Teti was murdered, who gained? Some think Userkare was the plotters' man, a rival from another branch of the royal family. Others make him a harmless stand-in who held the throne while Pepi was too young. Either way he lasted only a year or two, and Pepi I never mentions him.

claims.text: Userkare was a usurper linked to Teti's murder.
claims.note: A guess built on the timing and on Manetho's murder story. No text links him to any plot.

claims.text: The Abydos king list names him as Teti's successor.
claims.note: His cartouche is the next one after Teti's in Seti I's list at Abydos. The Saqqara king list leaves him out.

reigns.hook: Userkare vanishes as quietly as he came. Teti's son Pepi I takes the throne, and he will soon find out that even his own harem can't be trusted.

reigns.tagline: The king who put Memphis on the map, plot and all
reigns.previously: Userkare's brief reign ends. Teti's son is ready.
paragraphs: Pepi I, son of Teti and Iput, reigned about 34 years and left his name on temples from the Delta to Elephantine. His pyramid at Saqqara was called Men-nefer, 'enduring and beautiful'. The name spread to the town nearby, and the Greeks turned it into Memphis.

Not everyone loved him. The official Weni, in his tomb at Abydos, says he alone was trusted to hear a secret case against a queen in the royal harem, and he never says what she did. Weni also led armies against the sand-dwellers north-east of Egypt five times. Pepi then married two sisters, both called Ankhnesmeryre, daughters of a noble family of Abydos. Each bore him a future king.
Copper statues of Pepi and a smaller figure were found at Hierakonpolis. When he died, his son Merenre, by the elder sister, took over.

claims.text: A queen plotted against Pepi I and was tried in secret.
claims.note: Weni's inscription confirms a secret case against a queen. Her name, her crime and her fate are never given.

claims.text: Memphis takes its name from Pepi I's pyramid.
claims.note: The pyramid's name, Men-nefer, became the name of the city by the New Kingdom; Greek Memphis comes from it.

claims.text: Pepi changed his throne name after the harem plot.
claims.note: He did switch from Nefersahor to Meryre. Tying it to the plot is a modern guess.

reigns.hook: Pepi I is dead. His son Merenre is young and keen, and he has an explorer named Harkhuf ready to march into the unknown south.

reigns.tagline: A young king who looked south to Africa
reigns.previously: Pepi I dies after some 34 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Merenre, son of Pepi I and the elder Ankhnesmeryre, had only about nine years, but he spent them looking south. Old Weni, now governor of Upper Egypt, cut granite at Elephantine and dug five channels through the first cataract so boats could pass. Merenre himself came down to Aswan, and rock carvings there show Nubian chiefs bowing to him.

His explorer Harkhuf made long trips to the land of Yam, deep in Africa, and came back with donkeys loaded with incense, ebony, leopard skins and ivory. In 1881 a mummy of a young man was found in Merenre's pyramid at Saqqara. Whether it is the king is still argued. His heir was his half-brother Pepi, a small boy.

claims.text: Weni dug five channels through the first cataract for Merenre.
claims.note: Weni says so in his own tomb inscription at Abydos. How big the channels were is not recorded.

claims.text: The mummy found in his pyramid is Merenre himself.
claims.note: Found in 1881. Some think the wrapping style points to a later burial reusing the tomb.

reigns.hook: Merenre is dead. The new king of Egypt is a little boy, and he may be about to reign longer than anyone in history.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who wanted a dancer more than gold
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Probably a son of Pepi I
reigns.previously: Merenre dies after a short reign. The heir is a small boy.
paragraphs: Pepi II came to the throne as a child, with his mother, Ankhnesmeryre II, close beside him. A little alabaster statue in the Brooklyn Museum shows him as a miniature king sitting on her lap. Manetho says he was six when he was crowned and reigned for 94 years.

The best story from his reign is a letter he wrote as a boy, which the expedition leader Harkhuf proudly carved on his tomb at Aswan. Harkhuf had sent word from the land of Yam, far to the south, that he was bringing home a dancing pygmy. The young king could barely contain himself. He wanted to see the dancer more than all the treasures of Sinai and Punt.

He ordered trusty men to sleep beside the dancer on the boat and check on him ten times a night, so he could not fall into the river. Over Pepi's long reign, though, the provincial governors grew rich and built grand tombs at home, acting more like local princes than royal servants. When the old king finally died, the Old Kingdom was running out of road.

claims.text: Pepi II reigned for 94 years, the longest reign in history.
claims.note: Manetho says so and the Turin king list also gives him over 90 years, but some Egyptologists think the dates from his reign point to about 64.

claims.text: The boy king's letter to Harkhuf is genuine.
claims.note: Harkhuf had it carved on the front of his tomb at Qubbet el-Hawa, Aswan, where it can still be read.

claims.text: Powerful provincial governors brought down the Old Kingdom.
claims.note: Their growing wealth is clear from their tombs. How much it caused the collapse, against low floods or a weak succession, is argued.

reigns.hook: Pepi II is dead and his heirs are short-lived. The Old Kingdom falls apart, and Egypt splits between rival kings, hungry provinces and a vengeful queen.

reigns.title: The First Intermediate Period
reigns.tagline: Seventy kings in seventy days, and a vengeful queen
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Pepi II's son, then obscure heirs
reigns.cameToPower: Pepi II died after a long reign
reigns.previously: Pepi II dies after a record reign, and the old order starts to crack.
paragraphs: Pepi II had reigned so long that hardly anyone alive remembered another king. When he died, the machine he left behind seized up. His son Merenre II lasted about a year. After him the kings at Memphis came and went so fast that later writers lost count. This is the start of the First Intermediate Period, and for over a century Egypt would have no single master.

Manetho gives this moment a 7th Dynasty of seventy kings who reigned for seventy days, most likely a garbled memory of a crowd of short reigns. The king list at Abydos names a string of them, men like Netjerkare, Menkare and Neferkare II, with almost nothing to show for any of them. Out in the provinces the governors were already little kings, with their own soldiers, granaries and grand tombs.

The best story from these years is a legend. Herodotus heard of a queen, Nitocris, whose brother the king had been murdered. She built a vast underground hall, invited his killers to a banquet and let the river in to drown them, then threw herself into a room full of ashes. Low Nile floods and hungry harvests may have made the real troubles worse.

claims.text: Queen Nitocris avenged her murdered brother by drowning his killers at a banquet in a secret underground hall, then threw herself into a room full of ashes.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, some 1,700 years later. A name once read as Nitocris in the Turin king list now looks like a misreading, so she may never have existed.

claims.text: The 7th Dynasty was seventy kings who reigned for seventy days.
claims.note: This comes from Manetho, as quoted by Africanus. It is probably a garbled memory of many short, weak reigns, not a real count.

claims.text: Egypt was gripped by famine caused by failing Nile floods.
claims.note: Governors' tombs of the following decades describe starvation, but boasting of feeding the hungry was a stock way to praise yourself. How far climate caused the collapse is still argued.

reigns.hook: Seventy kings in seventy days, or so the story goes. Then one Memphis king, Qakare Ibi, lasts long enough to build a pyramid: a small one, with the old spells inside.

reigns.tagline: The last pharaoh of the old days to build a pyramid
reigns.previously: Pepi II's heirs fade fast. Kings at Memphis barely last a year.
paragraphs: Qakare Ibi was one of the 8th Dynasty kings who still ruled from Memphis after Pepi II's long reign. Most of them are just names. Ibi is different, because he built a pyramid. It stands at south Saqqara near Pepi II's, and was excavated by Gustave Jéquier around 1930.

It is tiny, but inside the burial chamber the old spells are carved on the walls, just as in the pyramids of Unas and Teti. It is the last pyramid of the Old Kingdom that we know. The Turin king list seems to give him about four years. Then the throne passed to Neferkaure.

claims.text: Ibi's pyramid is the last known Old Kingdom pyramid with Pyramid Texts.
claims.note: Jéquier found the texts in its burial chamber. More may lie unfound, so 'last known' is the safe wording.

claims.text: He reigned about four years.
claims.note: The figure comes from a damaged part of the Turin king list, as Kim Ryholt reads it. Shaw gives no per-king dates here.

reigns.hook: Ibi is buried with the old spells. His successor Neferkaure holds Memphis, but the real power is drifting south to the priests and governors of Coptos.

reigns.tagline: A Memphis king who ruled by royal decree
reigns.previously: Qakare Ibi dies, buried in the last small Old Kingdom pyramid.
paragraphs: Neferkaure is one of the last kings in the Abydos king list before it skips straight to the Middle Kingdom. We know him mainly from a single document, a royal decree of his fourth year found at Coptos, the temple town of the god Min in Upper Egypt.

The Coptos decrees show how these late Memphis kings still worked. They protected temple staff and land, and handed out posts and honours to the powerful family who ran Coptos. Real strength now lay with such families more than with the king. Neferkaure reigned about four years, and the next king, Neferkauhor, leaned on that same family even harder.

claims.text: A decree of Neferkaure's fourth year was found at Coptos.
claims.note: It belongs to the group of royal decrees dug up in the Min temple at Coptos, published by Hans Goedicke.

claims.text: He reigned about four years.
claims.note: Based on the year 4 decree and a reading of the damaged Turin king list. Shaw gives no per-king dates here.

reigns.hook: Neferkaure's short reign ends. The next king, Neferkauhor, will pour out decrees in a single year to win over one family: the vizier Shemay's.

reigns.tagline: A king who married his daughter to the real power
reigns.previously: Neferkaure's short reign ends, leaving decrees at Coptos.
paragraphs: Neferkauhor Khuwihapi left more paperwork than most kings of his age. Eight of his decrees, found in the temple of Min at Coptos, were issued in one busy stretch. They pile honours on Shemay, the vizier, who already ran the south from Coptos, and on his wife Nebet, the king's eldest daughter.

Their son Idy was made overseer of Upper Egypt, and another decree gave a post in the Min temple to Idy's brother. A king who has to buy loyalty this way is not strong. The Turin king list gives him a little over two years. Then came Neferirkare II, the last of the Memphis line.

claims.text: Neferkauhor's daughter Nebet was married to the vizier Shemay.
claims.note: The Coptos decrees name her as the king's eldest daughter and Shemay's wife.

claims.text: He reigned a little over two years.
claims.note: From the Turin king list, but which damaged entry is his is a matter of reading. Shaw gives no per-king dates here.

reigns.hook: Neferkauhor's decrees bought him Coptos, but not much time. The last king of Memphis, Neferirkare II, is about to meet a new power from Herakleopolis.
