reigns.tagline: The last king of the old Memphis line
reigns.previously: Neferkauhor dies after about two years of handing out favours.
paragraphs: Neferirkare II is often counted as the last king of the Old Kingdom. His name is the final cartouche of the 8th Dynasty in Seti I's king list at Abydos. The very next name is Mentuhotep II, more than a century later, as if everything in between had never happened.

He seems to have reigned only a year or so. Little else survives. Meanwhile, at Herakleopolis, south of Memphis, a family of local rulers had grown strong enough to claim the crown for themselves. Their kings would rule the north for over a century.

claims.text: Neferirkare II is the last Old Kingdom king in the Abydos list.
claims.note: His is the last name before the list jumps to Mentuhotep II of the 11th Dynasty.

claims.text: He reigned about a year and a half.
claims.note: From the damaged Turin king list, as Kim Ryholt reconstructs it. Shaw gives no per-king dates here.

reigns.hook: Memphis is finished. Kings from Herakleopolis, most of them named Khety, take over the north, and their founder is remembered as a tyrant who came to a very bad end.

reigns.tagline: A crown with no fixed home, and a lot of Khetys
reigns.previously: Neferirkare II fades away, and Memphis is finished as a royal city.
paragraphs: With the Memphis kings gone, the crown moved south up the Nile to Herakleopolis, near the mouth of the Faiyum. Its rulers, Manetho's 9th and 10th Dynasties, called themselves kings of all Egypt. Several of them were named Khety. Their founder, Khety I, left only a handful of objects, but Manetho remembered him as a brute who ruled by terror until he went mad and was eaten by a crocodile.

Herakleopolis held the north and leaned on loyal governors in the south. The toughest was Ankhtifi of Mo'alla, who ran Hierakonpolis and Edfu and marched against Thebes. In his tomb he boasts that the whole south was starving while his province alone had bread. Another Khety, Nebkaure, became the king in a famous story, the Tale of the Eloquent Peasant, in which a robbed farmer argues so beautifully that the king has him kept talking so his speeches can be written down.

The kings kept a court, wrote wise books and buried their governors grandly at Asyut. One of them left his son Merikare a famous book of royal advice. But the south was slipping away. At Thebes the local lords had stopped taking orders, and around 2125 BC their leader, Intef, declared himself king. Herakleopolis would fight on for decades, but Egypt now had two crowns again.

claims.text: Khety I went mad and was killed by a crocodile.
claims.note: Only Manetho tells it, as quoted by Africanus and Eusebius, nearly 2,000 years later. Nothing from the time says so.

claims.text: The Teaching for King Merikare was written by his father, a king named Khety.
claims.note: The text survives only in copies made centuries later, and many think it was composed in the Middle Kingdom as political literature.

claims.text: Southern Egypt suffered a terrible famine.
claims.note: Ankhtifi's tomb says so, but claiming to feed the starving was a stock boast for governors. How bad it really was is argued.

reigns.hook: At Thebes a family of local lords has had enough of taking orders from the north. Their leader, Intef, writes his name like a pharaoh's and dares Herakleopolis to stop him.

reigns.tagline: The Theban lord who promoted himself to king
reigns.previously: Herakleopolis rules the north, but Thebes has stopped listening.
paragraphs: Thebes was a small provincial town when Intef I was born, ruled by a family of local lords. His father was probably Mentuhotep, later remembered as the clan's ancestor and given a royal title after his death. Intef went one step further while still alive. He took a Horus name, Sehertawy, which means 'he who pacifies the Two Lands', and claimed to be king of Egypt. In practice he ruled a handful of southern provinces.

That was a direct challenge to Herakleopolis and its allies, and the south turned into a war zone. Governors loyal to the north, like Ankhtifi of Mo'alla, marched against the Thebans. Intef held on. He was buried across the river from Thebes at el-Tarif, in a 'saff' tomb, a long courtyard cut into the ground with a row of doorways along the back. He reigned about 13 years, and his brother took over the fight.

claims.text: Intef I was the first ruler of Thebes to call himself king.
claims.note: His Horus name Sehertawy survives, carved at Tod by Mentuhotep II. The earlier Theban lords used only local titles.

claims.text: Ankhtifi of Mo'alla fought against Intef I.
claims.note: Ankhtifi's tomb describes battles with Thebes, but it never names the Theban ruler, so the match is an educated guess.

reigns.hook: Intef I is dead. His brother, also called Intef, takes the Theban crown, and he will keep it for half a century, fighting Herakleopolis every step of the way.

reigns.tagline: Fifty years of war, and a king who loved his dogs
reigns.previously: Intef I dies after about 13 years as Thebes's first king.
paragraphs: Intef II, whose Horus name Wahankh means 'enduring of life', lived up to it. He reigned about 50 years and spent much of it at war. He pushed the Theban border north to Abydos and fought for the old holy ground of Thinis, where Egypt's first kings were buried. The fighting there went back and forth, and the Herakleopolitan side admitted that sacred tombs were wrecked in the struggle.

Between campaigns he built at Thebes, and some of the earliest royal work at Karnak bears his name. He also adored his hunting dogs. On a stela from his tomb at el-Tarif he stands with his hounds around his feet, each one named, some apparently in Libyan (Berber) words. A thousand years later, when inspectors checked the royal tombs for robbers, they noted the stela with the king and his dog Behka between his feet, and found the tomb intact.

His treasurer Tjetji left a stela of his own, now in the British Museum, saying he served both Intef II and his son. Near the end of his long reign the old king could claim that Thebes ruled from Elephantine to well north of Abydos. His son Intef III inherited the war.

claims.text: Intef II named his dogs on his stela.
claims.note: The 'dog stela' from his tomb, now in Cairo, shows the hounds with their names written beside them.

claims.text: Inspectors under Ramesses IX found his tomb intact, with the dog Behka on its stela.
claims.note: The Abbott Papyrus records the inspection of the Theban royal tombs around 1110 BC and mentions the stela and the dog by name.

reigns.hook: The old king dies with Abydos in Theban hands. His son Intef III has a shorter time and a harder job: hold the line against Herakleopolis.

reigns.tagline: The short reign between two great Theban kings
reigns.previously: Intef II dies after about 50 years, with Abydos in Theban hands.
paragraphs: Intef III, crowned as Nakhtnebtepnefer, inherited a kingdom at war. The front line with Herakleopolis ran through Middle Egypt north of Abydos, and his job was to hold it. He seems to have done so, keeping his father's gains for about eight years. His father's old treasurer Tjetji stayed on to serve him, and the Theban state kept growing into a real royal government.

He is best remembered as a father. His wife Iah bore him a son, Mentuhotep, who would finish the war his grandfather had started. Years later, in a rock carving at Shatt er-Rigal near Gebel el-Silsila, the grown-up Mentuhotep II had himself shown towering over his mother Iah and his father Intef III. Intef III was buried at el-Tarif like the kings before him, and his son took the crown.

claims.text: Intef III was the father of Mentuhotep II.
claims.note: Mentuhotep II names his mother Iah, and the Shatt er-Rigal relief shows his father as King Intef.

claims.text: He reigned about eight years.
claims.note: The figure comes from the damaged Turin king list. Shaw's 2063-2055 BC follows it, but other scholars give slightly different lengths.

reigns.hook: Intef III is dead. His son Mentuhotep inherits a war that has dragged on for generations, and means to end it with one king over the whole Nile.

reigns.tagline: The Theban who glued Egypt back together
reigns.previously: Intef III dies, holding the line against Herakleopolis.
paragraphs: Mentuhotep II began as one of two kings. His Thebans held the south and the kings of Herakleopolis held the north, and the old war over the middle of the country flared up again. Some time before his 39th year he broke through. Herakleopolis fell, the north submitted, and for the first time in over a century one pharaoh ruled from the Delta to Aswan. He took a new name meaning 'he who unites the Two Lands'. This is the start of the Middle Kingdom.

Then he built. Across the river from Thebes, at Deir el-Bahri, he raised a terraced tomb-temple against the cliffs, unlike anything before it. Nearby lay a tomb packed with about 60 soldiers, many with arrow wounds, killed in some battle and buried with honour. Later Egyptians never forgot him. Their king lists and temple scenes set him beside Menes and Ahmose as one of the great founders of Egypt.

Howard Carter's horse, the story goes, stumbled into a hole in front of the temple. When he dug there in 1900, he found a hidden shaft and a painted sandstone statue of the king, black-skinned, in a white robe and the red crown. Mentuhotep reigned about 51 years. His son Mentuhotep III carried on, but under Mentuhotep IV the family line ran dry, and a vizier named Amenemhat was waiting in the wings.

claims.text: Howard Carter found the hidden statue when his horse stumbled into a hole.
claims.note: Carter's own story, and the reason the spot is called Bab el-Hosan, 'Gate of the Horse'. Nobody else saw it happen.

claims.text: He reunited Egypt around his 39th year.
claims.note: The date is pieced together from changes in his royal names. When and how the war with Herakleopolis ended is not recorded.

claims.text: The 60 soldiers in the nearby tomb died in his war with Herakleopolis.
claims.note: Herbert Winlock, who found them in the 1920s, thought so. Others link them to a different campaign, and some date the burial later.

reigns.hook: After half a century, the old king is dead. His son Mentuhotep III takes over a united, peaceful Egypt, and looks east, to the Red Sea and the land of incense.

reigns.tagline: He sent 3,000 men across the desert to the Red Sea
reigns.previously: Mentuhotep II dies after about 51 years, Egypt reunited.
paragraphs: Sankhkare Mentuhotep was the son of the great Mentuhotep II and his wife Tem. His father had reigned for half a century, so he was probably no youngster when his turn came. He kept the peace his father had won and built temples across the south, at Abydos, Armant, Medamud and Elephantine, and a small temple on a hilltop in western Thebes.

His big moment came in his 8th year. His steward Henenu led 3,000 men from the Nile valley through the Wadi Hammamat to the Red Sea, digging a dozen wells on the way and clearing out raiders. From the coast an expedition set out for Punt, the land of incense somewhere to the south, the first known voyage there since the Old Kingdom. Henenu came home with incense and perfumes.

Mentuhotep began a tomb-temple at Deir el-Bahri near his father's, but it was never finished. He reigned about 12 years. The king after him is so obscure that the Turin king list leaves seven years with no name at all.

claims.text: Henenu took 3,000 men across the desert to launch an expedition to Punt.
claims.note: Henenu's own rock inscription in the Wadi Hammamat. The numbers are his boast, but the expedition is not in doubt.

claims.text: Mentuhotep III was already old when he became king.
claims.note: A guess from his father's 51-year reign; nothing gives his age.

reigns.hook: Next comes Mentuhotep IV, a king the later king lists leave out. His vizier, a man named Amenemhat, is about to be sent into the desert for a stone coffin.

reigns.tagline: The king the lists forgot, and the vizier who saw omens
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Probably a son of Mentuhotep III
reigns.previously: Mentuhotep III dies after about 12 years.
paragraphs: Nebtawyre Mentuhotep is a king later Egyptians chose to forget. The Turin list records seven years with no king named, and the king lists carved in the New Kingdom jump straight from Mentuhotep III to Amenemhat I. His mother Imi is called 'king's mother' but never queen, which suggests she was a lesser wife of the king before him.

Yet he was real, and busy. Rock inscriptions in the Eastern Desert record his men quarrying amethyst at Wadi el-Hudi and working on the Red Sea coast. The grandest are in the Wadi Hammamat. There, in his second year, a force of 10,000 men under the vizier Amenemhat came to cut a block for the lid of the king's sarcophagus.

The vizier's inscriptions tell of wonders. A pregnant gazelle walked up to the chosen block and gave birth on it. A sudden rainstorm revealed a well of fresh water. The question was whose luck these omens showed. Within a few years Mentuhotep IV had gone, nobody knows how, and a man called Amenemhat was king.

claims.text: The vizier Amenemhat is the same man as King Amenemhat I.
claims.note: Widely accepted, given the name and the timing, but no text links the two directly.

claims.text: Amenemhat seized the throne by force.
claims.note: There is no evidence either way. Later 12th Dynasty texts present him as a saviour, which may hint that his claim needed defending.

reigns.hook: The vizier now wears the crown. Amenemhat I will found the 12th Dynasty, move the capital north and, after 30 years, meet a violent end.

reigns.tagline: The vizier who became king, and died in the dark
reigns.previously: Mentuhotep IV vanishes. His vizier Amenemhat is ready.
paragraphs: Amenemhat was most likely the vizier who had led Mentuhotep IV's men into the Wadi Hammamat and come home with tales of wonders. Within a few years that king had vanished from the record, and a King Amenemhat was founding the 12th Dynasty. How the crown changed hands is a mystery: no text tells of a war, or of a peaceful handover.

A new man needed a good story, and his scribes wrote one. The Prophecy of Neferti, set back in the days of Sneferu, foretells an age of chaos ended by a saviour king called Ameny, son of a woman from the south. Everyone knew who that meant. Amenemhat moved the capital north from Thebes to a new city, Itjtawy, near Lisht, and built his pyramid there.

After about 30 years it ended at night. A later text puts words in the dead king's mouth, telling his son how armed men came for him after supper while he rested, and no one came to his aid. His son Senusret was away fighting in Libya. Whether the attackers had won, and who would hold the throne, was suddenly up for grabs.

claims.text: Amenemhat was murdered in a palace plot.
claims.note: The Instruction of Amenemhat has his ghost describe the attack, but it was written as political literature in his son's reign. Most Egyptologists think he really was killed.

claims.text: The vizier Amenemhat of the gazelle inscriptions is the same man as King Amenemhat I.
claims.note: The name and timing fit, and most historians accept it, but no text says so outright.

claims.text: Senusret I was already ruling beside his father as co-king.
claims.note: Some monuments carry dates in both reigns, which once suggested a ten-year co-regency. Many scholars now doubt it.

reigns.hook: In the Libyan desert, a messenger reaches the crown prince Senusret with news of his father's death. He tells no one, and slips away for home.

reigns.tagline: He raced home from a murder and ruled for 45 years
reigns.cameToPower: Rushed home on his father's death
reigns.previously: Amenemhat I is attacked in his palace at night.
paragraphs: Our best picture of how he took power comes from a story. The Tale of Sinuhe opens with Senusret leading his army home from Libya when messengers bring word that the old king is dead. He sets off at once, quietly, with only his own men. A courtier called Sinuhe overhears and panics so badly that he flees to Canaan, where he lives for decades as a desert chief before coming home as an old man to beg the king's pardon.

Whatever happened that night, Senusret held on, and reigned about 45 years. He pushed south into Lower Nubia and built forts such as Buhen near the second cataract to guard the routes to the gold mines. He built temples all over Egypt. At Heliopolis one of his obelisks still stands. At Karnak his elegant White Chapel was later pulled down and used as rubble inside a pylon, and in the 20th century it was rebuilt from its original blocks.

The Greeks later remembered kings of his name as Sesostris. Senusret died around 1911 BC, leaving a rich, settled kingdom to his son Amenemhat II. The 12th Dynasty had survived its bloody start and was set to rule for another century and a half.

claims.text: Senusret secretly rushed home from Libya when his father was murdered.
claims.note: This comes from the Tale of Sinuhe, a work of literature, though it is set in real events and real places.

claims.text: His obelisk at Heliopolis is the oldest standing obelisk in Egypt.
claims.note: It is often called that, and it still stands in place in Cairo's Matariya district, but older, broken obelisks are known.

claims.text: He conquered Lower Nubia as far as the second cataract.
claims.note: A stela from Buhen records a campaign in his 18th year, but how far earlier kings had already pushed is debated.

reigns.hook: Senusret I dies after some 45 years. His son Amenemhat II, already crowned at his side, will keep the peace for decades.

reigns.tagline: Annals of gifts and raids, and princesses' gold
reigns.previously: Senusret I dies after some 45 years, Egypt rich and settled.
paragraphs: Amenemhat II was the son of Senusret I and Queen Neferu, and he seems to have shared the throne with his father for a couple of years before ruling alone. He reigned about 35 years, a long, quiet stretch in which Egypt traded more than it fought. Many of his statues were later taken over by other kings, which makes him easy to overlook.

One find changed that. Blocks reused at Memphis carry part of his annals, a year-by-year record of the court. They list expeditions to Lebanon and the Sinai, gifts from foreign lands, an army sent against two towns in the Levant, and captives brought home. At Tod, near Luxor, chests with his name, buried under a temple, were packed with silver cups and lapis lazuli from far beyond Egypt.

He took the royal cemetery back to Dahshur with his White Pyramid, named for its pale limestone, most of it later carted away. Beside it in the 1890s Jacques de Morgan found tombs of royal women that robbers had missed, with gold crowns and jewellery among the finest from ancient Egypt. Near the end he shared the crown with his son, Senusret II.

claims.text: Amenemhat II's annals record an army sent against towns in the Levant.
claims.note: The inscription found at Mit Rahina (Memphis) names the campaign and the captives. The towns' locations are argued over.

claims.text: He ruled jointly with his father for about two years.
claims.note: A stela dated to both reigns suggests it, but scholars disagree on how 12th Dynasty co-regencies worked.

claims.text: The silver of the Tod treasure was a gift from a foreign ruler.
claims.note: Its Aegean-style cups and Mesopotamian seals show long-distance contacts, but whether it came as tribute, trade or gift is unknown.

reigns.hook: His son Senusret II inherits a rich, peaceful kingdom. He turns to the Faiyum, the marshy basin west of the Nile, and builds his pyramid at its mouth.

reigns.tagline: The peacetime king of the Faiyum and the pyramid town
reigns.previously: Amenemhat II dies after about 35 years.
paragraphs: Senusret II seems to have been a king for peacetime: no war is recorded in his reign. He turned to the Faiyum, the great lake basin west of the Nile, and began works to bring water in from the Bahr Yussef, the branch of the Nile that feeds it, and to turn swamp into farmland. His grandson Amenemhat III would carry the work much further.

He built his pyramid at El-Lahun, at the mouth of the Faiyum, with a mudbrick core held in place by stone walls. Beside it stood the town for its workers and priests, which Flinders Petrie dug in 1889. It is one of the best-preserved towns from ancient Egypt, and it yielded a hoard of papyri: letters, accounts, census lists, and medical and veterinary texts.

In 1914 Guy Brunton found a hidden recess in the tomb of his daughter Sithathoriunet, full of jewellery robbers had missed, including a gold pectoral with her father's name. At Beni Hasan, a governor's tomb painted in Senusret's 6th year shows a party of 37 Asiatics, led by a chief called Abisha, arriving with eye paint to trade.

claims.text: His reign lasted far longer than the seven years given here.
claims.note: Estimates run from about 8 to 19 years, depending on how the co-regency with his father is counted.

claims.text: Abisha, in the Beni Hasan painting, is called 'ruler of foreign lands', the title later used by the Hyksos kings.
claims.note: The caption is painted in the tomb of the governor Khnumhotep II.

reigns.hook: Senusret II's reign is over. His son Senusret III will be a very different king: a hard soldier with his eyes fixed on Nubia.

reigns.tagline: The careworn warrior who walled off the Nile
reigns.previously: Senusret II dies, leaving a rich and peaceful Egypt.
paragraphs: Senusret III went to Nubia, and kept going back. His boats couldn't get easily past the rocks of the first cataract at Aswan, so he had a channel cut through them. Then he marched south, campaigning year after year, and built a chain of huge mudbrick forts around the second cataract, with thick walls, ditches and lookout posts, to control everything that moved on the river.

At Semna he set up a boundary stela with a blunt message for his heirs. Any son of his who held this border was truly his son. Any who gave it up was no son of his at all. The Nubians remembered him too: centuries later Thutmose III built a temple at Semna where Senusret was worshipped as a god. At home he seems to have cut the great provincial governors down to size.

His statues are unforgettable: a drawn, heavy-lidded face, lined with care, and big ears. Is it a true likeness, an old king's burden, or a message about a ruler who never sleeps? People still argue. The Greeks may have turned him into Sesostris, a hero who conquered the world. His son Amenemhat III inherited a safe, rich kingdom.

claims.text: Senusret III cut the power of the provincial governors.
claims.note: Their great provincial tombs stop being built around his reign. Whether he crushed them or simply drew their sons to court is unclear.

claims.text: His careworn statues were meant to show a king worn down by his duties.
claims.note: That's one reading. Others see a deliberate image of a watchful, all-knowing ruler, or simply a new court style.

claims.text: Sesostris, the hero Herodotus says conquered Asia and Europe, was really Senusret III.
claims.note: Herodotus's Sesostris is a blend of several kings and pure fiction. Senusret III is probably the main model, but he never campaigned beyond Nubia and Canaan.

reigns.hook: The borders are safe and the mines are open. Amenemhat III is about to preside over the richest years the Middle Kingdom ever saw.

reigns.tagline: Golden years, a sinking pyramid and a Labyrinth
reigns.previously: Senusret III dies with Nubia held by a wall of forts.
paragraphs: Amenemhat III had the luck to inherit peace, and he used it. He reigned about 45 years and Egypt was rich. His expeditions worked the turquoise and copper mines of Sinai harder than ever before. He poured effort into the Faiyum, the great lake basin west of the Nile, where swamp was turned into farmland. People there were still worshipping him as a god well over a thousand years later.

He built two pyramids. The first, at Dahshur, is called the Black Pyramid for its dark, crumbling core. It stood on soft ground and began to crack and sink, so he seems to have been buried in his second pyramid, at Hawara in the Faiyum. Beside it stood a vast temple with so many rooms and courts that Greek visitors called it the Labyrinth. Herodotus said it outdid even the pyramids.

His statues are among the most striking in Egypt. The Tanis sphinxes give him a lion's body and a great mane framing a hard, lined face. They were so unusual that scholars once took them for Hyksos work. After him Amenemhat IV reigned about nine years and left no son. The great family was down to its last royal woman.

claims.text: The Labyrinth had 3,000 rooms, half of them underground.
claims.note: Herodotus says so. He claims he toured the upper rooms but was refused entry to the lower ones, said to hold the tombs of kings and sacred crocodiles.

claims.text: He gave up the Black Pyramid because it was sinking and cracking.
claims.note: The damage is real and he probably lay at Hawara, but the Dahshur pyramid was still used for royal women's burials.

claims.text: The Tanis sphinxes were once thought to be portraits of Hyksos kings.
claims.note: Early Egyptologists, misled by later kings' names carved on them, credited them to the Hyksos. Their faces are now recognised as Amenemhat III's.

reigns.hook: The old king is dying. His heir Amenemhat IV is already crowned beside him, but the family that has ruled for two centuries is running out of sons.

reigns.tagline: The last king of a great family, with no son to follow
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Heir of Amenemhat III; perhaps grandson
reigns.reignEnded: Died with no son; Sobekneferu followed
reigns.previously: Amenemhat III dies after some 45 golden years.
paragraphs: Amenemhat IV shared the throne with the old king Amenemhat III for a time before he ruled alone. His mother Hetepti was called 'king's mother' but never queen, so he may have been a grandson of Amenemhat III, or a son by a lesser wife. The Turin king list gives him 9 years, 3 months and 27 days.

He kept the old king's projects going. Expeditions went to the turquoise mines of the Sinai and to Wadi el-Hudi for amethyst, and objects with his name reached Byblos on the Lebanese coast. In the Faiyum he finished the temple at Medinet Madi, begun under Amenemhat III, for the harvest goddess Renenutet and the crocodile god Sobek. It is one of the best-preserved temples of the Middle Kingdom.

His tomb has never been identified; one of two unfinished pyramids at Mazghuna, south of Dahshur, is a guess. When he died he left no son, and the throne passed to Sobekneferu, probably a daughter of Amenemhat III.

claims.text: Amenemhat IV was not Amenemhat III's son.
claims.note: Argued from his mother's lack of a queen's title. He may still have been a son by a minor wife, or a grandson.

claims.text: Amenemhat IV and Sobekneferu were husband and wife.
claims.note: A guess based on her taking the throne after him. No text says so.

reigns.hook: Amenemhat IV dies with no son to follow him. For the first time we can be sure of, a woman is about to take the throne of Egypt as king.

reigns.tagline: The first woman we know for sure ruled Egypt as king
reigns.previously: Amenemhat IV dies after about nine years, leaving no son.
paragraphs: Her name means 'beauty of Sobek', after the crocodile god of the Faiyum, and she was probably a daughter of Amenemhat III. When Amenemhat IV died without a son, she took the throne herself. Other women may have ruled Egypt before her, but she is the first we can say for certain ruled as king in her own right, with the full set of royal names.

She made no secret of being a woman, or of being king. A headless statue in the Louvre shows her in a woman's dress, with a king's kilt over it and a royal headcloth falling to her shoulders. Her titles mix female grammar with kingly roles. She added to the great temple at Hawara, honouring Amenemhat III, the father who had made her world.

Her reign was short. The Turin king list, written down centuries later, gives her just under four years. How it ended, nobody knows, and no tomb has been found that is certainly hers. With her, the 12th Dynasty, a family that had held Egypt for about two centuries, came to an end.

claims.text: Sobekneferu was the first woman to rule Egypt as king.
claims.note: She is the first certain one. Merneith of the 1st Dynasty may have ruled as regent, and Nitocris may be a misreading or a legend.

claims.text: She reigned 3 years, 10 months and 24 days.
claims.note: That is the Turin king list's figure, but the papyrus was copied about 500 years later and is badly damaged in places.

claims.text: She was buried in one of the two pyramids at Mazghuna, near Dahshur.
claims.note: Some scholars have suggested the northern Mazghuna pyramid, but nothing found there names her.

reigns.hook: Sobekneferu is gone, and her great family with her. The next king, Sobekhotep I, opens a dynasty of dozens of kings, most of whom barely have time to unpack.

reigns.tagline: First of a dynasty of very short reigns
reigns.previously: Sobekneferu's reign ends, and the great 12th Dynasty with it.
paragraphs: With Sobekneferu gone there was no one left of the old royal family to take over, and a new dynasty began, the 13th. Its first king was probably Sekhemre Khutawy Sobekhotep, who also called himself Amenemhat Sobekhotep. That double name may mean 'Sobekhotep, son of Amenemhat', a hint that he was linked by blood to the great kings before him. This is where many books begin the Second Intermediate Period.

He kept the old machine running. A household census from the town of Lahun is dated to his first year, and officers at the Nubian forts carved the height of the Nile flood in his years 2, 3 and 4. At Medamud, near Thebes, he added to the temple of the war god Montu, and a carved lintel there shows him offering to the god. After about four years he was gone, and the throne began to change hands fast.

claims.text: Sobekhotep, not Wegaf, founded the 13th Dynasty.
claims.note: The Turin king list starts the dynasty with Wegaf. Kim Ryholt argued in 1997 that the scribe mixed up two similar names, and most now follow him.

claims.text: He was the first king called Sobekhotep.
claims.note: Older books call him Sobekhotep II and number the later kings differently. This deck follows Ryholt's order and numbering.

claims.text: His highest known year is year 4.
claims.note: A Nile-flood record carved at the fort of Kumma in Nubia is dated to his fourth year.

reigns.hook: Sobekhotep's Egypt is not whole. Out in the eastern Delta, rulers with Canaanite names are calling themselves kings and stamping their own seals.

reigns.title: The Fourteenth Dynasty
reigns.tagline: Delta kings with Canaanite names
reigns.cameToPower: Broke away in the eastern Delta
reigns.previously: Sobekhotep I takes the throne at Itjtawy as the 13th Dynasty begins.
paragraphs: While the 13th Dynasty ruled from Itjtawy, the eastern Delta slipped out of its hands. Shaw's scheme dates this rival line, the 14th Dynasty, from about 1773 to 1650 BC; some scholars start it near 1720 BC, and Kim Ryholt as early as 1805 BC. Its kings sat at Avaris, or at Xois if Manetho is right, and many had West Semitic names: Yakbim, Ya'ammu, Qareh ('the bald one') and 'Ammu.

Most are known only from scarab seals, and the order of the early kings is Ryholt's, worked out from the style of those seals and much disputed. The best attested is Sheshi, whose names are on almost 400 seals found from Canaan to Nubia; two impressions even turned up at Carthage, in a layer about 1,500 years younger. Ryholt makes him husband of a Nubian princess, Tati, and father of Nehesy, 'the Nubian', who ruled briefly and left monuments at Avaris.

After Nehesy the Turin list runs through dozens of names with reigns of a year or two: Merdjefare, Sewadjkare III, Nebdjefare, Webenre and many more, some lost in gaps. Both Bietak and Ryholt think famine, and perhaps plague, struck the Delta. Around 1650 BC the Hyksos took power at Avaris, and the 14th Dynasty was gone.

claims.text: Yakbim founded the dynasty, and Sheshi and Nehesy were father and son.
claims.note: Kim Ryholt's reconstruction from seal styles. The early kings are missing from the Turin list, and von Beckerath and others put several of them in the 16th Dynasty.

claims.text: Sheshi was Salitis, the Hyksos conqueror named by Manetho.
claims.note: Nicolas Grimal, William Hayes and Donald Redford make the match; Ryholt puts Sheshi here, and others make him a later Hyksos king or vassal.

claims.text: The 14th Dynasty had 76 kings who ruled from Xois.
claims.note: Manetho's figure, known only through later quotations. The Turin list names only about 56 kings for this line and has no room for more than about 70.

reigns.hook: Back at Itjtawy the 13th Dynasty rolls on. Sobekhotep I is gone after about four years, and the next king, Sonbef, may have been his brother.

reigns.tagline: A king who may have been two kings, or one
reigns.previously: The Delta goes its own way. At Itjtawy, Sobekhotep I dies.
paragraphs: Sekhemkare Amenemhat Sonbef is a king we know mostly from a few small objects: a cylinder seal now in the Metropolitan Museum, a scarab, and two inscribed blocks from Tod, south of Thebes. Like Sobekhotep I he used a double name, and 'Amenemhat Sonbef' may mean 'Sonbef, son of Amenemhat'. If so, he and Sobekhotep could have been brothers, sons of Amenemhat IV.

Nile-flood records at the Nubian forts of Askut and Semna, dated to years 3 and 4 of a king Sekhemkare, may be his. The trouble is that a later king, Amenemhat V, used the same throne name, Sekhemkare, so nobody can be sure whose they are. Some Egyptologists think there was only ever one king, and that Sonbef and Amenemhat V are the same man.

claims.text: Sonbef and Amenemhat V were the same king.
claims.note: Detlef Franke and Stephen Quirke thought so. Kim Ryholt and Jürgen von Beckerath keep them apart as two kings with the same throne name.

claims.text: Sonbef was a son of Amenemhat IV.
claims.note: It rests on reading his double name as 'son of Amenemhat'. Double names were also simply a fashion of the age.

reigns.hook: After Sonbef comes Nerikare, a king so obscure that his name was misread for decades. One lost stela and one Nile flood mark are almost all he left.

reigns.tagline: The king whose name was read as a duck
reigns.previously: Sonbef's few years on the throne come to an end.
paragraphs: Nerikare is a king who almost slipped out of history. The Turin king list has a gap where he should be. What survives is a stela dated to his first year, copied by the Prussian expedition of Karl Richard Lepsius in the 1840s and since lost, and a Nile flood mark cut into the rock at Semna in Nubia.

For years the Semna mark was read as a king 'Djefakare'. Kim Ryholt pointed out that the first sign is a vulture, not a duck, which turns the name into Nerikare. If he is right, Nerikare was the third king of the dynasty, and he probably lasted about a year. Flood marks like his stop soon after this, as if the frontier forts were no longer reporting home.

claims.text: Nerikare reigned for only about a year.
claims.note: Ryholt's estimate. The Turin list gives 6 years for the gap where he probably sat, but Ryholt argues that figure was a scribe's filler for lost entries.

claims.text: The Semna flood record names Nerikare, not a king 'Djefakare'.
claims.note: Ryholt's rereading of one hieroglyph, accepted by Darrell Baker; the first editors read the name differently.

reigns.hook: Next comes Amenemhat V, who left something much better than a flood mark: a fine stone statue of himself at the temple of Elephantine.

reigns.tagline: A king in two pieces, Vienna and Aswan
reigns.previously: Nerikare is gone after about a year, known from one lost stela.
paragraphs: Sekhemkare Amenemhat V is one of the few kings of this run whose face we can see. He dedicated a statue of himself to Satet, goddess of Elephantine at the first cataract. In the 19th century the head and shoulders turned up in the ruins of the shrine of Heqaib on the island and went to Vienna. The body, with his names carved on it, was found in 1932 and is in the Aswan Museum.

A papyrus from Lahun dated to year 3 of a king Sekhemkare may be his, and the Turin list gives an Amenemhat 3 years. The catch is Sonbef, two cards back, who used the same throne name, Sekhemkare. Some scholars think the two are one man. In Ryholt's order, used here, they are separate kings, and Amenemhat V's family may have held on to the crown after him.

claims.text: Amenemhat V and Sonbef were different kings.
claims.note: Ryholt, von Beckerath and Baker keep them apart. Detlef Franke and Stephen Quirke think 'Amenemhat Sonbef' was simply one king's double name.

claims.text: He reigned about 3 years.
claims.note: Based on a Turin king list entry for an Amenemhat with 3 years and a Lahun papyrus dated to year 3 of Sekhemkare; neither certainly belongs to him.

claims.text: The statue from Elephantine shows Amenemhat V.
claims.note: The inscription on the body in Aswan names Sekhemkare Amenemhat, beloved of Satet, lady of Elephantine.

reigns.hook: His successor, Ameny Qemau, carries the short form of Amenemhat inside his own name. Was he Amenemhat V's son? He at least leaves a pyramid.

reigns.tagline: A pyramid in the desert with his name inside
reigns.reignEnded: Unknown; reigned a year or two
reigns.previously: Amenemhat V dies, leaving his statue at Elephantine.
paragraphs: Ameny Qemau is one of the few 13th Dynasty kings whose tomb we can point to. In 1957 the explorer Charles Muses dug into a ruined pyramid at southern Dahshur, near the great pyramids of the 12th Dynasty. Its upper parts had long been stripped for stone, but inside were pieces of canopic jars, the containers for a mummy's organs, carved with the name of King Ameny Qemau.

Beyond the pyramid we know very little. His double name may mean 'Qemau, son of Ameny', and Ameny was a short form of Amenemhat, so he may have been a son of Amenemhat V. Even a reign of a year or two was enough to start a pyramid, which shows the royal workshops near the capital were still running smoothly.

claims.text: The southern Dahshur pyramid is Ameny Qemau's.
claims.note: Canopic jar fragments naming him were found in its burial chamber, published by Charles Muses and later studied by Egyptologists.

claims.text: He was a son of Amenemhat V.
claims.note: Kim Ryholt's reading of the double name as a family link. It is plausible but unproven.

reigns.hook: Ameny Qemau's son takes the throne with a mouthful of a name, Qemau Siharnedjheritef. A ceremonial mace bearing his name will turn up in a tomb far away in Syria.

reigns.tagline: His name turned up in a prince's tomb in Syria
reigns.previously: Ameny Qemau dies, leaving a half-ruined pyramid at Dahshur.
paragraphs: His throne name was Hotepibre, and his personal name is a sentence: Qemau Siharnedjheritef, 'Qemau's son, Horus who avenges his father'. That makes him almost certainly a son of Ameny Qemau. He reigned only a couple of years, but he left a seated statue, found in the eastern Delta, and a scatter of other objects.

His most surprising relic turned up far from Egypt. At Ebla, in Syria, Italian archaeologists digging a royal tomb known as the 'Tomb of the Lord of the Goats' found a ceremonial mace with his name on it. Whether he sent it as a gift to a Syrian ruler, or it travelled there later, is unknown. Either way, even these short-lived kings still had contacts and prestige well beyond the Nile.

claims.text: A mace bearing Hotepibre's name was found in a royal tomb at Ebla.
claims.note: Found by Paolo Matthiae's Italian mission at Tell Mardikh (Ebla), now in a Syrian museum.

claims.text: The mace was a royal gift from Egypt to the ruler of Ebla.
claims.note: A tempting guess, but it could have reached Syria by trade or as loot. No text explains it.

reigns.hook: Next on the throne is Amenemhat VI, a king with three names, and maybe three generations of his family packed into them.

reigns.tagline: Three names, a few stones, and two short years
reigns.reignEnded: Unknown; reigned a year or two
reigns.previously: Hotepibre Qemau Siharnedjheritef dies after a couple of years.
paragraphs: Seankhibre Amenemhat VI went by a string of names, Ameny Antef Amenemhat. Kim Ryholt has read them as a family tree: Amenemhat, son of Antef, son of Ameny. If he is right, the king was a grandson of an earlier ruler and part of a family that kept passing the crown around.

Little else survives. His name appears on an offering table, a stone slab for gifts of food to the gods, and on a stela, and later Egyptians included him in the list of ancestor kings carved for Thutmose III at Karnak. He reigned only a short time, and the crown passed again, this time to a king called Nebnuni.

claims.text: His three names record three generations: Amenemhat, son of Antef, son of Ameny.
claims.note: Ryholt's reading. Others see a plain triple name, which some kings of the age used without any family meaning.

claims.text: He appears in the Karnak king list of Thutmose III.
claims.note: The 'Chamber of Ancestors' from Karnak, now in the Louvre, includes his throne name Seankhibre.

reigns.hook: Next comes Semenkare Nebnuni, another king of a couple of years. In this dynasty a short reign is the rule, not the exception.

reigns.tagline: A king who survives as one line in a list and one stone
reigns.previously: Amenemhat VI is gone after a year or two. The queue moves on.
paragraphs: His full name was Semenkare Nebnuni, and nearly all we know about him fits on a postcard. The Turin king list, a papyrus written out about 500 years later, gives him roughly two years. Kim Ryholt, who rebuilt the order of this dynasty from that battered list, makes him its ninth king. He ruled from Itjtawy, the royal city near el-Lisht that the 12th Dynasty had founded.

That was how the 13th Dynasty worked. Kings followed each other every year or two, often with no sign of being related, while viziers and scribes kept the country running underneath them. Taxes were collected, Nile floods were measured and letters were filed. Nebnuni was one more name at the top of a machine that barely noticed who was in charge.

claims.text: The Turin king list gives Nebnuni a reign of about two years.
claims.note: The entry is read this way by Ryholt, but the papyrus is broken and its numbers are often patched together from fragments.

claims.text: Kings of this dynasty were picked in turn from a few powerful families.
claims.note: A theory proposed by Stephen Quirke to explain the short reigns. No ancient text describes such a system; coups and early deaths are other explanations.

reigns.hook: Next comes Sehetepibre, whose name turns up on a seal made for the ruler of Byblos, far away on the coast of Lebanon.

reigns.tagline: His seal went all the way to Byblos
reigns.previously: Nebnuni is gone after a couple of years. The queue moves on.
paragraphs: Sehetepibre took the Horus name Sewesekhtawy, 'he who enlarges the Two Lands', which was a bold claim for a king who lasted about two years. The Turin list names two kings called Sehetepibre in this dynasty, and scholars argue over which is which. Ryholt thinks one of them is a copying slip, which makes this king the tenth of the dynasty.

His best traces are far from home. A stela bearing his names was found at Gebel Zeit on the Red Sea coast, where Egyptians mined galena for black eye paint. A lapis lazuli cylinder seal in the Metropolitan Museum carries his name, a prayer to 'Hathor, lady of Byblos', and, in cuneiform, the name of Yakin-Ilu, a ruler of Byblos. Egypt's kings were still worth knowing on the Lebanese coast.

claims.text: The cylinder seal shows Sehetepibre was in contact with the rulers of Byblos.
claims.note: The Met seal pairs his cartouche with the name of Yakin-Ilu of Byblos in cuneiform; how the seal was used is unknown.

claims.text: He was the tenth king of the dynasty and reigned about 2 years.
claims.note: Ryholt's reconstruction of the Turin list. Franke and von Beckerath put him fifth.

reigns.hook: Next comes Sewadjkare, a king so fleeting that only a few days of his reign survive in the Turin list.

reigns.tagline: A king who exists in one line of papyrus
reigns.previously: Sehetepibre dies after about two years.
paragraphs: Sewadjkare is a name and nothing more. No statue, no seal, no stela of his has ever been found. All we have is one line in the Turin king list, a papyrus copied some 500 years later under the Ramesside kings. Even there the length of his reign has crumbled away, leaving only part of the figure for the days.

A king who left nothing behind was probably not on the throne long. In this stretch of the dynasty that was normal: the crown changed hands every year or two, and the government of viziers and scribes carried on beneath it. Two later kings used the same throne name, including Hori near the end of the dynasty, so he is sometimes called Sewadjkare I.

claims.text: Sewadjkare reigned only a short time, perhaps weeks or months.
claims.note: Ryholt's estimate from the space left in the damaged Turin entry; only part of the days figure survives.

claims.text: He is known only from the Turin king list.
claims.note: No contemporary object with his name has been identified.

reigns.hook: Then comes Nedjemibre, whose name means something like 'pleasing of heart to Ra'. The Turin list gives him seven months.

reigns.tagline: Seven months, then a Sobekhotep moves in
reigns.previously: Sewadjkare comes and goes, leaving only a line in the king list.
paragraphs: Nedjemibre is another king we know only from the Turin list, and there he gets seven months and some lost days. His birth name is unknown. Some have wondered if it was Amenemhat, which would make him the father of the later king Renseneb, but nothing proves it.

What happened next is the interesting part. The king who followed him, Khaankhre Sobekhotep, is well attested but never names his parents. In an age when kings' sons liked to say whose sons they were, that silence suggests a man not born royal. Kim Ryholt thinks Sobekhotep pushed Nedjemibre aside and took the throne for himself.

claims.text: Nedjemibre reigned 7 months.
claims.note: The figure comes from the Turin king list, copied centuries later; there is no other record of him.

claims.text: His successor Sobekhotep II seized the throne from him.
claims.note: Ryholt's inference from Sobekhotep's silence about his parents; there is no record of a coup.

reigns.hook: The next king is a Sobekhotep with no royal father to boast of. He still finds the means to build at Abydos.

reigns.tagline: One of many Sobekhoteps, and one who built for Osiris
reigns.previously: Nedjemibre is gone after seven months. A Sobekhotep moves in.
paragraphs: His throne name was Khaankhre, and his birth name honoured Sobek, the crocodile god of the Faiyum. Plenty of 13th Dynasty kings had the same idea, which makes them a headache to tell apart. Scholars number the Sobekhoteps differently. In Kim Ryholt's scheme, used here, this one is Sobekhotep II, but older books may give him a different number.

He left more than his neighbours in the list did. Carved blocks with his names have turned up at Abydos, the holy city of Osiris, where every king liked to be seen building. Abydos mattered more than ever in this age: making the pilgrimage and setting up a stela by the god's processional road was what every official hoped for. How long he ruled and how his reign ended, nobody knows.

claims.text: Khaankhre is the king called Sobekhotep II.
claims.note: This is Ryholt's numbering. Other scholars number the 13th Dynasty Sobekhoteps differently, so the same Roman numeral can mean different kings in different books.

claims.text: He put up buildings at Abydos.
claims.note: Architectural pieces carved with his names come from Abydos; how big the building was is unclear.

reigns.hook: The next king, Renseneb, lasts just four months. His only trace outside the king list is a glazed bead, last seen in a Cairo antiques shop in 1929.

reigns.tagline: Four months on the throne and one lost bead
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Perhaps son of a king Amenemhat
reigns.previously: Sobekhotep II dies after about two years.
paragraphs: Renseneb's name means 'my name is healthy', which did him little good: the Turin list gives him a reign of four months. His throne name is unknown. Apart from the king list, one object survived, a glazed steatite bead reading 'Renseneb Amenemhat, given life'. Percy Newberry saw it in a Cairo antiques shop in 1929, and it has not been seen since.

Kim Ryholt reads the bead as 'Renseneb, son of Amenemhat', which would make him a king's son taking his turn. Others read it simply as a double name. Either way, he did not last. The king after him, Hor, never mentions a royal father either, and Ryholt suspects another takeover.

claims.text: Renseneb reigned four months.
claims.note: From the Turin king list, copied centuries later; no dated document from his reign survives.

claims.text: Renseneb was the son of a king Amenemhat.
claims.note: Ryholt's reading of the double name on the lost bead; Stephen Quirke and others do not accept it.

reigns.hook: Hor follows him and is king only a few months too. But Hor is about to become one of the most famous faces of the whole dynasty.

reigns.tagline: Months on the throne, then forever in a wooden statue
reigns.previously: Renseneb lasts four months. The throne passes again.
paragraphs: Awibre Hor was king for a matter of months and then he died. On paper he is one of this dynasty's forgettable names. What rescued him was his grave. He was buried at Dahshur in a modest shaft tomb inside the enclosure of Amenemhat III's pyramid, beside the great king of a century before. Maybe he was family. Maybe he just chose good company.

In 1894 the French archaeologist Jacques de Morgan cleared the tomb and found a wooden shrine. Inside stood a striding wooden statue of the king, nearly life-size, with inlaid eyes. On its head rise two raised arms, the hieroglyph for ka, the life force that needed a body to come home to. Now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, it is one of the most haunting faces to survive from ancient Egypt.

claims.text: Hor reigned only a few months.
claims.note: The short reign comes from Ryholt's reading of the damaged Turin king list; the hurried, modest burial fits it.

claims.text: He was buried beside Amenemhat III because he descended from him.
claims.note: A guess from where the tomb is. No text names Hor's parents.

claims.text: His ka statue was found standing in its own wooden shrine.
claims.note: Jacques de Morgan's excavation report on Dahshur, 1894; the statue is in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

reigns.hook: Hor's son may already be at his side. Khabaw, whose name is carved next to Hor's on a granite beam, takes the throne next.

reigns.tagline: Hor's son, carved in granite beside him
reigns.previously: Hor dies after a few months and is buried at Dahshur.
paragraphs: The Turin list skips him, but Sekhemrekhutawy Khabaw left more behind than most kings around him. Two granite architraves carry his names, one found at Bubastis in 1891 and now in the British Museum, the other at Tanis, where his name stands beside Hor's. Both were probably carved for buildings at Memphis and dragged north by later kings.

His seals turn up at the Nubian fortresses of Uronarti and Mirgissa, so the frontier garrisons still took orders from him. The pairing with Hor led Ryholt and Darrell Baker to suggest he was Hor's son, perhaps crowned while Hor was still alive. That would make him one of the few kings in this dynasty to follow his own father.

claims.text: Khabaw was Hor's son and perhaps his co-ruler.
claims.note: Ryholt and Baker's reading of the Tanis architrave that names both kings; no text calls Khabaw Hor's son.

claims.text: His name dropped out of the Turin list because its source was already damaged.
claims.note: Ryholt argues the Ramesside copyist found a gap marked 'missing' where Khabaw should be.

reigns.hook: Next comes another of Hor's sons, Djedkheperew. His name will end up on a black stone statue of the god Osiris lying on his bier.

reigns.tagline: His name on the bed of Osiris, half scratched out
reigns.previously: Khabaw dies after a year or two.
paragraphs: Djedkheperew is known by his Horus name; his throne and birth names are lost. Eleven of his seal impressions were found at the Nubian forts of Uronarti and Mirgissa, lying with Khabaw's. His great monument is the 'Bed of Osiris', a black stone sculpture of the god lying on a lion-headed bier, found in the 1st Dynasty tomb of Djer at Abydos, which Egyptians by then believed was the tomb of Osiris himself.

Someone later scratched out his birth name on it, carelessly, and the traces seem to begin with the name Hor. Ryholt takes that as a sign that he called himself Hor's son, making him Khabaw's brother and successor. The sculpture was long credited to King Khendjer before closer study of the inscription. It is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

claims.text: The Bed of Osiris was made for Djedkheperew.
claims.note: Anthony Leahy once attributed it to Khendjer; later study of the erased inscription points to Djedkheperew.

claims.text: He was a son of Hor and brother of Khabaw.
claims.note: Ryholt's inference from the erased name and from seals found together at Uronarti.

reigns.hook: After Djedkheperew the line of Hor's sons fades out. The next king, Amenemhat VII, may carry yet another father's name inside his own.

reigns.tagline: Amenemhat, son of Kay? A king with his father in his name
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Perhaps son of an earlier king, Kay
reigns.cameToPower: Followed kings known only from seals
reigns.reignEnded: End unknown, after a year or two
reigns.previously: Djedkheperew dies, his name later scratched off Osiris's bed.
paragraphs: His full name was Sedjefakare Kay-Amenemhat, and that double birth name is the puzzle. Kim Ryholt argues that names like this were family labels, meaning something like 'Amenemhat, son of Kay'. If he is right, the king's father was a man called Kay, perhaps one of the shadowy kings just before him. Several 13th Dynasty kings may have used the trick to show that royal blood did run in their veins.

He left a few real monuments, which is more than many of his neighbours managed. Inscribed pieces with his name come from temples in the south. They are short and formal and tell us nothing about the man. His reign lasted a couple of years at most, and then the crown moved on to a king the ancient list had filed somewhere else entirely.

claims.text: Amenemhat VII was the son of a king called Kay.
claims.note: Ryholt reads 'Kay-Amenemhat' as 'Kay's son Amenemhat'. Others think the double name is just a name, and it says nothing of his father.

claims.text: Some 13th Dynasty kings put their father's name in front of their own.
claims.note: Ryholt's theory of 'filiative' names, also used for Qemau Siharnedjheritef; widely discussed, not proven.

reigns.hook: Next comes Wegaf. The Turin list puts his name at the very top of the dynasty. Was the ancient scribe wrong, or are the modern scholars?

reigns.tagline: The king the ancient list may have filed in the wrong place
reigns.previously: Amenemhat VII, perhaps the son of a king Kay, passes on.
paragraphs: The Turin king list, the papyrus that holds most of what we know about this age, opens the 13th Dynasty with Khutawyre Wegaf. For a long time historians took it at its word. Then Kim Ryholt noticed that the dynasty's real founder, Sobekhotep I, had an almost identical throne name, Sekhemre Khutawy. His idea: the scribe mixed the two up, and Wegaf really belongs about twenty kings later.

Wherever he sits, his reign probably gave us one text we can still read. Stelae set up at Abydos mark out the sacred road along which the god's image was carried in procession, and forbid anyone to build a tomb on it, on pain of punishment. Everyone wanted to be buried close to the god, and the king had to keep the crowds off his path. The Turin list gives him a little over two years.

claims.text: The Turin list puts Wegaf first in the 13th Dynasty by mistake.
claims.note: Ryholt's argument from the near-identical throne names; many accept it, but some still place Wegaf at the start of the dynasty.

claims.text: Wegaf banned tomb-building on the god's processional road at Abydos.
claims.note: The Abydos boundary stelae (Cairo) were reinscribed for Neferhotep I; the erased first owner is usually read as Wegaf, though some suggest King Seth.

claims.text: He reigned 2 years and 3 months.
claims.note: The Turin list's figure, read by Ryholt; the papyrus is damaged here.

reigns.hook: His successor will carry a name no Egyptian king had used before. It may be foreign, and it may mean 'boar'.

reigns.tagline: A king nicknamed 'Boar' who built a real pyramid
reigns.previously: Wegaf, the king the Turin list put first, has had his two years.
paragraphs: Khendjer is not an Egyptian name. Kim Ryholt linked it to the Semitic word for boar or pig, which would make him a king of Canaanite descent ruling Egypt about a century before the Hyksos. That is less strange than it sounds: people from the Levant had been living and working in Egypt for years, and some rose high. Under the throne name Userkare, he ruled from Itjtawy as a fully Egyptian king.

Unlike most of his dynasty, he got a pyramid finished. It stands at South Saqqara and was dug by the Swiss archaeologist Gustave Jéquier around 1930. The burial chamber was cut from a huge single block of quartzite, and the black granite capstone is now in Cairo. At Abydos his officials had the temple of Osiris cleaned and repaired, and the stelae they set up to boast about it survive in the Louvre.

claims.text: Khendjer's name comes from a Semitic word for 'boar'.
claims.note: Ryholt's suggestion. Others doubt the etymology, so whether he was of foreign descent is uncertain.

claims.text: His officials restored the temple of Osiris at Abydos.
claims.note: Two stelae of the official Amenyseneb, now in the Louvre, describe the work and name the vizier Ankhu.

claims.text: He reigned about five years.
claims.note: Dated records from his reign reach his fifth year; the Turin list entry is damaged.

reigns.hook: After Khendjer, a man whose name means 'general' takes the throne. He will leave two giant statues, and a Hyksos king will one day carve his own name on them.

reigns.tagline: His name meant 'general', and maybe so did his old job
reigns.reignEnded: End unknown, after a short reign
reigns.previously: Khendjer dies, a king with a foreign name and a finished pyramid.
paragraphs: Imyremeshaw is less a name than a job title: it means 'overseer of the army', in other words 'general'. Whether he was born with it or came to the throne straight from command, nobody can say. In a dynasty where kings came and went every few years, a soldier taking his turn would be no surprise. His throne name was Smenkhkare, and he did not last long.

He is remembered for two colossal seated statues of himself in granite, found at Tanis in the Delta and now in Cairo. They were not made there; later kings hauled old statues to Tanis by the dozen. Along the way, the Hyksos king Apepi had his own name carved on one, and Ramesses II added his too. Recycling a dead king's statue was the cheapest way to look grand.

claims.text: Imyremeshaw was an army general before he became king.
claims.note: His name is the title for 'general', which suggests it, but Egyptians were sometimes given titles as personal names.

claims.text: The Hyksos king Apepi and later Ramesses II carved their names on his statues.
claims.note: The added inscriptions are on the two colossi from Tanis, now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

reigns.hook: Next comes Intef IV. The Turin list measured his reign, but the years and months are torn away. Only three days survive.

reigns.tagline: Only the last three days of his reign survive
reigns.previously: Imyremeshaw dies, his statues later hauled north to Tanis.
paragraphs: Sehetepkare Intef took a name famous from the old Theban kings who had fought their way to power three centuries before. The Turin list includes him, but the years and months of his reign are torn away; only '3 days' is left. In the Faiyum, the lower half of a seated statue of him was found in the temple of the harvest goddess Renenutet at Medinet Madi.

A palace account from this time, Papyrus Boulaq 18, describes a royal household with a queen named Aya, a prince Redienef, three daughters and ten of the king's sisters. Ryholt thinks the king was either Intef or his predecessor Imyremeshaw. Intef's reign ended under a cloud: his successor Seth never named a royal father, and both Ryholt and von Beckerath think Seth seized the throne.

claims.text: Intef reigned less than ten years.
claims.note: Ryholt gives about 10 years in all to Imyremeshaw, Intef and Seth together; Intef's own figure is lost in the Turin list.

claims.text: His successor Seth usurped the throne.
claims.note: Inferred from Seth's lack of a royal father's name; no text describes what happened.

reigns.hook: The man who takes Intef's place is named after Seth, the god of chaos and storms. His reign leaves almost nothing but six days in the king list.

reigns.tagline: A king named after the god of chaos
reigns.previously: Intef IV's reign ends, perhaps not by his own choice.
paragraphs: Meribre Seth carried the name of Seth, god of storms, deserts and disorder, and the murderer of Osiris in myth. It was a rare choice for a king. The Turin list records him, but all that remains of his reign length is '6 days'. He never named a royal father, which is why scholars think he took the crown from Intef rather than inheriting it.

No object is certainly his. Ryholt thinks a stela at Abydos, later taken over by Neferhotep I, was first carved for Seth, and that his successor Sobekhotep III recarved some of his building blocks at Medamud near Thebes. Von Beckerath even tracked him down in a much later family tree, where the scribe swapped the Seth sign for a donkey. If so, Seth's name was still being dodged a thousand years later.

claims.text: Seth reigned less than five years.
claims.note: Ryholt's estimate from the 10 years he gives Imyremeshaw, Intef and Seth together; only '6 days' survives in the Turin list.

claims.text: Sobekhotep III recarved Seth's monuments at Medamud.
claims.note: Rests on almost erased signs on blocks from Medamud; the evidence is weak.

claims.text: The king 'Aaqen' in a 22nd Dynasty genealogy is Seth.
claims.note: Von Beckerath's idea that a donkey sign replaced the hated Seth animal; it remains a guess.

reigns.hook: Seth vanishes. The next king is the son of a commoner and a commoner's wife, and he is not ashamed to carve their names on his seals.

reigns.tagline: The king who put his commoner parents on show
reigns.cameToPower: Followed King Seth; not born royal
reigns.previously: Meribre Seth's short reign ends; nobody knows how.
paragraphs: Most kings liked to pretend they were born to rule. Sekhemre Sewadjtawy Sobekhotep did the opposite. On his monuments he named his father Mentuhotep, a man with no royal title, and his mother Iuhetibu, and gave room to his wife and daughters as well. Rock inscriptions in the far south show the family together. He came from the ruling class, not the royal family, and he was proud of it.

His reign, about four years by the Turin list, also gives a rare look inside ordinary homes. A papyrus now in the Brooklyn Museum lists the servants of one household, and dozens of them have Asiatic names: people from Canaan and Syria, some given Egyptian names alongside their own. This was the slow migration that would end, within a century, with foreign kings ruling the north.

claims.text: Sobekhotep III openly named his non-royal parents, Mentuhotep and Iuhetibu.
claims.note: Their names and the absence of royal titles appear on his own monuments and rock inscriptions.

claims.text: A household in his time had dozens of Asiatic servants.
claims.note: Papyrus Brooklyn 35.1446, published by William C. Hayes in 1955; part of it is dated to his reign, though the list itself may be older.

reigns.tagline: The king who went back to the old books for Osiris
reigns.previously: Sobekhotep III dies after about four years, with no son to follow.
paragraphs: Khasekhemre Neferhotep was another king who openly named his non-royal parents, Haankhef and Kemi. With him the throne finally steadied. The Turin list gives him eleven years, an age by this dynasty's standards, and his name turns up from the Delta to Aswan. Even a ruler of Byblos, on the coast of today's Lebanon, had himself carved seated before Neferhotep's name, a sign that Egypt still counted abroad.

His most famous text is a great stela at Abydos. In it the king tells how he had the temple's house of books opened and searched the ancient writings of the creator god Atum, so that a new statue of Osiris could be made exactly as the god had been in the beginning. Then he sailed to Abydos and took part in the god's festival in person. It is the voice of a king who wanted to do things properly.
He had two brothers. One, Sihathor, was crowned beside him near the end of his reign, and the two died within a short time of each other. Then the throne went to the other, Sobekhotep.

claims.text: Neferhotep's Abydos stela says he searched the ancient writings before remaking the statue of Osiris.
claims.note: His own account on the great Abydos stela. It is royal propaganda, but it shows how kings wanted to be seen.

claims.text: A king of Byblos was Neferhotep's loyal vassal.
claims.note: A relief from Byblos shows its ruler Yantin before Neferhotep's name. Whether that means real control or just respect is argued.

claims.text: His brother Sihathor briefly ruled with him.
claims.note: Sihathor appears with royal names, but whether he ever really reigned, even as a junior partner, is uncertain.

reigns.hook: In his last months Neferhotep crowns his brother Sihathor beside him. The Turin list gives Sihathor a few months of his own. Did he ever rule alone?

reigns.tagline: The middle brother who was king for months
reigns.reignEnded: Died within months, before his brother
reigns.previously: Neferhotep I dies after 11 years, his brother already crowned.
paragraphs: Sihathor was one of three brothers who held the crown: Neferhotep I, Sihathor and Sobekhotep IV, sons of Haankhef and Kemi. Rock inscriptions on the islands of Philae and Sehel, carved for Neferhotep, show him in the family group. On two statues at the shrine of Heqaib on Elephantine he is only a 'king's son'. On a cylinder seal in the Petrie Museum he is king.

The Turin list puts him right after Neferhotep with a reign of a few months, though the number itself is lost. Most scholars think those months were spent as co-king in Neferhotep's last year and that Sihathor died first, so he never ruled alone; this card simply follows the king list's order. At Abydos, Josef Wegner's team found an unfinished royal tomb wedged between the great tombs of the other two brothers. It may well be his.

claims.text: Sihathor ruled only as Neferhotep's co-king and died before him.
claims.note: The usual view, from his place in the Turin list and the later statue that calls him only 'king's son'; Ryholt and others weigh it differently.

claims.text: The unfinished tomb between tombs S9 and S10 at Abydos was his.
claims.note: Wegner's suggestion, based on its position between the tombs thought to belong to his brothers.

claims.text: He was the son of Haankhef and Kemi.
claims.note: Neferhotep I's rock inscriptions at Philae and Sehel name the family.

reigns.hook: Both brothers are dead within months of each other. The crown passes to the last of them, Sobekhotep IV, who says he was born in Thebes.

reigns.tagline: The third brother, and the dynasty's last high point
reigns.previously: Neferhotep I and his brother Sihathor are dead. The third steps up.
paragraphs: Khaneferre Sobekhotep was the third of the brothers, after Neferhotep I and the short-lived Sihathor, and he kept the family's run going. A stela he set up at Karnak tells of his birth in Thebes and lists his gifts to the temple of Amun. He reigned about a decade, long enough to leave statues and inscriptions across the country.

Big granite statues of him were later carried to Tanis in the Delta, and some now sit in the Louvre, proof he could still command serious work from the quarries. Broken inscriptions hint at a war in Nubia, where the kingdom of Kush was growing stronger. After him the dynasty's grip began to slip, and the north drifted out of reach.

claims.text: Sobekhotep IV was born in Thebes.
claims.note: He says so on his stela from Karnak, now in Cairo.

claims.text: He fought a campaign in Nubia.
claims.note: Fragmentary inscriptions from Karnak seem to mention it, but the texts are too broken to be sure.

reigns.hook: His son, Merhotepre Sobekhotep V, takes the throne. His mother's name on his seals is what tells him apart from all the other Sobekhoteps.

reigns.tagline: The Sobekhotep we know by his mother's name
reigns.previously: Sobekhotep IV dies after about ten years on the throne.
paragraphs: Merhotepre Sobekhotep's place in the Turin list is lost in a hole in the papyrus, right below Sobekhotep IV. He gives himself away on his seals. Like the three brothers before him, he named his parents on them, and his mother was the king's mother Nubhotepti. That sets him apart from the other Sobekhoteps, and suggests he may have been Sobekhotep IV's son.

His monuments cluster around Thebes. A seated granodiorite statue in Cairo carries both his royal names, and a striding statue comes from Karnak. A legal stela from Thebes quotes a decree of a year 1 of 'Merhotepre', probably him. Older books merge him with a later king, Merhotepre Ini, who had the same throne name, and call him Sobekhotep VI.

claims.text: Merhotepre Sobekhotep and Merhotepre Ini were two different kings.
claims.note: Ryholt separates them, placing Sobekhotep in the lost line after Sobekhotep IV; Franke and von Beckerath thought they were one king.

claims.text: He reigned about 3 years.
claims.note: Ryholt's estimate; the Turin entry is lost.

claims.text: His mother was named Nubhotepti.
claims.note: Seals naming a King Sobekhotep with the king's mother Nubhotepti; Ryholt assigns them to him.

reigns.tagline: A reign the king list measured to the very day
reigns.previously: Sobekhotep V dies after about three years.
paragraphs: Khahotepre Sobekhotep is one of those kings we know mostly by a number. The Turin list gives him four years, eight months and 29 days, which shows how carefully the scribes kept count even when they lost track of almost everything else. Scarabs and seals with his name, a kneeling statue now in Berlin and a few mentions on officials' monuments are about all he left behind.

Kim Ryholt numbers him Sobekhotep VI; other books call him Sobekhotep V. By his time the dynasty was ruling a shrinking kingdom. In the eastern Delta, the rulers of the 14th Dynasty ran their own affairs from Avaris, and the Canaanite families settled there were growing in number and in wealth.

claims.text: He reigned 4 years, 8 months and 29 days.
claims.note: That is the reading of his Turin king list entry, but the papyrus was copied centuries later and its order here depends on Ryholt's reconstruction.

claims.text: A rival 14th Dynasty ruled the eastern Delta from Avaris in his time.
claims.note: Ryholt dates the 14th Dynasty this early; others put it later or doubt it was ever a real dynasty.

reigns.hook: Next comes Ibiau, who will last longer than anyone since the three brothers: more than ten years.

reigns.tagline: Ten quiet years in a dynasty of revolving doors
reigns.previously: Sobekhotep VI's reign of not quite five years is over.
paragraphs: Wahibre Ibiau gave the 13th Dynasty one of its longer breathing spaces: the Turin list gives him ten years and eight months. For a dynasty that sometimes changed kings twice in a year, that counts as stability. Seals and scarabs with his name are common, and officials of his reign set up stelae of their own.

Egypt under Ibiau was still one country on paper, but it was quietly coming apart. The king's writ ran in Memphis and the south, while Avaris in the eastern Delta looked more and more to its own rulers. His reign also turns up in a later legal record from Karnak, which traces how the governorship of the town of El Kab passed down and was sold within one family. Offices outlasted the kings.

claims.text: Ibiau reigned 10 years and 8 months.
claims.note: The reading of his entry in the Turin king list, a later copy that is damaged in many places.

claims.text: The Juridical Stela from Karnak mentions his reign.
claims.note: The stela, a 17th Dynasty record about the governorship of El Kab, names a King Wahibre; most identify him with Ibiau.

reigns.hook: Next comes Merneferre Ay, who will reign longer than any king of the dynasty: more than twenty years.

reigns.tagline: The last king whose writ ran the whole Nile
reigns.reignEnded: End of the longest reign in the line
reigns.previously: Ibiau dies after about ten years, a long run for this dynasty.
paragraphs: Merneferre Ay broke the pattern. In a dynasty where most kings barely lasted a year or two, the Turin king list gives him 23 years and 8 months, the longest reign of the whole 13th Dynasty. Shaw gives no dates for single kings in this age, so the years on this card are only a rough fit, about 1694 to 1671 BC.

His scarabs turn up in big numbers, and his name is found in both the south and the far north. His black granite pyramidion, the capstone of a pyramid, shows him in a boat before the god Horus. It turned up at Faqus in the eastern Delta, not far from Avaris. So he planned a proper royal pyramid, though nobody has found it. He is the last 13th Dynasty king with clear traces in both halves of the country.

After him, things slip fast. The eastern Delta was drifting out of the dynasty's reach, into the hands of local lords and Canaanite settlers around Avaris. Ay's successors would rule a shrinking kingdom from the old capital, Itjtawy, near the Faiyum.

claims.text: The Turin king list gives Merneferre Ay 23 years and 8 months, the longest reign of the dynasty.
claims.note: The papyrus is broken and pieced together; the figure follows Ryholt's reading. Shaw gives no per-king dates.

claims.text: His pyramidion was found at Faqus in the eastern Delta.
claims.note: Now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo. His pyramid has never been found, so the stone may have been moved from elsewhere.

claims.text: He was the last 13th Dynasty king who ruled both Upper and Lower Egypt.
claims.note: Based on where his objects turn up. Scarabs travel, so finds in the Delta don't prove he governed it.

reigns.hook: Ay's long reign is over. The next king, Ini, gets about two years, and the north keeps slipping away.

reigns.previously: Merneferre Ay dies after nearly 24 years, the dynasty's longest reign.
paragraphs: Merhotepre Ini is one of those kings who survive almost only as a line in a list. The Turin king list, copied out some 450 years later, gives him about two years. Kim Ryholt, who rebuilt the order of these kings, thought he may have been a son of Merneferre Ay, but nothing written at the time says so.

What we can see is the world he ruled. In the eastern Delta a rival line, which Manetho's lists call the 14th Dynasty, ran its own affairs from Avaris. One of its kings, Nehesy, whose name means 'the Nubian', left monuments there. The kings at Itjtawy still held the Nile valley, but their reach was shrinking with every short reign.

claims.note: From the damaged Turin king list, as Ryholt reads it. Shaw gives no per-king dates for this dynasty.

claims.text: Ini was a son of Merneferre Ay.
claims.note: A suggestion by Ryholt from the order of names. No monument names his father.

reigns.previously: Ini dies after about two years on the throne.
paragraphs: Sankhenre Sewadjtu is a puzzle with most of the pieces missing. The Turin king list gives him about three years and two months. Beyond that, almost nothing with his name has been found that experts agree on. No statue, no tomb, no family. He is a name on a 3,000-year-old scrap of papyrus, and a number next to it.

That is what much of the late 13th Dynasty looks like. The papyrus now in Turin was a list of every king the scribes knew, with the years each one ruled. It was in many fragments by the time it reached Europe, and scholars still argue over how the pieces fit. Sewadjtu's place in the order comes from one of those reconstructions.

claims.note: From the Turin king list as Ryholt reads it; the papyrus is badly damaged at this point.

claims.text: The Turin king list reached Europe broken into many fragments.

reigns.tagline: One king, or two names for the same man?

reigns.previously: Sewadjtu dies, leaving almost nothing behind but his name.
paragraphs: Mersekhemre Ined gets about three years in the Turin king list. That would make him one more forgettable king, except for a puzzle. Two statues from Karnak name a king Mersekhemre Neferhotep, usually called Neferhotep II. Same throne name, same era. Ryholt argued they are one and the same man, with Ined as a short or private name.

If he is right, Ined left real monuments at Thebes, the great temple city of the south. Temples there were still being given statues by the kings at Itjtawy. That matters, because Thebes was about to become the heart of Egypt's fight for survival. For now, though, it was still a provincial town loyal to a fading court.

claims.text: Ined and the king of the Karnak statues, Neferhotep II, were the same man.
claims.note: Ryholt's view, from their shared throne name Mersekhemre. Others count two different kings.

reigns.previously: Ined dies after about three years. The court is still at Itjtawy.
paragraphs: Sewadjkare Hori gets about five years in the Turin king list. In this stretch of the 13th Dynasty that counts as a solid reign. Of the man himself, almost nothing is known: no family, no tomb, and only faint traces of his rule outside the list itself.

Kings like Hori ruled from Itjtawy, the capital founded by Amenemhat I nearly 300 years before. The officials still filed their papers. But Avaris in the Delta was growing richer and more independent with every decade, and the kings of the south no longer controlled the trade routes to Canaan that had made the Middle Kingdom wealthy.

paragraphs: Merkawre Sobekhotep was named after Sobek, the crocodile god, like so many kings of his dynasty. Scholars number him Sobekhotep VII, though the numbering of the Sobekhoteps changes from book to book. The Turin king list gives him about two years.

A statue from Karnak carries his names. He is one of the last 13th Dynasty kings with a known name and length. Right after him the Turin papyrus breaks into damaged entries: kings whose names are half lost or whose years are missing. The dynasty was not dead yet. But Egypt was splitting, and the next few kings would leave so little behind that no one can give them a card of their own.
