reigns.title: The Last Kings of the Thirteenth Dynasty
reigns.tagline: Half-erased names as the old kingdom ran out
reigns.cameToPower: Unknown; names lost in the king list
reigns.previously: Sobekhotep VII dies. The king list breaks into lost names.
paragraphs: By about 1655 BC the 13th Dynasty was running on fumes. Over roughly 120 years it had gone through 50 kings or more, from Sobekhotep I and the brothers Neferhotep I and Sobekhotep IV to Merneferre Ay with his 24 years. Now the Turin king list breaks into damaged entries: names with no years, years with no names, and kings like Senusret IV and Dedumose who are known from a stela or two.

Their realm had shrunk to the Nile valley south of Memphis. The eastern Delta answered to Avaris, where rulers of Canaanite descent held power. Later Egyptians remembered this as the moment disaster struck. Manetho, quoted by Josephus, says that under a king he calls Tutimaios 'God was displeased with us', and men of obscure race swept in from the east and took the land without a battle.

The truth was slower. The newcomers had been living in the Delta for generations. But around 1650 BC their chiefs took the title of king and pushed south to Memphis. The court at Itjtawy was finished. In Thebes, local lords carried on, and their line would one day strike back.

claims.text: Manetho's Tutimaios, under whom the invaders came, was the late 13th Dynasty king Dedumose.
claims.note: The names look alike, and Dedumose is attested on stelae from the south. The match is a modern guess.

claims.text: Foreigners took Egypt in a sudden invasion without a fight.
claims.note: Manetho's story, written some 1,400 years later and known only through Josephus. Digs at Avaris show a slow takeover by settlers.

reigns.hook: The kings at Itjtawy are gone. In the Delta, the rulers of Avaris crown themselves. The Egyptians call them rulers of foreign lands, and history will call them the Hyksos.

reigns.title: The Hyksos
reigns.tagline: The foreigners who crowned themselves at Avaris
reigns.previously: Kings come and go fast, and settlers from Canaan fill Avaris.
paragraphs: Their name comes from the Egyptian heqau khasut, 'rulers of foreign lands'. They were West Semitic people from Canaan, and by about 1650 BC their kings, the 15th Dynasty, ruled the north from Avaris in the eastern Delta. This is the Second Intermediate Period: Egypt split again, with foreigners in the north and a line of Theban kings in the south.

The first Hyksos kings are shadowy. Manetho names a founder, Salitis. On the ground, a door jamb from Avaris names a ruler Sakir-Har as 'ruler of foreign lands', and scarabs give names like Semqen and Aperanat. Manetho, quoted by Josephus, describes a savage invasion that burned cities and wrecked temples. The ground tells a quieter tale.

Manfred Bietak's digs at Avaris, today's Tell el-Dab'a, show a Canaanite town growing over generations, with its own temples and graves, some with donkeys buried at the tomb door. Horses and chariots spread in Egypt in this age. In the south a line of Theban kings, Kim Ryholt's 16th Dynasty, held the valley from Hu to Edfu, and a few kinglets may have ruled for a while at Abydos.

claims.text: The Hyksos swept into Egypt in a savage invasion, burning cities as they came.
claims.note: That's Manetho, quoted by Josephus. Excavation at Avaris points instead to settlers already living there gradually taking power.

claims.text: The Hyksos were the Israelites of the Bible's Joseph and Exodus stories.
claims.note: Josephus made the link in the 1st century AD to prove the antiquity of the Jews. No evidence connects the two.

claims.text: The Hyksos brought the horse and chariot to Egypt.
claims.note: Both appear in Egypt around this time, but how much the Hyksos had to do with it is debated.

reigns.hook: The Hyksos hold the north. At Thebes a new line of kings starts up, and one of the first, Djehuti, has himself carved in the red crown of a north he will never rule.

reigns.tagline: Crowned for a north he never ruled
reigns.cameToPower: Followed a king whose name is lost
reigns.reignEnded: Unknown; about 3 years on the throne
reigns.previously: The Hyksos take Memphis, and the old court at Itjtawy falls.
paragraphs: With the Hyksos holding Memphis and the north, the south had to fend for itself. Kim Ryholt's reading of the battered Turin king list finds a new line of kings at Thebes, which he calls the 16th Dynasty. Djehuti, throne name Sekhemre Sementawy, is the first of them whose name survives, and the list gives him three years. Shaw gives no dates for single kings in this age, so the years on these Theban cards are Ryholt's.

His name turns up along the Nile from Deir el-Ballas, north of Thebes, down to Edfu. On a painted block at Edfu he wears the red crown of Lower Egypt, a claim on a north he never ruled. His queen was called Mentuhotep. A chest inscribed as his gift to her, with cosmetic boxes inside, was dug up near Thebes in the 1820s and went to Berlin. It may first have been made for the king's own burial.

claims.text: Djehuti was an early king of a Theban 16th Dynasty.
claims.note: Kim Ryholt's reconstruction, followed by Darrell Baker. Others put him at the very end of the 13th Dynasty or early in the 17th.

claims.text: His queen's coffin carried some of the earliest known Book of the Dead spells.
claims.note: The coffin is lost and known only from copies made by John Gardner Wilkinson around 1832. It may have belonged to a different queen of the same name.

claims.text: The unfinished southern pyramid at South Saqqara was built for him.
claims.note: Based on a scrap of inscription that may be part of his Horus name. The pyramid lies far north of the stretch of Nile where he is attested.

reigns.hook: Djehuti is gone after three years. His successor, Sobekhotep VIII, will walk into a flooded temple at Karnak and play the god who ordered the waters back.

images.alt: Line drawing of a carved block: a king in the tall red crown receives the ankh sign of life from a god, with hieroglyphs above

reigns.tagline: The king who waded into the flood at Karnak
reigns.reignEnded: Unknown; 16 years in the Turin list
reigns.previously: Djehuti dies after three years on the Theban throne.
paragraphs: Sobekhotep VIII, throne name Sekhemre Seusertawy, is known from a single stone, but it is a good one. In the last days of his fourth year the Nile rose so high that it swamped the temple, probably Karnak. His stela tells how the king came to the flooded hall. John Baines reads the scene as the king playing the creator god, who drove the waters back from the first mound of dry land at the beginning of the world.

The stela survived because later builders broke it up and packed it inside the Third Pylon at Karnak during Amenhotep III's works, as fill. If Ryholt has matched him to the right entry in the Turin list, Sobekhotep reigned 16 years. That may be generous, as nothing else of his has been found. All the while the Hyksos held Memphis and pressed on the south.

claims.text: Sobekhotep VIII reigned for 16 years.
claims.note: Ryholt matches him to a damaged Turin list entry 'Sekhemre...' with 16 years. His only dated object is from his year 4.

claims.text: On the stela the king acts out the creation of the world.
claims.note: John Baines's reading. The stela itself records the flood and the king's visit to the temple.

claims.text: He belonged to the Theban 16th Dynasty.
claims.note: Ryholt and Darrell Baker say so; Jürgen von Beckerath and Labib Habachi placed him in the 13th Dynasty.

reigns.hook: After Sobekhotep, the Turin list gives Neferhotep III a single year. He will call Thebes 'my city' and boast of saving it from famine and foreigners.

images.alt: Line drawing of a stela scene: a king on the left faces Hapi, the Nile flood god, on the right, with hieroglyphs between them

reigns.tagline: He fed Thebes and called it 'my city'
reigns.reignEnded: Unknown; about a year on the throne
reigns.previously: Sobekhotep VIII dies; the Turin list gives him 16 years.
paragraphs: Neferhotep III's throne name, Sekhemre Sankhtawy, means roughly 'the might of Ra who nourishes the Two Lands'. It was not idle talk. On his one surviving stela, found at Thebes and now in Cairo, he boasts that he fed his city and saved it from famine. Hunger stalked Upper Egypt in these years.

The same stela says he raised his city up after it had sunk in strife with foreigners, most likely the Hyksos pushing south. He calls himself the guide of victorious Thebes, and over and over he calls it 'my city'. The text also gives the earliest known mention of the khepresh, the blue crown later worn by New Kingdom kings at war. The Turin list gives him a single year.

claims.text: The foreigners Thebes fought in his reign were the Hyksos.
claims.note: The stela names no enemy. Ryholt reads it as war with the Hyksos 15th Dynasty, which fits the times.

claims.text: His stela holds the earliest known mention of the khepresh crown.
claims.note: So scholars read the badly damaged text. A crude stela of the Abydos king Snaaib shows the crown being worn at about the same time.

reigns.hook: Neferhotep III is gone within a year. Another short-lived king, Mentuhotepi, takes over and hails Thebes as mistress of the entire land.

reigns.tagline: A one-year king who swore Thebes was his
reigns.reignEnded: Unknown; about a year on the throne
reigns.previously: Neferhotep III dies after a single year as king.
paragraphs: Seankhenre Mentuhotepi held Thebes for about a year, if Ryholt has read the torn Turin list rightly. He says so himself on a stela from Karnak: 'I am the king within Thebes, this is my city.' He hails Thebes as mistress of the entire land and city of triumph, bold words for a realm that ran only a short way up and down the Nile.

He claims he drove back the foreign lands, probably the Hyksos, though perhaps the Nubians to the south. His stela likens him to Sekhmet, the lioness goddess who burns her enemies with her fiery breath. Two limestone sphinxes of his were found at Edfu in 1924, one carved with each of his names. Older books call him Mentuhotep VI or VII.

claims.text: The 'foreign lands' he drove back were the Hyksos.
claims.note: His stela does not name them. Most read it as the Hyksos; the Nubians are the other candidate.

claims.text: He reigned only about a year.
claims.note: The Turin list entry is damaged, and Ryholt restores its name as Seankhenre. Older scholars put him in the 17th Dynasty.

reigns.hook: After Mentuhotepi comes Nebiriau I, the one king of this Theban line to last for decades. In his first year a provincial governor sells his job to pay off a debt in gold.

images.alt: Line drawing of a damaged stone sphinx, with a royal name in a cartouche carved between its front legs

reigns.tagline: Twenty-six years of calm in a broken land
reigns.reignEnded: Unknown; 26 years in the Turin list
reigns.previously: Mentuhotepi, the 'king within Thebes', dies after a year.
paragraphs: Nebiriau I, throne name Sewadjenre, is the one king of this Theban line who lasted. The Turin list gives him 26 years, and he seems to have had some peace. His realm reached at least from Hu in the north to Edfu in the south. A copper dagger with his name came out of a cemetery at Hu, found by Flinders Petrie in the 1890s.

His best monument is a legal record. The Juridical Stela, dated to his first year and found at Karnak in 1927, tells how Kebsi, governor of Elkab, owed 60 deben of gold, about 5.5 kg, to his relative Sobeknakht. Unable to pay, Kebsi sold him the governorship. The vizier checked that Kebsi really was the heir to the office, and the deal was sealed before witnesses.

Two of his seals turned up at Lisht, inside Hyksos territory, a hint of contact across the frontier. They are of clay and frit, not the usual steatite, as if no expeditions went out to the desert quarries. His namesake Nebiriau II, perhaps a son, followed him but left nothing except his name.

claims.text: Nebiriau I reigned 26 years.
claims.note: That is the Turin list figure. His highest dated object is from year 1, and finds are thin for so long a reign.

claims.text: Nebiriau II was his son.
claims.note: Assumed from the rare shared name. No source says so.

claims.text: His seals at Lisht show dealings with the Hyksos.
claims.note: Two seals were found there, inside the Hyksos realm, but how they got there is unknown.

reigns.hook: While Nebiriau rules Thebes, the north belongs to a far grander king. At Avaris, the Hyksos ruler Khyan calls himself son of Ra and sends his name as far as Crete and Baghdad.

reigns.tagline: The Hyksos king whose name went round the world
reigns.previously: Nebiriau I holds Thebes; the Hyksos at Avaris grow stronger.
paragraphs: Seuserenre Khyan is the best known of the Hyksos kings, and he travelled further than any of them, at least on paper. A granite lion with his name turned up in Baghdad. A stone lid with his name was found in the palace at Knossos on Crete. Shaw puts him about 1600 BC.

At first he called himself 'heqa khasut', ruler of foreign lands, the old Egyptian label that became our word Hyksos. Later he took the full titles of a pharaoh, including 'son of Ra'. A stela from Avaris calls a man named Yanassi 'eldest king's son' of Khyan. Yanassi may have reigned after him briefly, but the crown went to Apepi.

In 2011 a team led by Nadine Moeller reported sealings of Khyan at Edfu, deep in the south. They lay in the same building as sealings of the 13th Dynasty king Sobekhotep IV. If the two really were near neighbours in time, the dates of this whole age need a shake-up.

claims.text: Objects with Khyan's name reached Crete and Mesopotamia.
claims.note: The lid from Knossos is in the Heraklion museum and the lion from Baghdad is in the British Museum. How they got there, by trade, gift or later looting, is unknown.

claims.text: Khyan's sealings at Edfu show he lived much closer in time to Sobekhotep IV than the usual dates allow.
claims.note: Moeller and Marouard argued this from the find. Others think old sealings were simply kept and thrown out together.

reigns.hook: At Thebes a new king, Bebiankh, sends miners to the Red Sea hills. At Avaris, Khyan dies, his son's hopes fade, and Apepi is waiting for the throne.

reigns.tagline: A Theban king who dug for ore by the Red Sea
reigns.reignEnded: Unknown; 12 years in the Turin list
reigns.previously: Khyan rules at Avaris; at Thebes, Nebiriau's heirs barely last.
paragraphs: After Nebiriau I, Thebes went through two kings in quick succession: Nebiriau II, known only from his name, and Semenre, known from one bronze axe head. Then came Bebiankh, throne name Seuserenre, and the Turin list gives him 12 years. For a king of this shrunken realm he left a surprising amount behind.

He sent men to Gebel Zeit on the Red Sea coast, where miners dug galena, the lead ore Egyptians ground into black eye paint, and they left a modest stela with his names. He added to the temple of the war god Montu at Medamud, just north of Thebes. A bronze dagger from Naqada, now in the British Museum, reads 'Son of Ra, Bebiankh, given life'.

Danger came from the south too. In the tomb of Sobeknakht II at Elkab, son of the man who bought the governorship under Nebiriau, an inscription tells how 'vile Kush' came north with Nubians, Puntites and Medjay. Some date that raid to Bebiankh's reign or just after.

claims.text: Kush invaded Upper Egypt in Bebiankh's time.
claims.note: Sobeknakht II's tomb text, published by Vivian Davies in 2003, names no king. Chris Bennett dates it to Bebiankh's reign or soon after.

claims.text: The Hyksos ended the Theban 16th Dynasty by taking Thebes.
claims.note: Ryholt's view. After Bebiankh the Turin list loses its names, and a new Theban line, the 17th Dynasty, appears around 1580 BC.

reigns.hook: Bebiankh's line is running out of time. In Avaris a new Hyksos king, Apepi, takes the throne, and he will rule the north for some forty years.

reigns.tagline: The Hyksos king who faced the Theban fightback
reigns.reignEnded: Reigned on as Thebes rose up
reigns.previously: Bebiankh rules Thebes; at Avaris, Khyan dies and Apepi steps in.
paragraphs: Apepi, whom the Greeks called Apophis, ruled the north from Avaris for about 40 years. He used three different throne names over that time and styled himself in full Egyptian fashion. In his 33rd year a scribe called Ahmose copied out a book of maths problems, fractions, pyramid slopes and grain sums. We call it the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, and it is now in the British Museum.

For decades he was master of Egypt. The Theban kings in the south seem to have paid him tribute, and his traders worked the whole Nile. He even took an old statue of the 13th Dynasty general-king Imyremeshaw and carved his own name on it. But Thebes was getting restless, and a later tale makes Apepi the one who picked the fight.

Shaw ends Apepi's reign about 1555 BC, so he outlived this card. He saw out Seqenenre Tao and faced Kamose too, whose men caught his messenger carrying a letter to the king of Kush. The last Hyksos king, Khamudi, reigned only briefly before Avaris fell.

claims.text: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus was copied in Apepi's 33rd year.
claims.note: The scribe Ahmose dates his copy to that year and says he worked from an older original of Amenemhat III's time.

claims.text: Apepi started the war by complaining about Theban hippos.
claims.note: From 'The Quarrel of Apophis and Seqenenre', written down centuries later. The papyrus breaks off before the end.

claims.text: Kamose's stela says his men caught Apepi's messenger with a letter asking the ruler of Kush to attack Thebes.
claims.note: The letter is quoted on Kamose's own victory stela at Karnak, which says his men caught the messenger.

reigns.hook: Apepi rules the north for decades. But go back to about 1580 BC, far up the Nile, where a Theban king named Rahotep is patching up temples the war has wrecked.

reigns.tagline: A Theban king with a broken country to mend
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Unknown; first of a new Theban line
reigns.previously: Apepi rules the north from Avaris, and Thebes bides its time.
paragraphs: While Apepi ruled the north from Avaris, Thebes had kings of its own. Rahotep may have been the first of them, the founder of what Manetho called the 17th Dynasty. He was a small king with a small realm, the Nile valley from around Abydos southward. Shaw gives no dates for single kings in this age, so the years on this card are only a rough fit, about 1580 BC.

What he left behind is a builder's boast. A stela found at Coptos says the king saw that the gates and doors of the temple of the god Min had fallen into ruin, and set his courtiers to put them right. At Abydos he renewed the walls of the temple of Osiris. A limestone stela in the British Museum, dated to his first year, shows him making offerings to Osiris for two of his officials.

Why were the temples in ruins? Nobody knows. Some think the Hyksos had raided the south and wrecked them. Others think the Theban kings were Apepi's vassals all along and the buildings had simply crumbled. Either way, Rahotep's line clung on, and the next kings took their names from Sobek, the crocodile god.

claims.text: Rahotep founded the 17th Dynasty at Thebes.
claims.note: That is Kim Ryholt's reconstruction. Others put him second in the line, or even back in the 13th Dynasty. He is missing from the Turin king list.

claims.text: He rebuilt temples the Hyksos had wrecked.
claims.note: His stela says the temple of Min had fallen into ruin but never says why. A Hyksos raid on the south is a modern theory.

claims.text: A late New Kingdom ghost story names a dead man who served as Rahotep's treasurer.
claims.note: The tale of Khonsuemheb and the Ghost has the ghost claim the job, but other details in it do not fit any known king, so it may be garbled.

reigns.hook: Rahotep's line holds on at Thebes. The next king, Sobekemsaf, will send men across the desert for stone and give his statues a long, proud stare.

images.alt: Line drawing of a carved stela: a king with raised arms makes an offering to the god Osiris, with two officials behind him and rows of hieroglyphs

reigns.tagline: The crocodile-god king who rebuilt Medamud
reigns.previously: Rahotep dies, after mending temples at Coptos and Abydos.
paragraphs: Sekhemre Wadjkhau Sobekemsaf was one of the busier Theban kings. His name means 'Sobek protects him', after the crocodile god. In his seventh year he sent a quarrying expedition into the Eastern Desert, to the dark stone of Wadi Hammamat, and the men carved his names on the rocks. At Medamud, just north of Thebes, he rebuilt the temple of the war god Montu, and a fine relief of him offering to the god still survives.

His statues show real money behind the throne. A red granite seated king in the British Museum carries his name. In the temple of Osiris at Abydos another statue showed a small boy standing between the king's legs: a King's Son, also called Sobekemsaf. Placing him there marked him out as the heir.

We know a little of his family. His chief wife was Queen Nubemhat, and their daughter married a king's son named Ameny. How long he reigned in the end is unknown. Shaw gives no dates for single kings here, so this card's years are only a rough fit.

claims.text: Sobekemsaf I reigned at least seven years.
claims.note: A rock inscription at Wadi Hammamat is dated to his year 7. No higher date is known.

claims.text: The prince on the Abydos statue became the next king, Sobekemsaf II.
claims.note: Daniel Polz and others think so. Kim Ryholt orders the kings differently, so even the numbers I and II are argued over.

reigns.hook: The little prince on the statue grows up. As Sobekemsaf II he will reign at Thebes and be buried in a pyramid, where tomb robbers will find him 450 years later.

reigns.tagline: Buried in gold, then robbed 450 years later
reigns.previously: Sobekemsaf I dies, with his son already named as heir.
paragraphs: Sekhemre Shedtawy Sobekemsaf took a throne name that says a lot about his times: 'Powerful is Ra, Rescuer of the Two Lands'. He was probably the young prince shown on his father's statue at Abydos. His own reign left only scraps: a painted block at Abydos with his names, a stela of a temple scribe, a ring. Shaw gives no dates for single kings here, so this card's years are only a rough fit.

He mattered most as a father. A door jamb from a desert temple on the road west of Thebes names a king Sobekemsaf as the father of King Intef, and two of his sons, both named Intef, would follow him on the throne. He was buried in a small pyramid at Dra Abu el-Naga in western Thebes, with his queen, Nubkhaes, in a chamber beside him.

About 450 years later, under Ramesses IX, a stonemason named Amenpanefer and his gang tunnelled into that pyramid. His confession survives. They found the king covered in gold, with a golden headpiece and amulets at his neck, stripped him and his queen, then set fire to their coffins. They were caught and put on trial.

claims.text: Tomb robbers stripped the gold from his mummy and burned his coffins.
claims.note: Amenpanefer's confession is preserved in the Leopold-Amherst Papyrus, and the inspection of the tomb in the Abbott Papyrus, both from Ramesses IX's reign.

claims.text: He was the father of Intef V and Intef VI.
claims.note: The door jamb names a King Sobekemsaf as father of an Intef but does not say which Sobekemsaf. Ryholt, Polz and Dodson all lean this way.

claims.text: The robbers' loot came to 160 deben of gold, about 14.5 kg.
claims.note: That is the figure Amenpanefer gives in his confession. Men in fear of execution may not have counted honestly.

reigns.hook: Sobekemsaf is laid in his pyramid. His elder son takes the throne as Intef, but he will not have long, and his brother is waiting with a coffin.

reigns.tagline: The elder brother, buried by the younger
reigns.previously: Sobekemsaf II is laid in his pyramid at Dra Abu el-Naga.
paragraphs: Sekhemre Wepmaat Intef called himself Intef-aa, 'Intef the Great', though his reign was probably short. He was a king's son by the king's chief wife, which makes him the obvious heir. Hardly anything from his reign survives except the things made for his burial. Shaw gives no dates for single kings here, so this card's years are only a rough fit.

Those burial goods tell the story. His coffin, now in the Louvre, is a rishi coffin, carved all over with feathers so the dead king lies wrapped in a bird's wings. Its inscription says it was given by his brother, King Intef. So the younger brother buried the elder and took his throne. The capstone of Intef-aa's small pyramid, with his name on it, is in the British Museum.

His pyramid itself is lost. Fragments of that capstone turned up in 2003 near his brother's pyramid at Dra Abu el-Naga, so it must have stood close by. In the 1800s local villagers found the coffin, and inside lay a papyrus, the Prisse Papyrus, holding some of the oldest wisdom texts in Egyptian literature.

claims.text: His coffin says it was a gift from his brother, King Intef.
claims.note: The inscription on Louvre coffin E 3019 says so, and the spelling fits Nubkheperre Intef. That is why the brother is thought to have succeeded him.

claims.text: The Prisse Papyrus was found inside his coffin.
claims.note: That is the usual account, but the coffin and papyrus were found by locals and sold off, and the details of the find are poorly recorded.

reigns.hook: Intef the Great is buried. His younger brother, Nubkheperre Intef, takes the crown and becomes the best-known Theban king of the age, and a frightening one to cross.

reigns.tagline: Builder, curse-writer, and the strongest Intef
reigns.reignEnded: Died; buried under a small pyramid
reigns.previously: Intef the Great dies. His brother buries him in a feathered coffin.
paragraphs: Nubkheperre Intef is the best attested king of the 17th Dynasty, named on more than twenty monuments from Abydos to Edfu. He built and rebuilt temples all over his realm, from a chapel for the god Min at Coptos to a new temple out on a desert road west of Thebes. His wife was named Sobekemsaf, and a son of his, Nakht, was head of the bowmen. Shaw gives no dates for single kings here, so this card's years are only a rough fit.

His most famous text is a curse. In his third year a temple official at Coptos named Teti, son of Minhotep, was found guilty of an offence against the god's temple. Nubkheperre had him thrown out of the temple, gave his job to the governor Minemhat, and laid a curse on anyone who ever tried to restore him or his family. The decree was carved in stone at the temple.

He was buried at Dra Abu el-Naga under a small, steep mudbrick pyramid. Robbers tunnelled in under Ramesses IX, but the inspectors found they had failed to reach him. Others did better in 1827, and his gilded coffin went to the British Museum. The tomb was then lost until Daniel Polz's German team found it again in 2001.

claims.text: Nubkheperre reigned much longer than three years.
claims.note: Year 3, on the Coptos decree, is his only known date. His many buildings and his tomb suggest a longer reign, but no figure survives.

claims.text: Ramesside inspectors found his tomb untouched.
claims.note: The Abbott Papyrus says robbers had tunnelled into the pyramid but had not reached the king, and records it as intact.

reigns.hook: Nubkheperre dies. A third Intef, Sekhemre Heruhirmaat, steps up, and his name barely survives at all.

reigns.tagline: The last Intef, a king of months
reigns.previously: Nubkheperre Intef dies, the strongest king Thebes has had.
paragraphs: Sekhemre Heruhirmaat Intef is the most shadowy of the three Intefs. His throne name, 'Powerful is Ra, Horus who is on his truth', survives on a coffin and on a block from Coptos. Even his number is a mess: some books call him Intef VII, others Intef VIII. Shaw gives no dates for single kings here, so this card's year is only a rough fit, and his reign may have lasted only months.

Where does he fit? Daniel Polz, who dug the Intef pyramids, puts him just after Nubkheperre, a short-lived king before a new family took over. The fine handwriting on his coffin matches Nubkheperre's way of spelling the name Intef, which ties the two together. After him the Intef line ends, and the throne passes to a man named Ahmose.

claims.text: Heruhirmaat Intef reigned only a few months.
claims.note: Nothing dated to his reign survives, which suggests it was very short. That is an argument from silence.

claims.text: He was Nubkheperre Intef's son.
claims.note: A guess from his place in the sequence and the spelling of his name. No text names his parents.

reigns.hook: The Intefs are finished. The new king, Senakhtenre Ahmose, starts a family that will one day throw the Hyksos out of Egypt, though he will not live to see it.

reigns.tagline: Grandfather of a conqueror, nearly lost to history
reigns.previously: Heruhirmaat Intef dies, and with him the line of the Intefs.
paragraphs: Senakhtenre Ahmose, sometimes called Ahmose the Elder, is the quiet first link in a famous chain. His wife was very probably Tetisheri, a commoner's daughter who lived to be honoured as the grandmother of the conqueror Ahmose I. Their son was most likely Seqenenre Tao, the next king. Shaw gives no dates for single kings here, so this card's years are only a rough fit; his reign seems to have been short.

For a long time he was little more than a throne name in a king list. Then in 2012 the Egyptologist Sebastien Biston-Moulin published a limestone door lintel from Karnak carrying both his names, and his personal name turned out to be Ahmose, the same as his famous grandson. He was building in the great temple of Amun, a sign Thebes was growing in confidence.

His tomb has never been found, and no mummy can be pinned on him. When he died, after what seems to have been a short reign, the crown passed to Seqenenre, who was about to receive a very strange message from Avaris.

claims.text: Tetisheri was his wife and Seqenenre his son.
claims.note: No text names Tetisheri's husband. A stela of Ahmose I at Abydos calls her the mother of his father and mother; the rest is the best fit.

claims.text: His personal name was Ahmose.
claims.note: A door lintel from Karnak, published by Sebastien Biston-Moulin in 2012, gives both his throne name and the name Ahmose.

reigns.hook: Senakhtenre is dead. Seqenenre Tao, most likely his son, becomes king at Thebes, and from Avaris comes a complaint about some very noisy hippos.

reigns.tagline: Noisy hippos, a war, and a king struck down
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by blows to the head
reigns.previously: Senakhtenre dies after a short reign. Thebes is ready to fight.
paragraphs: The story goes like this. Apepi, king at Avaris, sends a messenger all the way south to Thebes with a complaint: the hippos in Seqenenre's pool are making so much noise that Apepi can't sleep. Avaris is hundreds of miles away. It's an insult dressed up as an order, and Seqenenre and his court are left speechless. Then the papyrus breaks off, just as it's getting good.

The tale was written down long after, but it seems to remember a real clash, because Seqenenre's own body shows how he died. His mummy, found in the royal cache at Deir el-Bahri that came to light in 1881, has terrible head wounds from an axe, a spear or dagger, and a club. He was about 40. Some of the wounds match the shape of axes used by the Hyksos.

Did he fall in battle, or die some other way? A 2021 CT study by Sahar Saleem and Zahi Hawass argued that his hands had been tied, and that he was captured and executed on the battlefield. Not everyone agrees. Either way, Thebes was now at war with Avaris, and the fight passed to the next king, Kamose.

claims.text: Apepi picked a quarrel by complaining that Theban hippos were keeping him awake.
claims.note: From 'The Quarrel of Apophis and Seqenenre', a tale on a papyrus written centuries later. It breaks off before the end.

claims.text: Seqenenre was captured and executed on the battlefield.
claims.note: The 2021 CT study by Saleem and Hawass reads his hands as bound. Others think he simply died fighting, or was attacked in his sleep.

claims.text: He was killed by Hyksos weapons.
claims.note: Some wounds match Hyksos-style axes, but Egyptian and foreign weapons of the time were not always so different.

reigns.hook: Seqenenre is dead, killed by enemy blows. Kamose takes the throne at Thebes, and his advisers beg him to keep the peace.

reigns.tagline: He refused to share Egypt, and caught a spy to prove it
reigns.previously: Seqenenre Tao dies of terrible head wounds, probably in battle.
paragraphs: Kamose told his own story on two stelae at Karnak, and it starts with a grumble. What use is being king, he asks, when he sits wedged between a foreigner at Avaris and a Nubian in Kush, each holding a slice of Egypt? His councillors told him to stay put. Things were fine as they were, they said, and the Hyksos weren't troubling Thebes. Kamose wouldn't hear it.

He sailed north with his army, wrecking towns that had sided with the Hyksos, and came right up to Avaris. On the way his men caught a messenger on a desert road, carrying a letter from Apepi to the new ruler of Kush. It urged the Nubian to attack while Kamose was busy in the north, so they could crush him between them and share out Egypt. Kamose sent the messenger back to Apepi.

Then, after only a few years as king, Kamose died. How, nobody knows. His painted wooden coffin was found at Dra Abu el-Naga in 1857, but the mummy inside is said to have fallen to pieces. The war was not over. It passed to Seqenenre's son Ahmose, still a boy.

claims.text: Kamose fought his way to the walls of Avaris.
claims.note: His stela boasts of it, but he plainly didn't take the city, and how far he really got is hard to judge.

claims.text: His mummy crumbled to pieces soon after the coffin was found.
claims.note: That is the usual account of the 1857 find, but records of it are thin.

claims.text: Kamose was Seqenenre's son.
claims.note: Some make him Seqenenre's brother, or Ahmose's elder brother. No text spells out how they were related.

reigns.hook: Kamose is dead and Thebes waits on a boy king, Ahmose. Up at Avaris, Apepi has a successor too, Khamudi, and he is about to find out what Thebes can do.

reigns.tagline: The last Hyksos king, with the Thebans at the gates
reigns.reignEnded: Avaris fell to Ahmose; fate unknown
reigns.previously: Kamose dies with Avaris still standing. Ahmose is a boy king.
paragraphs: Khamudi was the last of the Hyksos kings, Apepi's successor at Avaris. He is almost a ghost. His name sits at the end of the Hyksos kings in the Turin king list, and hardly anything else from his reign is known for certain. He came to the throne about the time Kamose was marching north, so his first years were spent with a Theban army loose on the Nile.

Then Thebes came back. The young Ahmose I sailed north with his fleet and laid siege to Avaris. A soldier named Ahmose son of Ebana, whose tomb at Elkab tells his life story, fought there more than once and won the king's 'gold of valour' for it. A note scrawled on the back of the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus records Heliopolis being taken in an 11th year, and the fortress of Sile after it, as an army closed in.

Avaris fell. The Hyksos who got away retreated to Sharuhen in southern Canaan, where Ahmose besieged them for three years. What happened to Khamudi himself, nobody knows. With his fall the 15th Dynasty ended, and Egypt was one kingdom again.

claims.text: The '11th year' on the Rhind Papyrus is Khamudi's.
claims.note: The note names no king. Many scholars think it is Khamudi's year, as Ahmose's army advanced, which would mean he reigned longer than Shaw's five years. Others give it to Ahmose.

claims.text: Khamudi is named in the Turin king list.
claims.note: The papyrus is badly broken. Kim Ryholt reads the last Hyksos name as Khamudi, and most now follow him.

reigns.hook: Khamudi holds Avaris, but not for long. In Thebes the boy Ahmose is growing up, and his mother is getting the army ready.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who drove out the Hyksos
reigns.previously: Khamudi holds Avaris, the last Hyksos king. Thebes has a boy king.
paragraphs: Ahmose was young when he became king, and in the early years others held things together. A stela at Karnak praises his mother, Queen Ahhotep, for caring for Egypt's soldiers, bringing back deserters and calming the south. Once Ahmose was grown, he went north to finish the war his father and Kamose had started. This is the founding of the 18th Dynasty and the start of the New Kingdom.

We know the campaign through an ordinary soldier. Ahmose son of Ebana, a fighting man from Elkab, had his life story carved in his tomb, and he keeps count of his rewards: gold for bravery, captives as slaves, and the hands he cut off dead enemies to prove each kill. He was there when Avaris fell. Then the army chased the Hyksos into southern Canaan and laid siege to Sharuhen for three years until it fell.

Ahmose turned south to Nubia too, and by the end of his reign, about 25 years later, Egypt was whole and on the road to empire. A strange stela from his time describes a terrible storm with rain and darkness. His queen, Ahmose-Nefertari, outlived him and was later worshipped as a goddess. Their son Amenhotep took the throne.

claims.text: Queen Ahhotep led Egypt's troops herself.
claims.note: The Karnak stela praises her for looking after the army and calming rebels. Gold flies, a military award, were found in a queen Ahhotep's burial, but there were two queens of that name and it's unclear whose it was.

claims.text: The storm on the Tempest Stela was the fallout of the volcanic eruption of Thera.
claims.note: An exciting idea, but the eruption's date is uncertain and the stela may describe a local storm, or use storm imagery for chaos.

claims.text: Ahmose son of Ebana fought at the fall of Avaris and the siege of Sharuhen.
claims.note: His tomb autobiography at Elkab tells it in his own words, listing every reward he won.

reigns.hook: Ahmose is gone and Egypt is whole. His son Amenhotep I inherits a quiet kingdom, and the workmen of Thebes are about to make him a saint.

reigns.tagline: The quiet king the tomb-builders turned into a god
reigns.previously: Ahmose has thrown out the Hyksos. Egypt is whole again and rising.
paragraphs: After his father's wars, Amenhotep I got something rare: about 20 fairly calm years. He was the son of Ahmose and Queen Ahmose-Nefertari, and his mother stayed a power at court for much of his reign. He built at Karnak, sent troops up the Nile into Nubia and kept the new state running. The records of his deeds are thin. His real legacy lay in one small village.

That was Deir el-Medina, home of the men who cut and painted the royal tombs at Thebes. Amenhotep and his mother became its patron saints, worshipped there for centuries after their deaths. When villagers fell out over a donkey, a debt or a stolen pot, they took the case to the deified king. Priests carried his statue out, and it gave its verdict by moving.

His mummy was rewrapped by priests about 3,000 years ago and has never been unwrapped since. In 2021 Sahar Saleem and Zahi Hawass unwrapped it digitally, with a CT scanner, without touching a bandage. Amenhotep left no surviving son. The crown passed to Thutmose, a tough army man.

claims.text: Amenhotep I founded the tomb-builders' village at Deir el-Medina.
claims.note: The villagers honoured him as their founder, but the oldest bricks there stamped with a king's name belong to Thutmose I.

claims.text: The deified king settled villagers' disputes as an oracle.
claims.note: Ostraca from Deir el-Medina record questions put to his statue and the answers it gave, for centuries after his death.

claims.text: The CT scan showed he died at about 35, with no sign of a violent death.
claims.note: Saleem and Hawass, Frontiers in Medicine, 2021. The age is an estimate from his bones and teeth.

reigns.hook: Amenhotep dies without a son. The new king, Thutmose, is a career soldier, and he wants to find out just how far Egypt's chariots can go.

reigns.tagline: The soldier king who planted a stone by the Euphrates
reigns.previously: Amenhotep I dies with no son. A soldier, Thutmose, takes the throne.
paragraphs: Thutmose I was probably not born into the main royal line. He seems to have been an army man, and once crowned he went looking for a fight. He sailed far up the Nile and smashed the kingdom of Kush. The soldier Ahmose son of Ebana, who was there, says the king came home with a Nubian chief hanging head-down from the prow of his ship.

Then he turned north-east. He marched through Canaan and Syria all the way to the Euphrates, a river that seemed to run backwards to Egyptian eyes, flowing south instead of north. On its bank he set up a stela to mark the edge of his world. Two generations later his grandson Thutmose III found it and set his own beside it.

He was probably the first king buried in the Valley of the Kings. His official Ineni dug the tomb and bragged that it was done with no one seeing and no one hearing. With his chief queen, Ahmose, he had a daughter, Hatshepsut. With a lesser wife, Mutnofret, he had a son, Thutmose II, who took the throne and married his half-sister.

claims.text: He sailed home with a Nubian chief hanging from the prow of his ship.
claims.note: Only Ahmose son of Ebana tells it, in his tomb autobiography at Elkab. An eyewitness, but a soldier who liked a boast.

claims.text: Thutmose I was the first king buried in the Valley of the Kings.
claims.note: Which tomb Ineni dug is still argued over, and the king's body was moved at least once in antiquity.

claims.text: He set up a stela on the bank of the Euphrates.
claims.note: Thutmose III's Annals at Karnak say he placed his own stela beside his grandfather's. Neither stone has been found.

reigns.hook: Thutmose II takes the throne, but he won't last long. Beside him stands his wife and half-sister, Hatshepsut, and she has plans of her own.

reigns.tagline: Husband of Hatshepsut
reigns.previously: Thutmose I dies after pushing Egypt's borders to the Euphrates.
paragraphs: Thutmose II was the son of Thutmose I by a lesser wife, and married his half-sister Hatshepsut to strengthen his claim. His reign was short, and historians still argue whether it lasted three years or thirteen.
His generals put down a revolt in Nubia in his name. When he died, his heir Thutmose III was a small child, and his widow Hatshepsut stepped in as regent.
reigns.hook: The new king is a toddler, and his stepmother Hatshepsut takes charge.

reigns.tagline: The queen who made herself king, false beard and all
reigns.reignEnded: Died; her images smashed years later
reigns.previously: Thutmose II dies young. His heir is a small boy, Thutmose III.
paragraphs: In 1479 BC her husband and half-brother Thutmose II died young. The heir was his small son by a lesser wife, Iset. The boy was crowned as Thutmose III, and Hatshepsut ran Egypt as his regent. Around 1473 BC she went further and had herself crowned king. The boy stayed king all along, and his reign is counted from 1479 BC, but for the next 15 years she was the senior king.

A woman king needed a story, and she carved one. Reliefs in her temple show the god Amun visiting her mother and fathering her. Her statues show her as a male king, false beard and all. Her temple, Djeser-djeseru, rises in terraces against the cliffs of Deir el-Bahri. Its walls show her fleet sailing to Punt and coming home with incense trees in pots, watched by Punt's very stout queen.

She raised two obelisks at Karnak, and one still stands. Her steward Senenmut, tutor to her daughter Neferure, rose from nowhere to huge power. When she died around 1458 BC, Thutmose III took over. About 20 years later her statues were smashed and her name chiselled off, probably to clear the way for his son Amenhotep II.

claims.text: Senenmut was Hatshepsut's lover.
claims.note: It rests mostly on a crude graffito in a quarry tomb near Deir el-Bahri. Nobody knows who drew it or whom it shows.

claims.text: Thutmose III wiped out her memory out of hatred.
claims.note: The attacks began some 20 years after her death, late in his reign. Securing his son's succession fits better than revenge.

claims.text: Her mummy was identified in 2007 by a single tooth.
claims.note: A molar in a box bearing her name matched a gap in a mummy from tomb KV60. Not every expert is convinced.

reigns.hook: Hatshepsut is dead, and the king she pushed aside is now a grown man. Thutmose III is about to make up for lost time, at the head of an army.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who waited 20 years, then conquered
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Thutmose II and Iset
reigns.previously: Hatshepsut dies after some 20 years in power.
paragraphs: Thutmose III had been king since 1479 BC, when he was a small child, and his years are counted from then. Only in 1458 BC did he rule alone. He wasted no time. In 1457 BC Canaanite princes led by the king of Kadesh gathered at Megiddo. His generals begged him to take a safe road. He chose the narrow Aruna pass instead, marched the army through in single file and burst out to surprise the enemy.

The enemy fled inside Megiddo, and he besieged it for seven months until it gave in. That was the first of about 17 campaigns in Canaan and Syria, written up in his Annals at Karnak. He even had boats carried overland to cross the Euphrates. At Karnak he carved the strange plants and animals he had seen abroad, a stone botanical garden. James Henry Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt.

Two of his obelisks from Heliopolis now stand in London and New York, both nicknamed Cleopatra's Needle. Late in life he made his son Amenhotep II co-ruler, and around then Hatshepsut's name was hacked off her monuments. He died around 1425 BC, 54 years after he was first crowned.

claims.text: He beat the enemy at Megiddo by marching through the Aruna pass against his generals' advice.
claims.note: The story comes from his own Annals at Karnak, drawn from a war diary. The heroic framing is the king's.

claims.text: His general Djehuty took Joppa by smuggling soldiers into the city in baskets.
claims.note: Told in Papyrus Harris 500, written down long after. Djehuty was real, but the tale reads like Ali Baba.

claims.text: He crossed the Euphrates with boats dragged overland from the coast.
claims.note: His own inscriptions, including a stela at Gebel Barkal, say so. The details can't be checked.

reigns.hook: The great conqueror dies. His son Amenhotep II takes over, a strapping athlete who wants everyone to know just how strong he is.

reigns.tagline: The strongman king who wanted the world to know it
reigns.previously: Thutmose III dies after 54 years as king, Egypt's greatest conqueror.
paragraphs: Amenhotep II was about 18 when he was first crowned, as junior partner to his ageing father Thutmose III, so Shaw counts his reign from 1427 BC. From about 1425 BC he ruled alone. He wanted everyone to know how strong he was. A stela he set up beside the Great Sphinx says nobody else could draw his bow, that he out-rowed 200 sailors, and that he shot arrows clean through thick copper targets from a racing chariot.

He took the army into Syria early in his reign. His Amada stela in Nubia says he sailed home with seven captured princes hanging head-down from the prow of his ship. Six were hung on the walls of Thebes. The seventh went up the Nile to hang on the walls of Napata, as a warning to the south. After that the wars died down, and his scribes boasted that the great kings of the north sent gifts.

He died around 1400 BC and was buried in tomb KV35 in the Valley of the Kings. In 1898 the French archaeologist Victor Loret opened it and found the king still lying in his own sarcophagus. In a side room lay a stash of other royal mummies, hidden there by priests centuries later to save them from robbers. One of them was his son, who had followed him as Thutmose IV.

claims.text: Amenhotep II out-rowed 200 sailors and shot arrows through copper targets.
claims.note: His own Sphinx stela at Giza says so. Bragging about the king's body was part of the job, so treat the numbers as boasts.

claims.text: He hung seven Syrian princes head-down from his ship and displayed their bodies on city walls.
claims.note: The Amada stela, with a copy at Elephantine, tells it. It is royal propaganda, though cruelty to rebels was a normal royal boast.

claims.text: Victor Loret found a hidden cache of royal mummies in his tomb in 1898.
claims.note: KV35 held Amenhotep II and, in a side chamber, kings including Thutmose IV, Amenhotep III, Merneptah and Seti II.

reigns.hook: Amenhotep II is dead. His son Thutmose IV takes the throne, and he has a story to explain why: the Great Sphinx itself promised him the crown.

reigns.tagline: The prince who dozed off under the Sphinx and woke up king
reigns.previously: Amenhotep II, the strongman king, dies around 1400 BC.
paragraphs: Thutmose IV was a son of Amenhotep II and Queen Tiaa, and probably not the son anyone expected to be king. He had a story ready. Between the paws of the Great Sphinx at Giza he set up a granite slab, the Dream Stela. As a prince out hunting, it says, he lay down at noon in the shade of the Sphinx, then half buried in sand. The god spoke to him in a dream: clear away the sand, and I will make you king.

Abroad he ended the long rivalry with Mitanni, the great power of northern Syria, and sealed the peace by marrying a Mitannian princess. Her family made him work for it. A later Mitannian king wrote that Thutmose asked for her again and again, and got her only on the seventh request. At Karnak he raised a giant obelisk his grandfather Thutmose III had left lying unfinished. It now stands in Rome, by the Lateran.

He died after about ten years, still young. Howard Carter found his tomb, KV43, in 1903, digging for the American Theodore Davis. Robbers had been there first, but they left the body of his chariot, and a note on the wall says officials of King Horemheb tidied up the burial decades later. The king's own thin mummy turned up in his father's tomb. His young son became Amenhotep III.

claims.text: The Sphinx promised a sleeping prince the throne if he cleared away the sand.
claims.note: Carved after he became king. It looks like a younger son justifying his claim, and the end of the text is broken.

claims.text: The Mitannian king only handed over his daughter on the seventh request.
claims.note: Tushratta of Mitanni says so of his grandfather Artatama in Amarna letter EA 29, written to Akhenaten. It is his side of the story.

claims.text: He died of a wasting illness.
claims.note: His mummy is very thin, which led early examiners to suggest a long illness. Nothing in the texts says what killed him.

reigns.hook: Thutmose IV is dead before his time. His young son Amenhotep III inherits an empire at peace and a treasury full of gold, and he means to spend it.

reigns.tagline: Egypt's richest king, and he wanted everyone to know
reigns.previously: Thutmose IV gets the crown he dreamt of, then dies young.
paragraphs: Amenhotep III ruled for about 38 years at the high noon of Egyptian wealth. His chief queen, Tiye, was not royal. Her parents, Yuya and Thuya, were a non-royal couple whose almost untouched tomb turned up in the Valley of the Kings in 1905. He announced the marriage on big carved scarabs sent out across the country, a kind of royal press release.

Other scarabs bragged of a wild bull hunt, a pleasure lake dug for Tiye, and 102 lions killed in his first ten years. He built Luxor temple and a vast temple on the west bank, whose giant guardians, the Colossi of Memnon, still sit there. In the Amarna letters he took Babylonian and Mitannian princesses as wives, but would not send a daughter abroad. No Egyptian king's daughter, he said, had ever been given away.

As he aged, the king of Mitanni sent him a statue of the goddess Ishtar, perhaps to heal him. Hundreds of statues of Sekhmet, the lioness goddess of plague and healing, may have had a similar job. He died around 1352 BC, and his son Amenhotep took the throne with some very new ideas.

claims.text: Amenhotep III refused to send a daughter abroad, saying no Egyptian king's daughter ever had been.
claims.note: Quoted back at him, with some irritation, by the Babylonian king in Amarna letter EA 4.

claims.text: One of the Colossi of Memnon 'sang' at dawn, and Roman tourists came to hear it.
claims.note: Greek and Latin graffiti on its legs record the sound after an earthquake cracked it. It fell silent after later repairs.

claims.text: The Mitannian king sent the statue of Ishtar to cure him.
claims.note: The letter (EA 23) says the goddess was sent to Egypt. It doesn't spell out why, so the healing idea is a guess.

reigns.hook: The old king is dead. His son Amenhotep IV seems ordinary at first. Within a few years he will change his name, shut the temples and build a new city in the desert.

reigns.title: Akhenaten & Nefertiti
reigns.tagline: The king who threw out the gods, and his famous queen
reigns.previously: Amenhotep III dies after nearly 40 glittering years.
paragraphs: He began as Amenhotep IV. Around his fifth year he became Akhenaten, devoted to the Aten, the sun disc whose rays end in little hands. Then came revolution. The old gods' temples were closed and Amun's name was hacked off monuments across Egypt. The court packed up and moved to a brand-new city, Akhetaten, built on empty desert. We call it Amarna.

Art changed too. The king appears with a long face and swollen belly, kissing and cuddling his six daughters. Always at his side was his queen, Nefertiti, worshipping beside him and even shown smiting enemies like a king. The Great Hymn to the Aten praises the sun as the maker of all life. Meanwhile Amarna letters from Canaanite vassals begged for troops that never came.

Nefertiti's painted bust was found at Amarna on 6 December 1912 by Ludwig Borchardt's team, in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose. It is in Berlin, and Egypt wants it back. She was long thought to vanish around year 12, but an inscription found in 2012 names her as queen in year 16. Akhenaten died around 1336 BC, and his revolution was left without a leader.

claims.text: Nefertiti ruled after Akhenaten as the female king Neferneferuaten.
claims.note: A woman did rule briefly under that name. Some Egyptologists think it was Nefertiti, others a daughter such as Meritaten.

claims.text: The strange art shows that Akhenaten had a disease.
claims.note: Ideas range from Marfan syndrome to hormone disorders. A 2010 DNA study found no sign, and the style may be religious.

claims.text: The Great Hymn to the Aten inspired Psalm 104.
claims.note: The likeness of theme and imagery is striking. Whether one text borrowed from the other can't be proved.

reigns.hook: After Akhenaten comes a blur of short reigns. Out of it steps a boy of about eight called Tutankhaten, and the old gods are waiting to come back.

reigns.tagline: The forgotten boy king who became the most famous of all
reigns.previously: Akhenaten dies. Short, murky reigns follow at Amarna.
paragraphs: He was born Tutankhaten, 'living image of the Aten', around 1345 BC, probably Akhenaten's son. Crowned at about eight or nine, he married his half-sister Ankhesenpaaten. Soon both changed names, to Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun. His Restoration Stela promised to reopen the old temples, and the court turned back to the old gods. Real power lay with the courtier Ay and the general Horemheb.

He died at about 18 or 19, around 1327 BC, and nobody knows why. A 2010 study found a broken leg, a deformed foot and traces of malaria. The old idea that he was murdered with a blow to the head is now rejected. A royal widow then wrote to the Hittite king Suppiluliuma, begging for one of his sons as a husband. He sent a prince, Zannanza, who died on the way.

Then the boy was forgotten, and so was his small tomb. On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter's team, paid for by Lord Carnarvon, found its first step. The burial chamber was opened on 16 February 1923. Inside a nest of gilded shrines and coffins, reached only in 1925, lay the king in a solid gold mask. Carnarvon died that April, and the papers had their curse.

claims.text: Asked if he could see anything, Carter replied: 'Yes, wonderful things.'
claims.note: That is the line in his published book. His own notes and others present give slightly different words.

claims.text: The widow who begged the Hittites for a husband was Tutankhamun's wife, Ankhesenamun.
claims.note: The Hittite text calls her only Dahamunzu, 'the king's wife'. Some argue for Nefertiti or Meritaten.

claims.text: A curse killed Lord Carnarvon and others who opened the tomb.
claims.note: Carnarvon died of an infection, and Carter lived until 1939. The curse was a newspaper sensation.

reigns.hook: Tutankhamun leaves no heir. The elderly Ay takes the throne, but the general Horemheb has been waiting a long time, and he has the army.

reigns.tagline: The mystery pharaoh of Amarna
reigns.previously: Akhenaten dies, and his new religion starts to crack.
paragraphs: Smenkhkare ruled briefly at the end of the Amarna period, either beside Akhenaten or just after him. Almost nothing about him is certain, not even who he was: some scholars think he was a son or brother of Akhenaten, others that the name hides Queen Nefertiti.
His reign lasted a year or two at most. He left almost no monuments, and the body sometimes linked to him, found in tomb KV55, is still disputed.
reigns.hook: The boy Tutankhaten comes to the throne and the court heads back to the old gods.

reigns.tagline: The old courtier who buried Tutankhamun
reigns.previously: Tutankhamun dies at about 19, leaving no heir.
paragraphs: Ay had served Akhenaten and Tutankhamun as a senior official. When the young king died without children, Ay performed his funeral rites, a role reserved for the heir, and so claimed the throne. He may have married Tutankhamun's widow Ankhesenamun.
He ruled for about four years. His successor Horemheb, the army's commander, later smashed his name from his monuments as part of wiping out the whole Amarna era.
reigns.hook: Ay dies, and General Horemheb takes the throne.

reigns.tagline: The general who cleaned house and erased the heretics
reigns.previously: Old Ay takes the throne after Tutankhamun and reigns about four years.
paragraphs: Horemheb had commanded the army under Tutankhamun. When the old courtier Ay died, around 1323 BC, Horemheb took the throne himself. He set out to fix a country he thought had gone rotten. His Great Edict went after corrupt officials and tax men who robbed the poor. The guilty would have their noses cut off and be sent into exile at Tjaru, a fortress on the desert frontier.

Then he went after the memory of Akhenaten. He pulled down the Aten temples and packed their blocks inside the pylons of Karnak as rubble. Later king lists jump straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb, as if Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ay had never been. The hidden blocks survived, though, and now help Egyptologists piece the Amarna story back together.

As a general he had built himself a splendid tomb at Saqqara, rediscovered in 1975. As king he had a new one dug in the Valley of the Kings. He had no surviving son, so he named his vizier and general Paramessu as heir, an old soldier who would rule as Ramesses I.

claims.text: His Great Edict punished corrupt officials by cutting off their noses.
claims.note: Carved on a broken stela at Karnak. How strictly it was enforced, nobody knows.

claims.text: Horemheb was the real power behind the boy king Tutankhamun.
claims.note: His Saqqara tomb gives him grand titles as the king's deputy, but he shared influence with Ay.

claims.text: Later Egyptians erased the Amarna kings from their king lists.
claims.note: The Abydos king list of Seti I goes straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb.

reigns.hook: Horemheb hands Egypt to an old comrade. Ramesses I barely lasts a year, but his son Seti is ready, and he means to win the empire back.

reigns.tagline: The soldier who founded a dynasty
reigns.previously: Horemheb dies without a son and names his vizier to follow.
paragraphs: Ramesses was a career soldier from a military family in the Nile Delta. Horemheb, who had no children, made him vizier and then heir, partly because he already had a grown son and grandson.
He reigned only about two years, but founded the Nineteenth Dynasty. His son Seti I and grandson Ramesses II made the family's name the most famous in Egyptian history.
reigns.hook: His son Seti I takes over and sets out to restore Egypt's empire.

reigns.tagline: The warrior who built the finest tomb in the Valley
reigns.previously: Horemheb's heir, the old soldier Ramesses I, reigns barely a year.
paragraphs: Ramesses I was already old when he took Horemheb's throne, and he reigned only about a year (1295 to 1294 BC). His son Seti inherited a new dynasty with no royal blood and something to prove. His name honours Seth, god of storms and chaos. He marched into Canaan and Syria to rebuild Egypt's empire, fought the Libyans and the Hittites, and for a time held the city of Kadesh.

At Abydos he built a beautiful temple with a famous list of 76 kings, showing him and his young son Ramesses honouring their ancestors. It quietly leaves out Hatshepsut and the Amarna kings. At Karnak the great Hypostyle Hall rose under his name, a forest of 134 giant columns.

His tomb, KV17, is among the longest and finest in the Valley of the Kings. Giovanni Belzoni found it in 1817, its paint still bright. His alabaster sarcophagus ended up in Sir John Soane's Museum in London. His mummy, found in the royal cache of 1881, still has a calm, handsome face. He had trained his son Ramesses well.

claims.text: Seti began the great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak.
claims.note: Some credit Horemheb or Ramesses I with the start. Seti decorated much of it and Ramesses II finished it.

claims.text: Seti captured Kadesh.
claims.note: His Karnak battle reliefs show it, but the city was soon back in the Hittite camp.

claims.text: His is one of the best-preserved royal mummies.
claims.note: A common verdict, though ancient robbers broke the head from the body.

reigns.hook: Seti dies, and his son steps up. Ramesses II will rule for 66 years, fill Egypt with his face, and fight the most famous battle of the age.

reigns.tagline: The king who fought a draw and carved it as a triumph
reigns.previously: Seti I dies, having restored Egypt's armies and its pride.
paragraphs: Ramesses II reigned for 66 years and made sure nobody would forget it. In 1274 BC, his fifth year, he marched on Kadesh in Syria against the Hittite king Muwatalli II. Two planted spies fed him a lie, and the Hittite chariots caught his army strung out on the march. Ramesses says he saved the day almost single-handed. At best it was a draw, but he carved his victory on temple walls all over Egypt.

In his year 21, about 1259 BC, he made peace with the next Hittite king, Hattusili III. Both versions survive, the Egyptian on temple walls and the Hittite on clay tablets. Later he married a Hittite princess. He built everywhere: a new Delta capital, Pi-Ramesses, and the rock temples of Abu Simbel, which were cut up and moved uphill in 1964 to 1968 to escape the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

He had over a hundred children and outlived many of his heirs. His queen Nefertari lies in a gorgeously painted tomb in the Valley of the Queens. Shelley's 1818 poem 'Ozymandias' takes its name from the Greek form of his throne name. He died around 1213 BC, aged about 90, and his 13th son took the throne.

claims.text: Ramesses won the battle of Kadesh almost single-handed.
claims.note: His own poem and reliefs tell it. Kadesh stayed Hittite, and Hittite sources suggest a stalemate at best.

claims.text: His treaty with the Hittites is the earliest surviving peace treaty.
claims.note: Often called so, and copies survive from both sides. Older Mesopotamian treaties exist, so it depends on definitions.

claims.text: In 1976 his mummy was issued a passport to fly to Paris.
claims.note: The mummy really did go to Paris for treatment against fungus. The passport story is widely told but hard to pin down.

reigns.hook: After 66 years, Egypt has a new king for the first time in most people's lives. Merneptah is already old, and enemies are gathering in the west.

reigns.tagline: The old prince whose stela first names Israel
reigns.previously: Ramesses the Great dies at about 90, after 66 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Merneptah had waited a very long time. He was the 13th son of Ramesses II, and the brothers ahead of him had all died before their father. By the time he was crowned he was probably in his sixties. There was no time to relax. In his fifth year, Libyan tribes pushed into the western Delta, joined by some of the Sea Peoples, raiders from around the Mediterranean. Merneptah's army crushed them.

He celebrated on a tall granite stela, which Flinders Petrie found at Thebes in 1896. Near the end it lists enemies beaten in Canaan, and boasts that Israel is laid waste and its seed is gone. It is the earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible. He also shipped grain to the Hittites, his father's old enemies, when famine struck them.

He died around 1203 BC. His mummy turned up in 1898, among the royal bodies hidden in the tomb of Amenhotep II. Older writers made him the pharaoh of the Exodus, though nothing backs that up. After him, the family of Ramesses began to tear itself apart.

claims.text: The Merneptah Stela is the earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible.
claims.note: The name is written with the sign for a people, not a place. Now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

claims.text: He sent grain to keep the Hittites alive in a famine.
claims.note: A Karnak inscription mentions shipping grain to Hatti. How much, and how bad the famine was, is debated.

claims.text: Merneptah was the pharaoh of the Exodus.
claims.note: A popular guess in older books. No Egyptian source mentions an Exodus, and the stela puts Israel already in Canaan.

reigns.hook: Merneptah's heirs turn on each other. First up is Amenmesse, a man of murky origins, who holds Thebes and the south as king.

images.caption: The Merneptah Stela in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo, carved in his reign. It is a monument, not a portrait.
images.alt: Tall granite stela with a rounded top, covered in rows of hieroglyphs and a relief scene at the top

reigns.tagline: The mystery king who seized the south, then was wiped out
reigns.reignEnded: Ousted by Seti II; fate unknown
reigns.previously: Merneptah dies an old man, his Libyan war won.
paragraphs: Merneptah's death set off a family feud, and Amenmesse is at the heart of it. Nobody is sure who he was. He may have been a son of Merneptah, or a grandson. Some think he was the same man as Messuy, a royal viceroy of Kush. Shaw's scheme gives him the throne from 1203 to 1200 BC, before Seti II. Many scholars think instead that he grabbed Thebes and Nubia while Seti II, the named heir, held the north.

Either way, for about four years he was king in the south. The tomb-builders at Thebes dated their records by his reign, and he began a tomb of his own in the Valley of the Kings, KV10. Then he was gone. Seti II's men chiselled his name off the temples and scraped the pictures off his tomb walls. Whether Amenmesse died, fled or was killed, no record says.

claims.text: Amenmesse ruled before Seti II, not as his rival.
claims.note: Shaw's scheme puts Amenmesse first, from 1203 to 1200 BC. Others think he rebelled in the south during Seti's reign. The monuments can be read both ways.

claims.text: He was the viceroy of Kush called Messuy before he took the throne.
claims.note: Suggested from a likeness of names and a Nubian power base. Many reject it; the evidence is thin.

reigns.hook: Amenmesse vanishes, and Seti II has the whole of Egypt. His first job: wipe every trace of his rival off the walls.

reigns.tagline: He beat his rival, then the palace slipped out of his hands
reigns.cameToPower: Merneptah's heir; took back the south
reigns.previously: Amenmesse vanishes from Thebes, his name chiselled off the walls.
paragraphs: Seti II was Merneptah's son, named crown prince while his father still lived. Whether he lost the south to Amenmesse or simply came after him, he ended up with all of Egypt and took his revenge in stone, hacking out his rival's name. In the first court of Karnak he built a small shrine of three chapels where the holy boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu could rest. It still stands.

Trouble was brewing at the tomb-builders' village of Deir el-Medina. The foreman Paneb was charged with stealing stone and tools from the king's own tomb as it was being dug, with beating people, and with seducing workmen's wives. At court a foreign-born official called Bay was rising fast and would soon be chancellor. Seti's chief wife, Tausret, was watching closely.

Seti died after about six years, and his tomb, KV15, had to be finished in a hurry. His mummy turned up in 1898 among the royal bodies hidden in the tomb of Amenhotep II. No grown son of his followed him. The crown went to a boy, Siptah, whose parentage is still argued over.

claims.text: The foreman Paneb stole from Seti II's tomb, beat people and seduced workmen's wives.
claims.note: All of it comes from a list of charges in Papyrus Salt 124, written by a rival, Amennakht. We never hear Paneb's side.

claims.text: The chancellor Bay was of Syrian birth.
claims.note: His second name looks Semitic and his rise was unusual, but no text says where he came from.

reigns.hook: Seti II dies. The new king is a boy with a twisted foot, and the real power sits with a widowed queen and a foreign-born chancellor.

reigns.tagline: The boy king with a twisted foot and a chancellor to fear
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Perhaps Seti II's or Amenmesse's son
reigns.cameToPower: Set up by the chancellor Bay
reigns.previously: Seti II dies after six years with no grown son to follow him.
paragraphs: Siptah was a boy when he was crowned, and his mummy shows why he could never have led an army: his left foot is badly twisted, maybe from polio. He was first named Ramesses-Siptah, then a year or two in renamed himself Merneptah-Siptah. Seti II's widow Tausret stood beside him, and so did the chancellor Bay, who boasted in an inscription that he had set the king on his father's throne. Bay was even given his own tomb in the Valley of the Kings.

He got too big. In Siptah's year 5 a message reached the tomb-builders at Deir el-Medina: Pharaoh had killed the great enemy Bay. Who gave the order is hard to say; the boy king was the one named. A year or so later Siptah himself was dead, at about 20. He was buried in tomb KV47, and his mummy later turned up with the others in the tomb of Amenhotep II. Tausret was left standing.

claims.text: Siptah had polio.
claims.note: His mummy has a deformed left foot. Polio is the usual guess; others think he was born with a club foot.

claims.text: The chancellor Bay was executed on Pharaoh's orders in year 5.
claims.note: A Deir el-Medina ostracon, published by Pierre Grandet in 2000, announces that Pharaoh has killed 'the great enemy Bay' in year 5.

claims.text: Siptah was a son of Amenmesse.
claims.note: Some argue this from his mother's name and the timing. Others make him a son of Seti II. No text names his father.

reigns.hook: Siptah is dead, and he leaves no heir. Seti II's widow Tausret has stood behind the throne for years. Now she means to sit on it, as king.

reigns.tagline: The widow who ruled as king, then disappeared
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Widow of Seti II; Siptah's regent
reigns.previously: Siptah dies young, the last of Seti II's line to wear the crown.
paragraphs: Tausret had been Seti II's chief wife, then the power behind the boy Siptah. When he died about 1188 BC she did not look for another man to crown. She took the throne herself, with a full king's names and titles, as Hatshepsut and Sobekneferu had done before her. She seems to have counted her years from Seti II's death, as if Siptah had never reigned. She began a temple for her own cult at Thebes and widened her tomb, KV14.

In 1908 a small pit in the Valley of the Kings, nicknamed the Gold Tomb, turned up earrings, rings and other jewellery bearing her name and Seti II's. After about two years as king she vanishes. Her tomb was taken over and extended by the next king, Sethnakht, who was buried in it. Her own mummy has never been identified. Sethnakht later claimed he had rescued Egypt from chaos and rebels.

claims.text: Tausret ruled as a full king in her own right.
claims.note: Her monuments give her a king's throne name and titles. She is one of very few women known to have done so.

claims.text: Sethnakht seized her tomb and was buried in it.
claims.note: KV14 shows her images plastered over or recut for him. What happened to her own body is unknown.

claims.text: Sethnakht rescued Egypt from rebels who bribed foreigners with stolen gold.
claims.note: His Elephantine stela says so, but it is the new king's own propaganda and never names Tausret.

reigns.hook: Tausret is gone, and nobody wrote down how. A man named Sethnakht, of unknown family, fights his way to the throne. His son will face invaders from the sea.

reigns.previously: Queen Tausret's reign ends in turmoil.
paragraphs: Setnakhte took the throne at the end of the Nineteenth Dynasty, a time of civil strife. His origins are unknown. On a stela at Elephantine he claimed to have driven out rebels and restored order to a land in chaos.
He ruled for only two or three years and founded the Twentieth Dynasty. His son became Ramesses III, the last great warrior pharaoh.
reigns.hook: His son Ramesses III takes over, and the Sea Peoples are coming.

reigns.tagline: He beat the Sea Peoples, then his own wife plotted murder
reigns.reignEnded: Throat cut in the Harem Conspiracy
reigns.previously: Tausret vanishes. Sethnakht grabs the throne in the chaos.
paragraphs: His father Sethnakht seized power in the chaos after Queen Tausret and held it for about two years. Ramesses III, first great king of the 20th Dynasty, modelled himself on Ramesses II, and he needed to. Libyans pushed into the Delta twice and were thrown back. In his year 8 came the Sea Peoples, raiders and migrants who had wrecked cities across the eastern Mediterranean. He fought them on land and in the mouths of the Nile, and won.

His temple at Medinet Habu, on the west bank at Thebes, shows it all: ships locked together, enemies tumbling into the water, scribes counting heaps of hands and penises cut from the dead. But the money was running out. In year 29 the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, their grain rations late, downed tools and marched on the temples to protest.

Then came the Harem Conspiracy. A lesser wife, Tiye, plotted to put her son Pentawer on the throne. The trial records survive: the guilty were sentenced to death or allowed to kill themselves, and some judges lost their noses and ears for partying with accused women. In 2012 a CT scan found a deep cut across the king's throat. The plotters probably got him, but not the crown. His son became Ramesses IV.

claims.text: The harem plotters succeeded in killing Ramesses III.
claims.note: A 2012 CT study by Zahi Hawass, Sahar Saleem and colleagues found a deep throat wound. The trial papers never say outright that the king died in the attack.

claims.text: 'Unknown Man E', a mummy wrapped in a goatskin, is Prince Pentawer.
claims.note: The same 2012 study found DNA showing a father-son link with Ramesses III. That fits Pentawer but cannot prove it.

claims.text: The Deir el-Medina walkout is the earliest strike on record.
claims.note: The Turin Strike Papyrus describes it day by day. 'Earliest' only means the earliest we know of.

reigns.hook: Ramesses III is dead, and his son Ramesses IV, the heir the plotters tried to push aside, takes the throne. He wants a long reign, and he will ask the gods for one.

reigns.tagline: He begged the gods for a 67-year reign and got six
reigns.cameToPower: Survived the harem plot as heir
reigns.previously: Ramesses III dies, probably murdered by harem plotters.
paragraphs: Ramesses IV was the heir the harem plotters wanted to push aside. They failed, and he took the throne with his father's killers on trial. The giant Papyrus Harris, listing every gift Ramesses III had made to the gods, was drawn up as he took over. He was in a hurry to make his own mark. In his year 3 he sent more than 8,000 men to the quarries of the Wadi Hammamat, deep in the eastern desert, to cut stone for his statues.

He doubled the gang of tomb-builders at Deir el-Medina to 120 men. On a stela at Abydos he made the god Osiris an offer: he had done more for the gods in four years than Ramesses II in 67, so please grant him a reign as long. The gods did not take the deal. He died after about six years, and was buried in tomb KV2. A plan of that tomb, drawn on papyrus at the time, survives in Turin. His son became Ramesses V.

claims.text: Ramesses IV asked Osiris for a reign as long as Ramesses II's 67 years.
claims.note: His Abydos stela makes the bargain in plain words. He reigned about six.

claims.text: His Wadi Hammamat expedition numbered more than 8,000 men.
claims.note: A rock stela at the quarry lists 8,368 men by job, from soldiers to stonecutters. It is the king's own count.

claims.text: An ancient plan of his tomb survives.
claims.note: A papyrus in the Museo Egizio, Turin, shows KV2 with its rooms and measurements, a rare architect's drawing.

reigns.hook: Ramesses IV's prayer goes unanswered. His son Ramesses V takes the throne, and his scribes measure Egypt field by field.
