reigns.tagline: The king of the great land survey, struck down by a pox
reigns.previously: Ramesses IV dies after six years, his prayer unanswered.
paragraphs: Ramesses V reigned only about four years, but one of his documents is a treasure. The Wilbour Papyrus, about ten metres long, records a survey of farmland in Middle Egypt in his year 4: who worked each plot, how big it was, and what it owed. Much of it belonged to the temples, above all to Amun of Thebes. Meanwhile the tomb-builders' journal records days when the gangs stayed home because of the enemy, Libyan raiders loose near Thebes.

His mummy has raised spots on the face, and doctors since the early 1900s have wondered if smallpox killed him. He was not buried at once. A note from Deir el-Medina puts his funeral in year 2 of the next king, his uncle, who also took over the tomb begun for him, KV9. Some think the uncle pushed him aside. Others think a deadly disease simply delayed the funeral.

claims.text: Ramesses V died of smallpox.
claims.note: Lesions on his mummy's face look like smallpox to many examiners. No sample has confirmed it.

claims.text: The Wilbour Papyrus surveys thousands of fields in his year 4.
claims.note: Now in the Brooklyn Museum; published by Alan Gardiner. It is the fullest land record from ancient Egypt.

claims.text: His uncle Ramesses VI forced him off the throne.
claims.note: Based on the delayed burial and the seized tomb. There is no direct evidence of a coup.

reigns.hook: Ramesses V is dead, or at least gone. His uncle, another son of Ramesses III, takes the crown, and the dead king's tomb with it.

reigns.tagline: The uncle whose tomb hid Tutankhamun for 3,000 years
reigns.previously: Ramesses V dies young, perhaps of smallpox, and lies unburied.
paragraphs: Ramesses VI had grown up as Prince Amenherkhepeshef, one of the many sons of Ramesses III. He was not young when the crown came to him. He took over his nephew's half-built tomb, KV9, and turned it into one of the grandest in the Valley of the Kings, its ceilings painted with the sky goddess Nut swallowing the sun at night. His workmen put up stone huts below it, right on top of a small, forgotten tomb.

That tomb was Tutankhamun's, and the huts and rubble kept it hidden until Howard Carter dug beneath them in 1922. Abroad the empire was slipping away. His is the last royal name found at the turquoise mines of Sinai. At home he made his daughter Iset God's Wife of Amun at Thebes, a powerful priestly post. He died after about seven years. Robbers later hacked his mummy to pieces looking for gold.

claims.text: Huts built by his tomb-workers hid the entrance to Tutankhamun's tomb.
claims.note: Howard Carter found the foundations of the workmen's huts over the entrance steps of KV62 in November 1922.

claims.text: He is the last pharaoh named at the Sinai turquoise mines.
claims.note: His is the latest royal name found at Serabit el-Khadim so far. New finds could change that.

claims.text: Robbers smashed his mummy apart.
claims.note: Found in 1898 in the tomb of Amenhotep II, the body was in pieces, bound by ancient priests onto a board.

reigns.hook: Ramesses VI dies. His son becomes Ramesses VII, just as the price of a sack of grain begins to soar.

reigns.tagline: Seven years of dear bread, and a body never found
reigns.reignEnded: Died with no son left alive
reigns.previously: Ramesses VI dies, buried in the grandest tomb of his age.
paragraphs: Ramesses VII reigned about seven years and left almost no buildings. What he did leave is a pile of shopping lists. The scribes of Deir el-Medina noted what things cost, and in his reign the price of grain climbed to its highest level in the whole New Kingdom. Workers were paid in grain, so when harvests failed or stores ran short, everyone felt it.

His tomb, KV1, sits near the entrance of the Valley of the Kings. It is small and was finished quickly, and it has stood open since ancient times: Greek and Roman visitors scratched their names on its walls. His mummy has never been found. A son named Ramesses seems to have died before him, so when the king died there was no son to follow.

claims.text: Grain prices peaked under Ramesses VII.
claims.note: Jac Janssen's study of Deir el-Medina prices shows grain at its dearest around his reign. The records are patchy, so the exact peak is uncertain.

claims.text: His mummy has never been found.
claims.note: It was not in either of the great royal caches found in 1881 and 1898, and KV1 was open and empty.

claims.text: His son died before him.
claims.note: A prince Ramesses, son of Ramesses VII, is known from a few objects. The date of his death is not recorded.

reigns.hook: Ramesses VII dies sonless. The crown goes back up the family tree, to an ageing uncle: one of the last living sons of Ramesses III.

reigns.tagline: The forgotten son of Ramesses III, king at last
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Ramesses III's son; Ramesses VII's uncle
reigns.cameToPower: Ramesses VII left no living son
reigns.previously: Ramesses VII dies with no son left to follow him.
paragraphs: As a young man he was Prince Sethherkhepeshef, one of the many sons of Ramesses III. You can still see him at Medinet Habu, walking in the long line of princes carved behind their father. A tomb was cut for him in the Valley of the Queens. Then four of his brothers and nephews wore the crown before him, and the years went by. When Ramesses VII died without a son, the old prince finally became Ramesses VIII.

He took the throne name Usermaatre Akhenamun, and then he almost vanishes. A few small objects carry his name, and no building of his is known. His royal tomb has never been found, and he was probably never buried in the prince's tomb either. Shaw's dates give him about three years; he may have had only one. With him the sons of Ramesses III ran out, and the crown moved to a new branch of the family.

claims.text: Ramesses VIII is the Prince Sethherkhepeshef shown among Ramesses III's sons at Medinet Habu.
claims.note: His royal name includes Sethherkhepeshef, matching the prince in the Medinet Habu procession of sons.

claims.text: He reigned for only about a year.
claims.note: So few objects name him that many scholars think his reign was very short; Shaw's scheme allows about three years.

reigns.hook: Ramesses VIII dies, and the crown leaves Ramesses III's sons for good. The next king will reign for 18 years, and his officials will catch a gang of robbers with royal gold.

reigns.tagline: The king whose men caught the tomb robbers
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Probably a grandson of Ramesses III
reigns.previously: Ramesses VIII, the last son of Ramesses III, dies after a short reign.
paragraphs: Ramesses IX reigned about 18 years, longer than anyone since Ramesses III. He built at Heliopolis and at Karnak, but at Thebes real power was sliding to the high priest of Amun, Amenhotep. A relief at Karnak shows the king rewarding him with gold, and the priest is carved as big as the king. That was new, and a warning.

In his year 16 came a scandal. Paser, mayor of east Thebes, accused the officials of the west bank of letting the royal tombs be robbed. An inquiry went from tomb to tomb and found that the pyramid of Sobekemsaf, a king of the 17th Dynasty, had been broken into. The stonemason Amenpanefer confessed that his gang had found the king and queen in their coffins, stripped off their gold and set fire to the coffins.

The case turned into a feud between Paser and Pawera, mayor of the west bank, and Paser came off worst. Ramesses IX was buried in a grand tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV6. His mummy later turned up in the great royal cache at Deir el-Bahri.

claims.text: Robbers confessed to stripping King Sobekemsaf and his queen and burning their coffins.
claims.note: The Leopold-Amherst papyrus records the stonemason Amenpanefer's confession, made under beating.

claims.text: The high priest Amenhotep had himself carved as large as the king.
claims.note: His reliefs at Karnak show him on the same scale as Ramesses IX, a break with all earlier custom.

claims.text: Ramesses IX was a grandson of Ramesses III.
claims.note: He is thought to descend through one of Ramesses III's sons, probably Montuherkhepeshef; no text says so outright.

reigns.hook: Ramesses IX is laid in the Valley of the Kings. The next Ramesses will barely leave a mark, while across the river the tomb-builders sit idle, afraid of the foreigners.

reigns.tagline: Barely a name, while the workmen sat idle
reigns.previously: Ramesses IX dies after 18 years and a tomb-robbery scandal.
paragraphs: Ramesses X is one of the least known kings of the New Kingdom. His throne name was Khepermaatre, and nobody is sure who his parents were. Shaw's scheme gives him about nine years, but the highest year found on any document is his year 3, and many think his reign ended not long after.

The best view of his reign comes from the journal kept by the scribes of the tomb-builders at Deir el-Medina. Day after day it notes the crews doing no work. Sometimes there was a festival. Sometimes the reason given is the 'foreigners', bands of Libyans on the Theban west bank. Royal Thebes was no longer a safe place.
His tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV18, was barely begun and may never have held him. His mummy has never been identified.

claims.text: The tomb-builders stayed home for fear of Libyan raiders.
claims.note: The Deir el-Medina journal blames idle days on 'foreigners'; whether they were raiders or settled Libyans is debated.

claims.text: Ramesses X reigned only three or four years.
claims.note: Year 3 is his highest known date; Shaw's scheme allows about nine.

reigns.hook: Ramesses X dies, all but forgotten. The next king will reign for 30 years, long enough to watch a viceroy, a general and a priest carve up his kingdom.

reigns.tagline: The last Ramesses, as generals and priests took over
reigns.previously: Ramesses X dies after a short, troubled reign.
paragraphs: Ramesses XI reigned about 30 years and held less of Egypt at the end than at the start. Early on, Thebes fell into chaos. Panehesy, the king's viceroy of Kush, came north with his Nubian troops, and for months the high priest of Amun, Amenhotep, was pushed aside. Then Panehesy was driven back south, where he held out for years.

In his year 19 the king announced a new era, the 'Repeating of Births', a fresh start. In practice the south now belonged to army men. The general Herihor, also high priest, carved royal titles for himself at Karnak. In one surviving letter the general Piankh orders two policemen drowned at night and kept quiet, and asks whose master Pharaoh is any more.

Ramesses XI's tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV4, was left unfinished, and he was probably buried somewhere else, perhaps in the north. When he died, Smendes, who already ran the Delta from Tanis, took the crown. The New Kingdom was over.

claims.text: The general Piankh ordered two policemen killed in secret.
claims.note: One of the Late Ramesside Letters, sent by Piankh, tells officials to drown them by night and tell no one.

claims.text: Panehesy's march on Thebes was a civil war, the 'War of the High Priest'.
claims.note: Pieced together from tomb-robbery papyri and letters; who fought whom, and when, is still argued over.

claims.text: Smendes was married to a daughter of Ramesses XI.
claims.note: A modern guess to explain how Smendes got the crown; no text names his wife Tentamun's father.

reigns.hook: Ramesses XI is gone. In the Delta, Smendes is crowned at Tanis. At Thebes the generals who serve as high priests of Amun accept him, on their own terms.

reigns.tagline: He ran the Delta for the last Ramesses, then took over
reigns.previously: Ramesses XI dies. The New Kingdom is over.
paragraphs: Welcome to the Third Intermediate Period. Smendes was a northerner whose name means 'he of the Ram of Mendes', a god of the Delta. Even before Ramesses XI died, he seems to have run the north from Tanis. In the Story of Wenamun, the envoy sent to Byblos for cedar reports first to 'Smendes and Tentamun' at Tanis, as if they were the real rulers.

As king he founded the 21st Dynasty and kept Tanis as his capital. Egypt was now split in two without a war. The Delta king ruled the north, and at Thebes the high priests of Amun, army generals all, ran the south, while still dating their records by his years. When the Nile flood threatened Luxor temple, Smendes sent thousands of men to quarry stone and repair it.

A stela of the high priest Menkheperre tells of rebels exiled to a western oasis being pardoned in a year 25, probably of Smendes. His tomb has never been found for certain, but his canopic jars survive. After about 26 years he was followed by the shadowy Amenemnisu.

claims.text: Smendes and Tentamun ruled the north while Ramesses XI was still king.
claims.note: It rests on the Story of Wenamun, which may be a work of fiction, and on how its dates are read.

claims.text: The pardon on the Banishment Stela happened under Smendes.
claims.note: The stela gives a year 25 but no king's name; most scholars assign it to Smendes.

reigns.hook: Smendes dies. His successor Amenemnisu will reign only about four years and leave behind little more than his name on a gold bow cap.

reigns.tagline: Four years, two bow caps and a mystery
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Unclear; no known tie to Smendes
reigns.previously: Smendes dies at Tanis after about 26 years.
paragraphs: Amenemnisu, whose name means 'Amun is king', is one of the most elusive pharaohs of all. Manetho remembered him as Nephercheres and gave him four years, and for a long time that was almost all anyone knew. His throne name, Neferkare, came with the title 'ruler of Thebes', perhaps a nod to the priests who ran the south.

Then in 1940 Pierre Montet opened the tomb of Psusennes I at Tanis. Among the king's weapons were two small gold caps from the ends of a bow, one with Amenemnisu's name and one with Psusennes's. Two kings on one bow suggests they ruled side by side for a while. Of Amenemnisu's own burial there is no trace. After about four years he died, and Psusennes I, son of the Theban high priest Pinedjem, ruled alone.

claims.text: Amenemnisu and Psusennes I reigned together for a time.
claims.note: The main evidence is the pair of bow caps from Psusennes's tomb, one for each king; it fits a co-regency but does not prove one.

claims.text: Manetho's 'Nephercheres' is Amenemnisu.
claims.note: The name is a Greek form of his throne name Neferkare, and the place in the list and four years fit.

reigns.hook: Amenemnisu dies. Psusennes I, a Theban priest's son on the throne of Tanis, will rule for nearly half a century and go to his grave in silver.

reigns.tagline: The priest's son who went to his grave in silver
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of the high priest Pinedjem I
reigns.previously: Amenemnisu dies after about four years at Tanis.
paragraphs: His name, Pasebakhaenniut, means 'the star that appears in the city'; the Greeks made it Psusennes. He was a son of Pinedjem I, the high priest of Amun who ran Thebes. For once the two halves of Egypt were in one family's hands: Psusennes as king at Tanis, his brothers as high priests in the south. Shaw's dates give him about 48 years.

He made Tanis a real capital, ringing its temple of Amun with a massive mudbrick wall. Inside that wall, by the temple, he built his tomb. For his outer sarcophagus he took a granite one carved for Merneptah more than 200 years earlier and had it shipped north from the Valley of the Kings.

In 1940 Pierre Montet found the burial untouched. Inside the granite lay a coffin of silver, a metal Egypt had to import, and on the king's face a mask of gold. With Europe at war, the find made far less noise than Tutankhamun had. Before he died, Psusennes had taken Amenemope as his partner on the throne.

claims.text: His outer sarcophagus was first made for Merneptah.
claims.note: Merneptah's names survive on the granite; Montet found it in Psusennes's burial chamber at Tanis.

claims.text: Silver was worth more than gold in Egypt at the time.
claims.note: Egypt had gold mines but imported its silver, and older lists put silver first; prices changed over the centuries.

reigns.hook: Psusennes I dies after nearly half a century. His partner Amenemope rules on alone, and will end up sleeping in the old king's tomb.

reigns.tagline: A gold mask in a borrowed tomb
reigns.reignEnded: Died after about 9 years as king
reigns.previously: Psusennes I dies after nearly 50 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Amenemope's name means 'Amun is in Opet', the great festival of Thebes. He was probably a son of Psusennes I. In Shaw's dates he was crowned in 993 BC, two years before the old king died, so for a while the two ruled together. This card starts when he ruled alone. His reign left few monuments.

His fame came almost 3,000 years later. When Pierre Montet worked through the royal tombs at Tanis in 1940, he found Amenemope's burial tucked into a small chamber of Psusennes I's tomb, a room first meant for a queen. He seems to have been moved there from his own smaller tomb nearby. Robbers had never found him. The damp Delta soil had rotted his wooden coffin, but his gold mask and jewellery came through.
After about nine years as king he died, and the throne passed to Osorkon, a man from a family of Libyan chiefs.

claims.text: Amenemope was first buried in his own tomb and moved into Psusennes I's later.
claims.note: Montet's finds suggest it: his name is in a small tomb nearby, while his burial lay in a chamber of Psusennes's tomb.

claims.text: He shared the throne with Psusennes I for about two years.
claims.note: Inferred from how the reign lengths fit and from objects naming both kings; Shaw's dates assume it.

reigns.hook: Amenemope dies. The next king, Osorkon, has a Libyan name and a Libyan family. He is a sign of things to come.

reigns.tagline: The forgotten first Libyan king of Egypt
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No known kin; son of a Libyan chief
reigns.previously: Amenemope dies, buried in a borrowed chamber at Tanis.
paragraphs: For centuries this king was just a line in Manetho's list: Osochor, six years. Then in the 1970s the French scholar Jean Yoyotte spotted a fragment of the priests' annals at Karnak naming a King Osorkon whose mother was called Mehtenweskhet. She was already known as the wife of a Libyan chief named Shoshenq and the grandmother of a later king, Shoshenq I.

So Osorkon the Elder was the son of a Great Chief of the Meshwesh, Libyans whose families had settled in the Delta as soldiers generations before. How he got the crown nobody knows; no war is recorded. The Libyan clans were simply the strongest power in the north, and the Tanis kings needed their swords.

Very little from his reign survives: a few objects with his throne name, Aakheperre, long credited to a much later Osorkon. After about six years he died and the crown went to Siamun. But Osorkon's nephew Shoshenq was growing up in the family business.

claims.text: Osorkon the Elder was the son of the Libyan chief Shoshenq and Mehtenweskhet.
claims.note: A Karnak priestly annal names his mother; a later family tree makes her the chief Shoshenq's wife. Jean Yoyotte made the link in 1977.

claims.text: Objects naming Aakheperre Osorkon belong to him, not to Osorkon IV.
claims.note: Long given to the 8th-century Osorkon IV; Aidan Dodson and others have reassigned them to Osorkon the Elder.

reigns.hook: Osorkon dies after about six years. The crown passes to Siamun, who will build at Tanis and perhaps send an army to the Philistine coast. The Libyan clan waits its turn.

reigns.tagline: The Tanis king who may have given Solomon a bride
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Unknown; not known to be kin
reigns.cameToPower: Followed Osorkon the Elder at Tanis
reigns.previously: Osorkon the Elder, the first Libyan king, dies after a short reign.
paragraphs: After a brief spell with a Libyan on the throne, Tanis had a king with a proper Egyptian name again. Siamun means "son of Amun", and he lived up to it. In about 19 years he enlarged the great temple of Amun at Tanis and built for the same god at Memphis. He is one of the better known kings of the 21st Dynasty, which is not saying much.

A carved block from Tanis shows him in the old pose, smiting a kneeling enemy who clutches an unusual axe. Some scholars think the axe is Aegean in style, which would make the enemy a Philistine. Set that beside the Bible's story of a pharaoh who burned the town of Gezer and handed it to his daughter as a wedding gift when she married King Solomon, and you have a tempting match.

Down at Thebes the priests were still moving the royal dead to keep them from robbers. Ink notes on the coffins of Seti I and Ramesses II are dated to his reign, logging another move on their way to the hiding place at Deir el-Bahri found in 1881. Siamun died about 959 BC, and the crown passed to Psusennes II.

claims.text: Siamun was the pharaoh who took Gezer and gave it to his daughter, Solomon's wife.
claims.note: 1 Kings 9:16 tells the story but never names the pharaoh. Siamun is the usual guess because of the Tanis smiting scene.

claims.text: The Tanis relief records a real war against the Philistines.
claims.note: The axe looks Aegean to some scholars. Others see a standard smiting scene with no particular battle behind it.

claims.text: Royal mummies were moved between hiding places in his reign.
claims.note: Dockets written in ink on the coffins of Seti I and Ramesses II name his regnal years.

reigns.hook: Siamun dies with no famous son. The last king of Tanis, Psusennes II, may also be high priest at Thebes, and his daughter is about to marry into a Libyan family.

reigns.tagline: The last Tanis king, who married into the Libyans
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Unknown; maybe a Theban priest's son
reigns.previously: Siamun dies after about 19 years of building at Tanis.
paragraphs: Psusennes II was the last king of the 21st Dynasty, reigning about 14 years from about 959 BC. Very little is known about him. Many Egyptologists think he was the same man as Psusennes, the high priest of Amun at Thebes. If so, he was the one king of the age who held the north and the south in his own hands, the crown at Tanis and the god's estate at Thebes.

His real legacy was a marriage. His daughter Maatkare became the wife of Osorkon, son of Shoshenq, the great chief of the Libyans and the strongest man in the army. When Psusennes died about 945 BC with no son to follow him, Shoshenq took the crown himself. Thanks to that wedding, the new Libyan dynasty could say it had the old royal blood in its family.

claims.text: Psusennes II was also the high priest of Amun at Thebes.
claims.note: It rests on the shared name and the timing. No text clearly calls one man both king and high priest.

claims.text: His daughter Maatkare married Shoshenq I's son Osorkon.
claims.note: A statue dedicated by Osorkon I's son names his mother Maatkare as a daughter of a King Psusennes. Which Psusennes is debated.

reigns.hook: Psusennes II dies with no son to follow him. His daughter's father-in-law, a Libyan army chief named Shoshenq, is ready to take the crown for himself.

reigns.tagline: The Libyan chief who may have looted Solomon's temple
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Libyan army chief, no son of the last
reigns.previously: Psusennes II dies, last of the Tanis kings. A Libyan chief steps up.
paragraphs: Shoshenq came from a family of Libyan chiefs, the Meshwesh, settled at Bubastis in the Delta for generations. They were soldiers, Egyptian in religion but proud of their roots. As commander of the army he took the throne and founded the 22nd Dynasty. To bring Thebes into line, he made his son Iuput high priest of Amun.

Then he went to war. He marched into Canaan and Israel and carved a long list of the towns he took on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak. A broken piece of his victory stela turned up at Megiddo. He's usually taken to be the biblical Shishak, who carried off the treasures of Solomon's temple in Jerusalem. Oddly, Jerusalem isn't on his surviving list.
He began a vast new court at Karnak to show off his victories, but the reliefs on the portal were never finished. He died after about 21 years, and his son Osorkon I took over a rich, united kingdom.

claims.text: Shoshenq is Shishak, who took Solomon's treasures in Rehoboam's fifth year.
claims.note: The names and timing fit, but Jerusalem is missing from the Karnak list as it survives. Some think the city paid him off.

claims.text: He was a nephew of the earlier king Osorkon the Elder.
claims.note: Pieced together from family trees and a later genealogy. Most accept it, but it rests on thin evidence.

claims.text: A fragment of his victory stela was found at Megiddo.
claims.note: Excavators found it in the 1920s. It proves his army really reached the town.

reigns.hook: Shoshenq dies with Canaan humbled and the treasury full. His son Osorkon I inherits it all, and he is about to give a staggering share of it to the gods.

images.caption: The Bubastite Portal at Karnak, carved with Shoshenq I's names. A monument from his reign, not a portrait.
images.alt: Carved stone gateway at Karnak temple bearing the cartouches of Shoshenq I

reigns.tagline: The king who poured silver and gold into the temples
reigns.previously: Shoshenq I dies, leaving his son a rich, united kingdom.
paragraphs: Osorkon I took over the rich kingdom his father had built, and he spent like it. An inscription from the temple at Bubastis, his family's home town, lists his gifts to the gods in his first four years: gold, silver and lapis lazuli, entry after entry. Added up, it comes to a staggering weight of precious metal, quite possibly the loot from his father's raid into Canaan.

His name carried abroad. A statue of him went to Byblos on the Lebanese coast, where the local king Elibaal had his own dedication carved on it in Phoenician. At home he kept Thebes in the family: his sons served one after another as high priest of Amun, so the god's vast wealth stayed under the king's eye.

One son, Shoshenq, may have been made co-king and died before his father. In 1939 Pierre Montet found a king named Heqakheperre Shoshenq at Tanis, buried in a silver coffin with a falcon's head. Shaw calls him Shoshenq II. Osorkon I died about 889 BC, and another son, Takelot, took the throne.

claims.text: Osorkon I gave the temples hundreds of tonnes of silver and gold.
claims.note: The Bubastis list survives in pieces. Modern totals depend on how the damaged figures are restored and how much a deben weighed.

claims.text: A statue of Osorkon I at Byblos carries an inscription of the local king Elibaal.
claims.note: The statue, now in the Louvre, has Osorkon's names and a Phoenician dedication by Elibaal of Byblos.

claims.text: Shoshenq II, buried in a silver falcon coffin at Tanis, was Osorkon I's son and co-king.
claims.note: The burial is real. Making him Osorkon's son and co-ruler is a reconstruction from a high priest of the same name.

reigns.hook: Osorkon I's long reign is over. His son Takelot I takes the throne and then all but disappears: he is one of the most invisible kings Egypt ever had.

reigns.tagline: The king who nearly vanished from history
reigns.previously: Osorkon I dies after showering the gods with silver and gold.
paragraphs: Takelot I reigned about 15 years and left almost nothing behind: no temple, no statue anyone can be sure of. For a long time some scholars wondered whether he had really been king at all. His mother was Tashedkhonsu, a lesser wife of Osorkon I, and his half-brothers held the high priesthood of Amun at Thebes while he ruled in the Delta.

The proof he was king comes from a family tree. About a century and a half later a priest named Pasenhor set up a stela at the Serapeum, the burial place of the Apis bulls, listing his ancestors back to the first Libyan chief who settled in Egypt. Takelot sits there as king, between Osorkon I and Osorkon II.

In the tomb of Osorkon II at Tanis, Pierre Montet found a second burial, of a King Takelot, with a bracelet of Osorkon I among its grave goods. He took it for Takelot II, but many now think it is this Takelot, laid to rest by his son. Takelot I died about 874 BC.

claims.text: Pasenhor's stela lists Takelot I as a king between Osorkon I and Osorkon II.
claims.note: The genealogy, set up at the Serapeum in the reign of Shoshenq V, is now in the Louvre.

claims.text: The burial found in Osorkon II's tomb is Takelot I's.
claims.note: Montet thought it was Takelot II's. Later work on the throne names points to Takelot I, but the debate is not closed.

reigns.hook: Takelot I dies almost unnoticed. His son Osorkon II will make up for it, with a grand jubilee hall at Bubastis and a cousin at Thebes who calls himself king.

images.caption: The stone sarcophagus in Osorkon II's tomb at Tanis that many now credit to Takelot I. A burial, not a portrait.
images.alt: A large stone sarcophagus inside a ruined stone tomb chamber at Tanis

reigns.tagline: The king found in a silver coffin
reigns.previously: Osorkon I's long reign is coming to an end.
paragraphs: Shoshenq II is known almost entirely from his tomb, found intact at Tanis in 1939. He lay in a silver coffin with a falcon head, wearing a gold mask and fine jewellery.
He probably ruled only briefly, perhaps beside his father Osorkon I. Study of his skull found he died of an infection that spread from a head wound.
reigns.hook: Takelot I rules on, and the dynasty's grip on Egypt slowly weakens.

reigns.tagline: A grand jubilee, and a cousin who called himself king
reigns.previously: Takelot I dies, a king who left almost no trace.
paragraphs: Osorkon II ruled about 24 years and made sure people knew it. At Bubastis he built a hall for his sed festival, the jubilee meant to renew a king's strength, its granite gateway covered with scenes of the rites. Pieces of it are now in the British Museum and other collections.

Not everyone took orders from him. At Thebes his cousin Harsiese, son of a high priest of Amun, took a king's titles and a cartouche of his own. After Harsiese died, Osorkon put his own sons in the key posts: Nimlot as high priest of Amun at Thebes and Shoshenq as high priest of Ptah at Memphis.

An Assyrian inscription of Shalmaneser III lists 1,000 men from Musri among his enemies at the battle of Qarqar in Syria in 853 BC, perhaps a token force sent by Osorkon. He was buried at Tanis in a stone tomb inside the temple walls; when Montet opened it in 1939, robbers had been there first. Takelot II came next.

claims.text: His cousin Harsiese ruled at Thebes as a rival king.
claims.note: Harsiese's own monuments and burial at Medinet Habu give him royal titles. How much real power he had is less clear.

claims.text: Osorkon II sent troops to fight Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC.
claims.note: Shalmaneser III's Kurkh Monolith lists 1,000 men from Musri. Most read that as Egypt, but some think it means a land in Anatolia.

claims.text: His Bubastis festival hall was carved with the rites of his jubilee.
claims.note: Blocks excavated by Edouard Naville in the 1880s are now in London, Cairo and elsewhere.

reigns.hook: Osorkon II is dead. The next king, Takelot II, will make his own son high priest at Thebes, and Thebes will not take it lying down.

reigns.tagline: Thebes rises, and the crown prince strikes back
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son or grandson of Osorkon II
reigns.previously: Osorkon II dies and is buried in his stone tomb at Tanis.
paragraphs: Takelot II's reign is remembered for one thing: civil war at Thebes. In his year 11 he made his son, Prince Osorkon, high priest of Amun. The Thebans would not have him. The prince sailed south, beat the rebels, had the leaders brought before him and put to death, and had their bodies burned.

It did not last. In year 15 a strange omen, often read as an eclipse of the moon, came before years of fighting in which the prince was driven from Thebes again and again. We know all this because he had his own Chronicle carved on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak, so the rebels come off very badly.

Where Takelot himself ruled is a puzzle. Shaw counts him a 22nd Dynasty king in the north; others think he was a king of the south only. He died about 825 BC, and the throne at Tanis went to Shoshenq III, not to Prince Osorkon.

claims.text: Prince Osorkon executed the Theban rebels and had their bodies burned.
claims.note: His Chronicle at Karnak says so. It is his own account, carved to justify him.

claims.text: The year 15 omen was an eclipse of the moon.
claims.note: The Chronicle's wording about the sky and the moon is obscure. Reading it as an eclipse has been used to fix dates, and challenged.

claims.text: Takelot II ruled only in Upper Egypt, not from Tanis.
claims.note: David Aston and others argue for a Theban king; Shaw and Kitchen keep him in the Tanis line.

reigns.hook: Takelot II is dead, but his eldest son Osorkon does not become king. A man named Shoshenq III does, and the prince is left fighting for Thebes.

images.alt: Line drawing of a carved relief: a king on the left facing the seated god Amun-Ra on the right

reigns.tagline: A long reign while the kingdom split apart
reigns.reignEnded: Died after decades on the throne
reigns.previously: Takelot II dies. His son Osorkon is still fighting for Thebes.
paragraphs: Shoshenq III sat on the throne at Tanis for decades, about 52 years in Shaw's scheme. He may have been a younger son of Takelot II who pushed his brother, Prince Osorkon, out of the way. If so, the prince never forgot it.

He never ruled all Egypt. In his early years a rival named Pedubast I was proclaimed king in the south, and Theban records began giving the years of both kings side by side. Shoshenq kept the Delta and the old capital Memphis, where an Apis bull was buried in his year 28.

He spent his time at Tanis, where he built a temple gateway and a tomb inside the temple walls with a huge granite sarcophagus. Montet found it robbed. Shoshenq III died about 773 BC, and Pimay took the throne.

claims.text: Shoshenq III reigned for over 50 years.
claims.note: Shaw's dates give about 52 years, but his own dated records reach about year 39. A separate Shoshenq IV may fill the rest.

claims.text: He pushed aside his elder brother, Prince Osorkon.
claims.note: The family tie is a reconstruction. The prince was crown prince under Takelot II and yet did not succeed him.

claims.text: Theban records were dated by the years of two kings at once.
claims.note: The Nile-level records on the quay at Karnak pair Pedubast I's years with Shoshenq III's.

reigns.hook: Shoshenq III sits tight in the Delta. Up the Nile, Thebes has a king of its own: Pedubast I, who owes nothing to Tanis.

reigns.tagline: The rival king who split the crown in two
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival of Shoshenq III; origin unknown
reigns.previously: Shoshenq III rules at Tanis, but Thebes wants a king of its own.
paragraphs: Around 818 BC a man named Pedubast took the full titles of a pharaoh. Later tradition counts him as founder of a new line, the 23rd Dynasty, and Shaw places it at Leontopolis in the Delta. Many now think his real base was Thebes. Either way, Egypt now had two crowned kings at the same time.

Pedubast backed the Theban side against Prince Osorkon. His ally Harsiese held the office of high priest of Amun, and the prince's Chronicle tells of him being shut out of the city again and again. Pedubast also took a co-king, Iuput I, and records at Karnak give their years together.
He reigned about 25 years and died about 793 BC. A short-lived king named Shoshenq followed him in the south, and then a far more famous name.

claims.text: Pedubast's 23rd Dynasty ruled from Leontopolis.
claims.note: That follows Manetho's tradition as Shaw reads it. Many Egyptologists now see it as a line of kings based at Thebes.

claims.text: Iuput I ruled as Pedubast's co-king.
claims.note: A Nile-level record on the Karnak quay gives a year of Pedubast together with a year of Iuput.

reigns.hook: Pedubast dies. After a brief successor, the crown of the south passes to Osorkon III, very likely the same Prince Osorkon who fought Thebes for years.

reigns.tagline: The prince who fought for Thebes and won at last
reigns.reignEnded: Died; his son Takelot III ruled on
reigns.previously: Pedubast I dies. A short-lived Shoshenq follows him in the south.
paragraphs: Osorkon III ruled the south for about 28 years from about 787 BC. Many Egyptologists think he was Prince Osorkon himself, the crown prince passed over decades earlier, who had fought for Thebes most of his life. If so, he was an old man by now, and he had finally won.

Early in his reign the Nile rose higher than anyone could remember. An inscription from his year 3 describes Thebes swamped like a sea, with the temples standing in water. He placed his daughter Shepenupet I in the post of God's Wife of Amun, a princess who never married and ran the god's estate at Thebes.
Near the end he made his son Takelot III co-king, so the south passed smoothly to the family. Osorkon III died about 759 BC. In the Delta, meanwhile, the kings at Tanis kept changing.

claims.text: Osorkon III was the same man as Prince Osorkon of the Chronicle.
claims.note: Argued by David Aston and others from names and dates. It would make him very old as king, which some find hard to accept.

claims.text: A great flood swamped Thebes in his year 3.
claims.note: His inscription on the temple of Luxor describes it, paraphrased here.

claims.text: His daughter Shepenupet I became God's Wife of Amun.
claims.note: Her monuments at Karnak, some shared with her father and brother, give her the title.

reigns.hook: At Tanis, old Shoshenq III has finally died. The new king in the north has a name that probably means "the cat": Pimay.

reigns.tagline: A Delta king whose name meant "the cat"
reigns.previously: Osorkon III rules the south. At Tanis, Shoshenq III is dead.
paragraphs: Pimay reigned at Tanis for only about six years. His name probably means "the cat", fitting for a family from Bubastis, the city of the cat goddess Bastet. He was probably a son of Shoshenq III. By now the king at Tanis was just one ruler among several, with Osorkon III holding the south and local chiefs running much of the Delta.

His best record comes from the Serapeum at Saqqara. In his year 2 an Apis bull, the living sign of the god Ptah, was buried there with full honours, and officials left stelae dated to his reign. Pimay died about 767 BC, and his son Shoshenq V took over at Tanis.

claims.text: Pimay's name means "the cat".
claims.note: The usual reading is Egyptian Pa-miu, "the tomcat". It fits a family from Bubastis, but the reading is not certain.

claims.text: An Apis bull was buried in his year 2.
claims.note: Stelae from the Serapeum at Saqqara, found by Auguste Mariette, are dated to his year 2.

claims.text: Pimay was a son of Shoshenq III.
claims.note: Widely assumed from the order of kings at Tanis, but no text says so outright.

reigns.hook: Pimay dies after a few short years. His son Shoshenq V will reign at Tanis for almost four decades, while in the west the chiefs of Sais start to stir.

reigns.tagline: The quiet king at Tanis while Egypt came apart
reigns.reignEnded: Reigned on at Tanis to about 730 BC
reigns.previously: Pimay dies after a few short years at Tanis.
paragraphs: Shoshenq V, throne name Aakheperre, took over at Tanis from Pimay, probably his father, and then simply kept going. Shaw gives him 767 to 730 BC, about 37 years, one of the longest reigns of the age. On paper he was king of all Egypt. In practice his word counted in the north-eastern Delta and not much further, while Thebes looked to its own rival king, Osorkon III, and his family.

His years are easiest to follow through the sacred Apis bulls of Memphis. When a bull died it was buried in the vast catacomb of the Serapeum, and priests and pilgrims left dated stelae beside it. Shoshenq's year 11 and year 37 both turn up there. At Tanis he put up a chapel for his sed festival, the jubilee meant to renew an ageing king's strength.

The real action, though, was in the western Delta. The chiefs of Sais, led by an ambitious man named Tefnakht, were swallowing town after town. Shoshenq lived on at Tanis until about 730 BC, but by then Egypt's future was being decided by others, and his line ended with him or soon after.

claims.text: Shoshenq V reigned for at least 37 years.
claims.note: Apis stelae from the Serapeum at Saqqara, found by Auguste Mariette, are dated to his years 11 and 37.

claims.text: He was the son of the previous king, Pimay.
claims.note: Assumed from the order of the Tanis kings; no surviving monument spells out the relationship.

claims.text: He built a jubilee chapel at Tanis for his sed festival.
claims.note: Blocks from a building named for his jubilee were found reused at Tanis. Whether the festival itself was held is less certain.

reigns.hook: Tefnakht of Sais is marching south and the princes of Middle Egypt are terrified. Far up the Nile, a king of Kush named Piye decides it is time to restore order, his way.

images.alt: A small round-topped stone stela with carved figures and hieroglyphs, from the Apis burials at Saqqara, in the Louvre.

reigns.tagline: He conquered Egypt, then fussed over the horses
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Kashta, king of Kush
reigns.previously: Shoshenq V rules at Tanis; Tefnakht of Sais is rising.
paragraphs: Piye, also written Piankhi, was king of Kush, ruling from Napata below the fourth cataract in what is now Sudan. The Kushites had taken Egyptian religion to heart and worshipped Amun at Gebel Barkal, their holy mountain. The Greeks later called them Ethiopians. When Tefnakht of Sais pushed south, Piye sent his army north and then came himself. He counts as the first of the 25th Dynasty, the Kushite 'black pharaohs'.

His great granite stela from Gebel Barkal tells the tale. He stopped at Thebes for the festivals, besieged Hermopolis and stormed Memphis. When King Nimlot of Hermopolis gave up, Piye toured the stables and was more upset that the horses had gone hungry than by the revolt. The Delta kings came to submit, but only Nimlot was let into the palace. The others ate fish, which made them unclean.
Then Piye sailed home to Napata, loaded with treasure, and as far as we know he never came back. He was buried under a pyramid at el-Kurru, with his horses buried nearby.

claims.text: Piye's horses were buried standing up.
claims.note: The horse burials at el-Kurru are real, but whether the animals were placed upright is an old description, not certain.

claims.text: Piye never returned to Egypt after his campaign.
claims.note: No source shows him back in Egypt, but the record is thin. It may just be silence.

claims.text: Piye's campaign came about 728 BC.
claims.note: The stela dates it to his year 21. Turning that into a BC date depends on when his reign began.

reigns.hook: Piye has gone home and left the beaten kings in place. One of them, Osorkon IV of Tanis, must now keep both Kush and the Assyrians happy.

reigns.tagline: A Delta king who bowed to Kush and sent horses to Assyria
reigns.reignEnded: Fades from view as Shabaqo takes over
reigns.previously: Piye goes home to Napata, leaving the beaten kings in place.
paragraphs: Osorkon IV, throne name Usermaatre, was the last king of the old Libyan line at Tanis. He held Tanis and Bubastis in the north-eastern Delta and little else. When Piye marched north, Osorkon joined the Delta lords who came to kneel before the Kushite. On Piye's Victory Stela he is 'King Osorkon in Bubastis', one of four rulers it calls kings. A block from Tanis may show his face.

His real problem lay to the east. Assyria was swallowing the kingdoms of the Levant. The Bible says Hoshea, the last king of Israel, sent messengers to 'So, king of Egypt' for help against Assyria, and got none. In 716 BC the Assyrian king Sargon II reached the Egyptian border, and a ruler of Egypt named Shilkanni sent him twelve big horses as a gift. Both may be Osorkon.
After that he disappears. Shabaqo of Kush came north and took the whole country, and the line of the Tanite kings ended with Osorkon IV.

claims.text: Osorkon IV is the biblical 'So, king of Egypt' whom Hoshea of Israel asked for help.
claims.note: 2 Kings 17:4. Many scholars make 'So' a garbled form of Osorkon, or of Sais; others say it is not a king at all.

claims.text: He is the 'Shilkanni' who sent Sargon II twelve horses in 716 BC.
claims.note: Sargon's annals name Shilkanni, king of Egypt. The name looks like Osorkon, and the date fits.

claims.text: He submitted to Piye.
claims.note: Piye's Victory Stela names him among the kings who came to submit.

reigns.hook: But one man never really gave up. Go back to about 727 BC: Tefnakht of Sais, the rebel Piye came north to crush, has sworn loyalty, and he is about to break his word.

reigns.tagline: Piye's great enemy, who crowned himself anyway
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Prince of Sais, rival of Piye
reigns.previously: Osorkon IV bows to Kush and woos Assyria. He fades from history.
paragraphs: Tefnakht started as a prince of Sais and 'Great Chief of the West'. By the 720s BC he had swallowed the western Delta and Memphis and was pushing south up the Nile. That brought Piye down from Kush. Piye's army smashed his allies, and Tefnakht fled to the islands of the Delta marshes, then sent a grovelling message: he could not bear to face the king's fury, so would Piye please accept his surrender from afar?

Piye sent two officials, and Tefnakht swore an oath of loyalty in a temple and handed over his treasure. Then Piye went home to Napata, and Tefnakht went straight back to work. He took a full set of royal names, Shepsesre Tefnakht, and ruled as a king at Sais. A stone stela of his from Sais, given to the goddess Neith and now in Athens, is dated to his eighth year as king.
Later Egyptians counted his family as Manetho's 24th Dynasty, though Manetho's lists, as they survive, skip Tefnakht. When he died, the crown of Sais passed to his son Bakenrenef.

claims.text: Tefnakht surrendered to Piye from hiding, without ever meeting him.
claims.note: That is the account on Piye's Victory Stela. It is Piye's own version, so Tefnakht's grovelling may be laid on thick.

claims.text: Tefnakht was a Libyan chief.
claims.note: The old view. A recently published statue of his names his grandfather Basa as a priest of Amun near Sais, which points to an Egyptian priestly family.

claims.text: He ruled as king for at least eight years.
claims.note: His donation stela in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens is dated to year 8. Shaw's dates allow him about seven.

reigns.hook: Tefnakht dies at Sais. His son Bakenrenef takes the crown and the Greeks will remember him as a wise lawgiver, which makes his ending all the worse.

reigns.tagline: The wise king of Sais, and a talking lamb
reigns.previously: Tefnakht dies, a king at Sais against Piye's will.
paragraphs: Bakenrenef, whom the Greeks called Bocchoris, ruled from Sais as king of Lower Egypt. Manetho counts him as the whole of the 24th Dynasty and gives him six years. A stela from the Serapeum at Saqqara marks the burial of a sacred Apis bull in his sixth year, which proves his writ ran as far as Memphis.

Later writers loved him. Diodorus calls him a great lawgiver who sorted out the law of contracts and debts, though he says the king was weak in body. Manetho adds that in his reign a lamb spoke. A later Egyptian text, the Prophecy of the Lamb, has the creature foretell centuries of foreign rule and misery for Egypt. A faience vase with his name even turned up in a tomb at Tarquinia in Italy.

The real end was brutal. Shabaqo, Piye's successor, came north to finish what Piye had left undone. Manetho says he took Bakenrenef prisoner and burned him alive. With that, the Kushite 25th Dynasty ruled all Egypt.

claims.text: Shabaqo burned Bakenrenef alive.
claims.note: Only Manetho says so, in quotations by later writers. No Egyptian record mentions how he died.

claims.text: A lamb spoke in his reign and prophesied disaster for Egypt.
claims.note: Manetho reports it, and a Demotic text of Roman date, the Prophecy of the Lamb, tells the story in full.

claims.text: He was one of Egypt's great lawgivers.
claims.note: Diodorus, writing some 650 years later, credits him with laws on contracts. No law of his survives.

reigns.hook: Bakenrenef is dead and Sais is crushed. Shabaqo of Kush now rules from the Delta to the fourth cataract, the first Kushite to hold all of Egypt.

images.alt: Old drawing of a small round-topped stela with a carved scene and hieroglyphic inscription

reigns.tagline: The Kushite who came north and stayed
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded Piye as king of Kush
reigns.previously: Bakenrenef of Sais falls to Shabaqo, Piye's successor from Kush.
paragraphs: Piye had beaten the Delta kings and then gone home. His successor Shabaqo, also written Shabaka and probably his brother, came north to finish the job and stayed. In the Delta, Bakenrenef of Sais, whom the Greeks called Bocchoris, had made himself king. Shabaqo swept him away, and for the first time a Kushite pharaoh ruled the whole Nile valley, from the Delta to the fourth cataract.

He played the Egyptian king to perfection. He built at Karnak and elsewhere around Thebes, and his son Haremakhet later rose to be high priest of Amun there. Finding an old religious text 'eaten by worms', he had it copied onto a stone slab so it would last. Centuries later the slab was used as a millstone. It is now the Shabaka Stone in the British Museum.

Next door, Assyria had become the superpower of the age, and Shabaqo kept a wary peace with it. Clay sealings bearing his name turned up in the royal palace at Nineveh. He died about 702 BC and was taken home to Kush, to be buried under a pyramid at el-Kurru near Piye.

claims.text: Shabaqo captured Bakenrenef (Bocchoris) of Sais and burned him alive.
claims.note: Only Manetho says so, as quoted by later writers. No Egyptian record mentions it.

claims.text: Shabaqo reigned before Shebitqo.
claims.note: That is the traditional order and Shaw's. New readings of Assyrian and Egyptian texts since 2013 have led some scholars to put Shebitqo first.

claims.text: Clay sealings with Shabaqo's name were found at Nineveh.
claims.note: Found in the palace there by Austen Henry Layard's team and now in the British Museum. What they once sealed, perhaps a gift or a treaty, is unknown.

reigns.hook: Shabaqo is buried in Kush. The new king, Shebitqo, inherits all Egypt just as the Assyrian army rolls towards Judah, and Judah's king is counting on Egyptian help.

reigns.tagline: The Kushite pharaoh who sent an army against Assyria
reigns.previously: Shabaqo dies, master of all Egypt, and is buried at home in Kush.
paragraphs: Shebitqo, also written Shabataka, was probably a son of Piye. He inherited an empire that stretched from the Delta to the fourth cataract, and a dangerous neighbour. Assyria had already swallowed the kingdom of Israel and was squeezing the small states of the Levant. When King Hezekiah of Judah and the coastal cities rebelled against Sennacherib, they looked to Egypt for help.

In 701 BC help came. A Kushite and Egyptian army, with chariots and archers, marched into Judah and met Sennacherib at Eltekeh. The Assyrian annals claim a clean victory, and Sennacherib went on to besiege Jerusalem, though he never took it. Shebitqo also summoned the young princes of Kush north to his court. One was his kinsman Taharqa, aged 20, who later boasted he was the king's favourite.

Shebitqo has since become the centre of a puzzle. An inscription of the Assyrian king Sargon II, carved at Tang-i Var in Iran, names him as the king who handed over the fugitive rebel Iamani of Ashdod in chains around 706 BC. If so, he was already on the throne before Shabaqo's reign, as Shaw dates it, had ended. Either way, he died in 690 BC and was buried at el-Kurru.

claims.text: Shebitqo reigned after Shabaqo.
claims.note: Shaw's order. Sargon II's Tang-i Var inscription names Shebitqo as king around 706 BC, which has led many scholars since 2013 to put him first.

claims.text: The Assyrians won the battle of Eltekeh in 701 BC.
claims.note: Our only account is Sennacherib's own annals, which never admit a setback.

claims.text: Taharqa came north aged 20 when the king summoned the princes of Kush.
claims.note: Taharqa's own stelae from the temple at Kawa in Sudan say so. They do not give the year.

reigns.hook: Shebitqo is dead. His kinsman Taharqa, the prince who once came north with the army, is crowned at Memphis, ready to build like Ramesses and to face the Assyrians himself.

reigns.tagline: The Kushite builder-king who took on Assyria
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Kush, Egypt slipping away
reigns.previously: Shebitqo dies. Assyria is on the march in the Levant.
paragraphs: Taharqa was Piye's son and the greatest builder of the Kushite pharaohs, with grand works at Karnak, Kawa and Gebel Barkal. In his year 6 the Nile rose higher than anyone could remember, and his stela boasts that it brought rich harvests and killed off the rats and snakes. The Bible remembers him as 'Tirhakah king of Kush', marching out against Sennacherib.

But Assyria was coming. In 671 BC King Esarhaddon took Memphis. Taharqa escaped, wounded according to the Assyrians, but his wife and his son Ushankhuru were taken. Taharqa won Memphis back, only for Ashurbanipal's army to drive him south again in 667 or 666 BC.
He died in 664 BC and was buried at Nuri under the biggest pyramid ever built in Kush. His claim to Egypt passed to his heir Tanutamani, who meant to win it back.

claims.text: A small kneeling prisoner on Esarhaddon's victory stela from Sam'al is Taharqa's son Ushankhuru.
claims.note: The figure wears Kushite-style dress and the capture is recorded, but the stela does not name him.

claims.text: Taharqa marched against Sennacherib, as 2 Kings and Isaiah say.
claims.note: In 701 BC he was not yet king. The Bible may be naming him by his later title, or mixing up campaigns.

claims.text: His pyramid at Nuri is the largest in Kush.
claims.note: It is the biggest at Nuri and usually called the largest Kushite pyramid, though it was enlarged in stages.

reigns.hook: Taharqa is dead and Tanutamani sweeps north to take Egypt back. But at Sais a local prince named Psamtik has thrown in his lot with Assyria.

reigns.tagline: The Delta prince caught between empires
reigns.previously: The Kushite pharaohs rule Egypt, and Assyria is coming.
paragraphs: Necho I was king of Sais in the Nile Delta while the Kushite pharaohs ruled Egypt. When the Assyrians invaded, he sided with them, was taken to Nineveh for plotting, then sent back as their vassal.
He was killed in 664 BC, probably fighting the Kushite king Tanutamani. His son Psamtik I went on to reunite Egypt and found the Twenty-sixth Dynasty.
reigns.hook: Necho's son Psamtik escapes to Assyria and waits for his chance.

reigns.tagline: Assyria's puppet who quietly took back all of Egypt
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Necho I of Sais
reigns.previously: Taharqa dies in 664 BC, with Egypt slipping from Kush's grip.
paragraphs: Psamtik's father Necho I, lord of Sais, died in 664 BC, probably fighting Taharqa's heir Tanutamani, who swept back into Egypt. The Assyrians answered by sacking Thebes in 663 BC, a disaster so famous that the prophet Nahum held it up as a warning to Nineveh. Psamtik, set up by Assyria as a vassal king, kept his head down.

Then, while Assyria was busy elsewhere, he quietly became his own master. He hired Greek and Carian mercenaries. By 656 BC he controlled Thebes, where his daughter Nitocris was adopted as the next God's Wife of Amun, a peaceful way to take over the south. Egypt was one kingdom again, under the 26th Dynasty, and the Late Period had begun.

Herodotus loved him. In one tale he had two babies raised by a shepherd who never spoke a word to them, to find the world's oldest language. Their first word was 'bekos', Phrygian for bread. Meanwhile his artists copied the styles of the Old Kingdom, as if Egypt wanted its golden age back.

claims.text: An oracle told Psamtik help would come from 'bronze men' rising from the sea, who turned out to be armoured Greek pirates.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, two centuries later. The Greek mercenaries were real; the oracle is a story.

claims.text: Psamtik's language experiment proved the Phrygians were older than the Egyptians.
claims.note: Herodotus heard it from priests at Memphis and says the Greeks told sillier versions.

claims.text: He besieged the city of Ashdod for 29 years.
claims.note: Herodotus calls it the longest siege he knew of. Nothing else backs up the number.

reigns.hook: Psamtik dies after 54 years. His son Necho II looks north, where Assyria is crumbling and Babylon is rising, and decides Egypt should join in.

reigns.previously: Taharqa dies, and his nephew wants Egypt back.
paragraphs: Tanutamani marched north from Kush and retook Memphis, killing Necho I. A dream stela tells how two serpents in a dream promised him both crowns of Egypt.
The Assyrians answered by sacking Thebes in 663 BC. Tanutamani fell back to Nubia, and by 656 BC Upper Egypt accepted Psamtik I. He ruled on in Kush, the last of his line to claim Egypt.
reigns.hook: Kush loses Egypt for good, and Psamtik I reunites the land.

reigns.tagline: The pharaoh who sent sailors all the way round Africa
reigns.previously: Psamtik I dies after 54 years, leaving Egypt rich and free.
paragraphs: Necho inherited a strong Egypt in a dangerous neighbourhood. Assyria, the old overlord, was collapsing under attack from Babylon and the Medes. Necho decided a weak Assyria was safer than a strong Babylon, so he marched north to help it. In 609 BC King Josiah of Judah came out to block his path at Megiddo, and was killed there.

For a few years Necho ran Syria and Canaan, even picking Judah's next king. Then in 605 BC the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar smashed his army at Carchemish on the Euphrates. Egypt's empire in Asia was gone almost overnight, and Necho fell back to guard his own frontier.

At home he thought big. He started digging a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea and built war galleys for both seas. Herodotus says he also hired Phoenician crews to sail right round Africa. Necho died in 595 BC, and his son Psamtik II took the throne.

claims.text: Phoenician sailors sent by Necho sailed round Africa in about three years, and saw the sun on their right as they went round the south.
claims.note: Only Herodotus tells it, and he didn't believe the sun detail. That detail is exactly what you would see south of the equator, which persuades many that the voyage really happened.

claims.text: Necho gave up his canal after 120,000 workers died and an oracle warned he was building it for a foreigner.
claims.note: Herodotus, writing about 150 years later. The 'foreigner' was taken to be Darius I, who did finish a canal there.

claims.text: Nebuchadnezzar crushed Necho's army at Carchemish in 605 BC.
claims.note: Recorded in the Babylonian Chronicle and echoed in the Bible (Jeremiah 46).

reigns.hook: Necho's son Psamtik II inherits a smaller empire, an army of Greek mercenaries, and a grudge against the Kushite kings who once ruled Egypt.

reigns.tagline: Six years, a war on Kush and a lot of chiselling
reigns.previously: Necho II dies. His empire in Asia is lost, but Egypt is still rich.
paragraphs: Psamtik II, Psammetichus to the Greeks, reigned only six years, and he spent the most famous of them settling an old score. In 593 BC his army marched south into Kush, the homeland of the Kushite pharaohs who had ruled Egypt two generations before. Egyptian troops and foreign mercenaries went together, and they struck deep into Kushite land.

On the way, some of the mercenaries stopped at Abu Simbel and scratched their names into the legs of Ramesses II's giant statues, in Greek and in Carian. One Greek graffito records that King Psammetichos had come to Elephantine, and names the officers who led the foreigners and the Egyptians. These scratches are among the earliest Greek writing that can be dated.

At home Psamtik had the names of the Kushite kings chiselled off monuments up and down Egypt, as if their dynasty had never been. He also kept Thebes in the family by having his daughter Ankhnesneferibre adopted as the future God's Wife of Amun. He died in 589 BC, leaving his son Apries a strong army and big ambitions.

claims.text: Greek and Carian soldiers carved their names on the colossi of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel.
claims.note: The graffiti are still there. The longest names Potasimto as leader of the foreigners and Amasis as leader of the Egyptians.

claims.text: His army smashed the statues of the Kushite kings at Kerma.
claims.note: Broken statues of Kushite kings found buried at Dukki Gel near Kerma in 2003 are often linked to this campaign, but how far the army went is argued over.

claims.text: Psamtik II had the Kushite kings' names hacked off monuments.
claims.note: Erased names of Shabaqo, Taharqa and others can be seen on many monuments, and most scholars date the damage to his reign.

reigns.hook: Psamtik II is dead after six years. His son Apries wants Egypt to count in Asia again, just as Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon is about to march on Jerusalem.

reigns.tagline: He backed Jerusalem against Babylon and lost his army
reigns.previously: Psamtik II dies after six years, his Kushite enemies erased.
paragraphs: Apries, the Hophra of the Bible, was a man in a hurry. He wanted Egypt back in the game in Asia, where Babylon now ruled. He encouraged King Zedekiah of Judah to rebel, and when Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, an Egyptian army marched out and the Babylonians pulled back for a while. Then they returned. Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC and its temple was burned.

Refugees from Judah poured into Egypt, the prophet Jeremiah among them, and he warned that Hophra too would be handed over to his enemies. In 570 BC Apries sent an army west against Cyrene, the Greek city in Libya. It was cut to pieces, and the survivors decided the king had sent them off to die so that he could rule the rest more safely.

The army mutinied. Apries sent his general Amasis to calm them, and instead the soldiers hailed Amasis as king. Apries fought back with his Greek mercenaries and lost. He lived on for a few years as a king without a kingdom, and died about 567 BC, probably killed trying to win his throne back.

claims.text: An Egyptian army made the Babylonians lift the siege of Jerusalem for a while.
claims.note: The Book of Jeremiah, chapter 37, says so. The Babylonian Chronicle is missing for these years, so nothing confirms it.

claims.text: When Apries's envoy Patarbemis came back without Amasis, Apries had his nose and ears cut off, and the outraged Egyptians went over to Amasis.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 2. A good story told over a century later, with no Egyptian evidence.

claims.text: Apries was killed around 567 BC while trying to win back his throne.
claims.note: A damaged stela of Amasis seems to describe a battle and Apries's burial with honours. Herodotus says the crowd strangled him. Dates and details differ.

reigns.hook: Apries is finished. Egypt's new king is the general Amasis, a soldier of humble birth who once answered a royal summons with a very rude noise.

reigns.tagline: The joking, drinking general the Greeks adored
reigns.reignEnded: Died just before the Persians came
reigns.previously: Mutinous troops crown the general Amasis. Apries is finished.
paragraphs: The Greeks called him Amasis, and they loved him. He was a soldier of humble birth, and Herodotus fills pages with stories about him: a joker, a drinker, a man who never pretended to be grander than he was. When Apries summoned him during the mutiny, he is said to have answered by breaking wind and telling the messenger to take that back.

As king he was shrewd. He made Naukratis in the Delta the official base for Greek traders, sent rich gifts to Greek temples and made friends with Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos. He took Cyprus. Egypt had rarely been so peaceful or so rich.

But to the east, Persia was swallowing everything. Cyrus the Great took Lydia and then Babylon, and Egypt was clearly next on the list. Amasis died in 526 BC, months before the blow fell, leaving his son Psamtik III to face it.

claims.text: Amasis melted down a golden footbath and made it into a statue of a god, to show his subjects that something humble could become worthy of honour, just like him.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 2. A lovely parable, but nothing outside Herodotus backs it up.

claims.text: He worked in the mornings and drank in the afternoons, telling critics that a bow kept strung all the time will snap.
claims.note: Herodotus again, who loved Amasis stories. Treat it as character sketch, not history.

claims.text: Amasis broke off his friendship with Polycrates after Polycrates threw away a precious ring and got it back inside a fish.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 3. Amasis supposedly decided a man that lucky was doomed. Polycrates did come to a grisly end.

reigns.hook: Amasis is dead. His son Psamtik III has barely settled on the throne when the Persian king Cambyses arrives at the edge of the Delta with the army of the greatest empire on earth.

reigns.tagline: The last pharaoh before the Persians
reigns.previously: Amasis II dies just as the Persians march on Egypt.
paragraphs: Psamtik III became king only months before the Persian king Cambyses II invaded. He lost the battle of Pelusium in 525 BC, and Memphis fell after a siege.
Herodotus says Cambyses first spared him, then forced him to drink bull's blood after he was caught plotting a revolt. Egypt became a Persian province.
reigns.hook: Egypt is now a province of Persia, ruled by Cambyses.

reigns.tagline: The Persian conqueror who put on the double crown
reigns.reignEnded: Died of a wound on the way home
reigns.previously: Amasis dies. His son Psamtik III inherits Persia at the door.
paragraphs: Cambyses, son of Cyrus the Great, came for Egypt in 525 BC. He met the new pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium, the gateway to the eastern Delta, and won. Memphis fell after a siege and Psamtik was taken prisoner. For the first time Egypt was a province of the Persian empire, and later king lists count Cambyses as the founder of the 27th Dynasty.

Egyptian records show him taking care to act the pharaoh. Udjahorresnet, who had commanded Egypt's navy, says on his statue that he gave Cambyses an Egyptian throne name and that the king cleared squatters out of the temple of Neith at Sais. Greek writers told a darker story, of a cruel madman who mocked Egypt's gods.

Herodotus adds an army lost in the desert and a failed march on Kush. In 522 BC news came of a rebellion back in Persia. Cambyses set off for home, but died on the way in Syria, from a wound in his thigh.

claims.text: Cambyses went mad and stabbed the sacred Apis bull, which died of the wound.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, but records from the Apis burial ground at Saqqara show a bull buried with full honours in Cambyses' reign.

claims.text: An army of 50,000 sent to the oasis of Siwa vanished in a sandstorm.
claims.note: Only Herodotus reports it. Explorers still hunt for the lost army, so far without convincing finds.

claims.text: At Pelusium the Persians drove cats and other sacred animals in front of their lines, so the Egyptians would not shoot.
claims.note: Told by the Greek writer Polyaenus some 700 years later. Herodotus, much closer in time, doesn't mention it.

reigns.hook: Cambyses is dead and Persia is in chaos. Out of it climbs Darius, a distant royal cousin, who will win over Egypt's priests by behaving like a true pharaoh.

reigns.tagline: The Persian who finished the pharaohs' canal
reigns.previously: Cambyses dies on the road home. Persia's throne is up for grabs.
paragraphs: Darius took the Persian throne in 522 BC by killing the man who held it, then spent a year crushing revolts across the empire. Egypt was one of the rebel provinces. Later, Herodotus says, Darius had his governor of Egypt, Aryandes, put to death for minting his own silver coins, a privilege that belonged to the king.

In Egypt, Darius played the pharaoh better than any Persian before or after. He sent Udjahorresnet home to restore the House of Life at Sais, a temple school for scribes and doctors. He built a temple to Amun at Hibis in the Kharga oasis, which still stands. Later Egyptians remembered him as a great lawgiver.

His proudest work was finishing Necho's canal from the Nile to the Red Sea. Along it he set up granite stelae in hieroglyphs and Persian cuneiform, boasting that ships now sailed from Egypt to Persia. After the Persian defeat at Marathon in 490 BC, Egypt rose in revolt again. Darius died in 486 BC before he could deal with it.

claims.text: Darius had Egypt's laws collected and written down.
claims.note: Reported by the Demotic Chronicle, written centuries later, and by Diodorus, who lists him among Egypt's great lawgivers.

claims.text: Aryandes was executed for striking his own silver coinage.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 4. Some historians think the real charge was rebellion, and the coins just a sign of it.

claims.text: A statue of Darius carved in Egypt, with hieroglyphs on its base, was found at Susa in Persia.
claims.note: Excavated at Susa in 1972 and now in Tehran. The base lists the peoples of the empire.

reigns.hook: Darius is dead and Egypt is in open revolt. His son Xerxes is coming, and he has none of his father's patience with Egyptian priests.

reigns.tagline: The Great King who crushed Egypt and took its fleet
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Darius I and Atossa
reigns.previously: Darius dies with Egypt in revolt. Xerxes inherits the problem.
paragraphs: Xerxes inherited the Persian Empire with Egypt in open revolt, and he dealt with Egypt before he looked at Greece. In his second year, 484 BC, his army retook the country. Herodotus says he left Egypt far more harshly ruled than it had been under Darius. He made his own brother Achaemenes governor, and unlike his father he made little effort to play the pharaoh.

What he wanted from Egypt was ships and men. When he invaded Greece in 480 BC, Egypt supplied 200 warships, Herodotus says, and Egyptian marines were praised as the best fighters on the Persian side at the sea battle of Artemisium. Then came the disaster at Salamis, and the Great King went home with his plans for Greece in ruins.

Egyptians remembered him badly. In 311 BC, over 170 years later, a stela set up for Ptolemy, then governor of Egypt, accused 'the enemy Xerxes' of taking land from the temple of Buto. In 465 BC Xerxes was murdered in his palace by his own courtiers, and the news would set Egypt stirring again.

claims.text: Xerxes left Egypt more harshly ruled than his father had.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 7, says so. Egyptian evidence from his reign is thin, though no temple building in his name is known.

claims.text: The Egyptians fought best of all Xerxes' forces at Artemisium.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 8. He gives the praise and the figure of 200 ships, and both are hard to check.

claims.text: A later stela blames Xerxes for seizing temple land at Buto.
claims.note: The Satrap Stela of 311 BC, now in Cairo, says so. It is Ptolemaic propaganda against Persia, so hardly neutral.

reigns.hook: Xerxes lies murdered. His young son Artaxerxes fights his way to the throne, and in the Delta men are whispering that Persia is weak.

reigns.tagline: Forty years on the throne, and a revolt that nearly won
reigns.cameToPower: Seized the throne after Xerxes' murder
reigns.previously: Xerxes is murdered in 465 BC. Persia's throne is up for grabs.
paragraphs: Artaxerxes was a younger son of Xerxes, and still young when his father was killed. In the bloody confusion that followed, his elder brother Darius was killed and so was the courtier Artabanus, who was blamed for the murder, and Artaxerxes took the throne. The Greeks called him Longimanus, 'long-handed', and Plutarch says his right hand really was longer than his left.

Egypt saw its chance at once. Around 460 BC a Libyan prince named Inaros led the Delta into revolt and called in an Athenian fleet. It took the king's best general, Megabyzus, and years of hard fighting to win the country back. After that, Artaxerxes left Egypt to his governors, and the province settled into a long, grudging calm.

That calm let Herodotus tour Egypt, quizzing priests at Memphis and Heliopolis. Far to the south, Jewish soldiers of the Persian garrison on Elephantine Island dated their marriage deeds and loans by Artaxerxes' years. He died in 424 BC, and within months two of his sons had been killed in the fight to succeed him.

claims.text: Artaxerxes' right hand was longer than his left, hence the name Longimanus.
claims.note: Plutarch, writing over 500 years later, explains the nickname this way. It may simply have meant a king with a long reach.

claims.text: His brother Darius was wrongly blamed for their father's murder and put to death.
claims.note: Ctesias and later Greek writers tell versions of the palace plot. They disagree on the details, and Persian records say nothing.

claims.text: The Elephantine papyri are dated by his regnal years.
claims.note: Aramaic contracts from the garrison, such as a marriage document of 449 BC now in the Brooklyn Museum, are dated in his reign.

reigns.hook: But go back to about 460 BC. In the western Delta a Libyan prince named Inaros has just thrown out the Persian tax collectors, and an Athenian fleet is on its way to help him.

reigns.tagline: The rebel prince who brought Athens to the Nile
reigns.cameToPower: Led a revolt from Marea, west Delta
reigns.previously: Artaxerxes I is king, but Egypt smells weakness in Persia.
paragraphs: Inaros, son of a man named Psamtik, was a Libyan prince from the western edge of the Delta. Around 460 BC he threw out the Persian tax collectors, and most of Egypt rallied to him. He knew Persia would come back in force, so he asked Athens for help. An Athenian fleet, campaigning off Cyprus with some 200 ships, sailed for the Nile instead.

At Papremis in the Delta, Inaros beat the Persian army and killed its commander Achaemenes, the governor of Egypt and the Great King's uncle. The Athenians sailed up to Memphis and took most of the city, trapping the Persian garrison in the citadel known as the White Wall. For a moment it looked as if Egypt was free.

Then Megabyzus arrived with a fresh army. He drove the Greeks out of Memphis and penned them on the island of Prosopitis for 18 months, until he drained the channel and marched across. Inaros was betrayed and handed over, and around 454 BC the Persians put him to death, impaled or crucified. Egypt was Persian again.

claims.text: Herodotus visited the battlefield of Papremis and found the Egyptian skulls far thicker than the Persian ones.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 3, says he saw the bones himself and blames the Egyptians' shaven heads baking in the sun. A traveller's tale.

claims.text: Megabyzus promised Inaros his life, but the queen mother Amestris later had him executed anyway.
claims.note: Ctesias, a Greek doctor at the Persian court, tells it. He is colourful and often unreliable, and Thucydides says only that Inaros was betrayed.

claims.text: Almost the whole Athenian expedition was lost, along with 50 relief ships that sailed into the Nile unaware.
claims.note: Thucydides, book 1. Historians argue over how big the force and its losses really were.

reigns.hook: Inaros is dead and the revolt is over. Artaxerxes reigns on until 424 BC, and after a vicious family scramble his son Ochus takes the throne as Darius II.

reigns.tagline: He killed his way to the throne, then lost Egypt
reigns.previously: Inaros is dead, and Artaxerxes I holds Egypt until he dies in 424 BC.
paragraphs: When Artaxerxes I died in 424 BC, Persia got three kings in a year. His heir Xerxes II was murdered after about six weeks by his half-brother Sogdianus. Then another half-brother, Ochus, son of a Babylonian concubine, raised an army, captured Sogdianus and had him put to death. Ochus took the name Darius II. Egypt, far away, simply changed the name at the top of its documents.

Egypt was run for him by the satrap Arsames, whose orders to his estate managers survive as letters on leather. On Elephantine Island, a Jewish garrison guarded the southern border. In 410 BC, with Arsames away, priests of the ram god Khnum got the local Persian commander to help them wreck the Jewish temple there. The garrison wrote to the governor of Judah, begging for help to rebuild it.
By the end of his reign the Delta was stirring. Darius died at Babylon in 404 BC, and his sons were soon fighting each other. In Egypt, a rebel prince of Sais was already acting like a king.

claims.text: Darius II had his rival Sogdianus executed by smothering him in hot ash.
claims.note: From Ctesias, a Greek doctor at the Persian court, whose history survives only in summaries and loves lurid detail.

claims.text: The Jews of Elephantine asked the governor of Judah to help rebuild the temple wrecked in 410 BC.
claims.note: Drafts of the petition, written in Aramaic in 407 BC, survive among the Elephantine papyri, with a note granting permission.

claims.text: Shaw ends his reign in 405 BC.
claims.note: The Oxford History gives 424 to 405 BC; Babylonian records put his death in 404 BC, the date used here.

reigns.hook: Darius II is dead, and in the Delta a prince of Sais named Amyrtaeus is ready to throw the Persians out.

reigns.tagline: The one-man dynasty that freed Egypt from Persia
reigns.previously: Darius II dies in 404 BC, and Persia's hold on Egypt starts to slip.
paragraphs: Amyrtaeus, Amenirdis in Egyptian, came from Sais in the western Delta, the old home town of the 26th Dynasty. When Darius II died and Persia's royal family turned on itself, he broke away. The timing was perfect. A Persian army gathering in Syria to retake Egypt was pulled away in 401 BC to deal with Cyrus the Younger, who was marching on his brother the king.

Slowly the whole country came over. Far south on Elephantine, Jewish soldiers who had served Persia started dating their contracts by the years of Amyrtaeus. He is the only king Manetho lists for the 28th Dynasty, with six years. Then a rival from Mendes, Nepherites, overthrew him. One Aramaic letter from Elephantine hints that Amyrtaeus was put to death at Memphis.

claims.text: Amyrtaeus was executed at Memphis by Nepherites.
claims.note: Based on one Aramaic letter from Elephantine. The wording is brief and its meaning is argued over.

claims.text: He was the grandson of the Amyrtaeus who fought the Persians alongside Inaros.
claims.note: Herodotus mentions an earlier Amyrtaeus holding out in the marshes. The family link is a modern guess from the name.

claims.text: Elephantine documents were dated by his reign.
claims.note: An Aramaic papyrus in the Brooklyn Museum is dated to his fifth year, showing the far south accepted him.

reigns.hook: Amyrtaeus is gone. The new king comes from Mendes, and his name is Nepherites. He knows Persia will be back, and he needs friends fast.
