reigns.tagline: He sent Sparta grain for a war with Persia
reigns.previously: Amyrtaeus is overthrown by a rival from Mendes in the Delta.
paragraphs: Nepherites, Nefaarud in Egyptian, founded the 29th Dynasty and ruled from Mendes in the eastern Delta. He knew Persia would try to win Egypt back, so he looked for allies among Persia's enemies. Sparta was at war with Persia in Asia Minor, and in 396 BC Nepherites sent its king Agesilaus grain and equipment for 100 warships.

The gift never arrived. The ships stopped at Rhodes, which had just gone over to the Persian side, and the cargo was seized. At home Nepherites built at Karnak and Memphis, and buried an Apis bull. He died after about six years. In the 1990s excavators at Mendes found what they believe is his tomb, its burial chamber smashed in ancient times.

claims.text: Nepherites sent Sparta grain and gear for 100 triremes, but the Rhodians seized it.
claims.note: Diodorus, writing over 300 years later. It fits Egypt's need for allies, but no Egyptian source records it.

claims.text: His tomb has been found at Mendes.
claims.note: Found by Donald Redford's team in the 1990s. The badly wrecked burial is identified by his name on objects, not by a body.

reigns.hook: Nepherites is dead, and the crown is up for grabs. The man who grabs it first is Hakor, the king the Greeks will call Achoris.

reigns.tagline: He lost his throne, won it back and beat Persia
reigns.previously: Nepherites I dies after six years. The crown is up for grabs.
paragraphs: Hakor, Achoris to the Greeks, made the 29th Dynasty count. His claim may have been shaky, since he took pains to call himself the heir of Nepherites and named his own son after him. About a year into his reign a rival called Psammuthes pushed him aside. Hakor got the throne back and later counted his years as if he had never lost it.

Then he went looking for friends. He sent help to Evagoras, the Greek king of Salamis in Cyprus, who was fighting Persia, and hired the Athenian general Chabrias with Greek mercenaries. In the 380s BC a Persian army attacked Egypt and after about three years gave up. Hakor built all over the country, from Karnak to Elkab. He died in 380 BC and his son took over.

claims.text: Hakor was pushed aside by Psammuthes for about a year and then took his throne back.
claims.note: Worked out by Egyptologists from Karnak inscriptions. Manetho's list puts Psammuthes after Hakor.

claims.text: A Persian invasion in the 380s BC was beaten off after a three-year war.
claims.note: The Athenian speaker Isocrates mentions it in passing. No Persian or Egyptian account survives.

claims.text: Hakor hired the Athenian general Chabrias to command his forces.
claims.note: Diodorus and the Roman writer Cornelius Nepos. Athens later called Chabrias home under Persian pressure.

reigns.hook: Hakor is barely a year into his reign when a rival named Psammuthes moves in on Karnak and starts calling himself king.

reigns.tagline: King for a year, then gone
reigns.previously: Hakor is barely a year into his reign when a rival steps up.
paragraphs: Psammuthes, Pasherienmut in Egyptian, is one of the shadowiest kings in this deck. Nobody knows who his family was or where he came from. Manetho gives him a single year. For that year, it seems, he was the one in charge, and Hakor was out.

He left his name at Karnak, the great temple of Amun at Thebes, where a small building bears his name. Later Hakor seems to have got rid of him and taken his throne back. What happened to Psammuthes after that, nobody wrote down.

claims.text: Psammuthes reigned in the middle of Hakor's reign, not after it.
claims.note: Manetho lists him after Hakor. Egyptologists reorder the kings from Karnak inscriptions; not everyone agrees.

claims.text: Psammuthes reigned for one year.
claims.note: Manetho's figure, preserved only in later copies. No dated document of his reign survives.

reigns.hook: Hakor is back, and rules until 380 BC. When he dies, his son Nepherites II takes over. He will last about four months.

reigns.tagline: Four months on the throne, then a general took it
reigns.previously: Hakor dies in 380 BC. His son Nepherites takes the throne.
paragraphs: Nepherites II was named after the founder of his dynasty, a sign of how much his father wanted to look like the rightful heir. He was crowned in 380 BC. Manetho gives him four months.

That was all he got. A general from Sebennytos in the Delta named Nakhtnebef seized the throne and started the 30th Dynasty. What happened to Nepherites nobody recorded. A late Egyptian text, the Demotic Chronicle, says his reign was cut short because he did not follow the law of the gods.

claims.text: Nepherites II ruled for only four months.
claims.note: Manetho's figure. Nothing dated to his reign has turned up.

claims.text: His reign was cut short as a punishment from the gods.
claims.note: The Demotic Chronicle, written under the Ptolemies, reads each king's fate as reward or punishment.

reigns.hook: A general from Sebennytos, Nakhtnebef, the Greeks' Nectanebo, has the crown. Now he must keep it, because Persia is coming with a huge army.

images.caption: Not a portrait: the small chapel of his father Hakor at Karnak. Almost nothing from Nepherites II's own short reign survives.
images.alt: Small ruined stone chapel in the forecourt of Karnak temple

reigns.tagline: Saved by a quarrel and a flood, then built everywhere
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Took the throne from the 29th Dynasty
reigns.previously: Nepherites II lasts four months. A general from Sebennytos strikes.
paragraphs: Nakhtnebef, to the Greeks Nectanebo, was a soldier from Sebennytos in the Delta. He founded the 30th Dynasty, the last line of native kings. His big test came in 373 BC, when the Persian commander Pharnabazus landed in the Delta with a huge army, joined by the Athenian general Iphicrates and his Greek mercenaries.

It should have been the end. Iphicrates wanted to dash straight for Memphis before the Egyptians were ready, but Pharnabazus insisted on waiting for the whole army. The two men fell out, the Egyptians dug in, and then the Nile began to rise and flood the Delta. The invaders gave up and sailed away.

Safe again, Nectanebo built all over Egypt. He lined the road leading from Luxor temple with sphinxes, and some of the earliest buildings on the island of Philae are his. A stela at Naukratis gave the goddess Neith a tenth of the taxes on Greek trade. He died in 362 BC and his son Teos took over.

claims.text: The Persian invasion of 373 BC failed because the generals quarrelled and the Nile flood caught them.
claims.note: Diodorus, book 15, writing centuries later and from the Greek side. Egyptian sources say nothing about it.

claims.text: Nectanebo I put up the earliest buildings that survive on Philae.
claims.note: His gateway and kiosk are the oldest standing remains there, but earlier temples may have stood on the island.

claims.text: The Naukratis stela gave the temple of Neith at Sais a tenth of the taxes on Greek trade.
claims.note: The stela was found at Naukratis in 1899 and is in Cairo. A twin copy was later found underwater at Thonis-Heracleion.

reigns.hook: Nectanebo's son Teos has big plans: take the war to Persia. To pay for it, he is about to tax everything in Egypt that moves.

images.caption: One of the sphinxes Nectanebo I set along the avenue at Luxor; the face is an idealised king, not a true likeness.
images.alt: Weathered stone sphinx with a human head, one of a row lining an avenue

reigns.tagline: He hired Sparta's king to fight for him and lost his crown
reigns.previously: Nectanebo I dies after beating off Persia. His son Teos takes over.
paragraphs: Teos, Djedhor in Egyptian, decided to attack Persia instead of waiting to be attacked. Armies cost money, so he squeezed the temples and taxed whatever he could. Then he hired the best soldiers he could find. Agesilaus II, the aged king of Sparta, came to lead the Greek mercenaries, and the Athenian Chabrias took charge of the fleet.

The Egyptians were not impressed at first. They expected a mighty warrior and found a small old man in plain clothes. The two kings then argued over who was in charge. Teos marched into Persian Syria anyway, leaving his brother to run Egypt.

That was his mistake. Back home the brother had his own son Nectanebo, Teos's nephew, proclaimed king. Nectanebo was with the army in Syria, and Agesilaus came over to his side. Teos was left with nothing. He fled to his enemy, the Persian king, and seems to have died in exile.

claims.text: The Egyptians laughed at Agesilaus when they saw the famous Spartan king was a small, plainly dressed old man.
claims.note: Plutarch, Life of Agesilaus, written over 400 years later. Agesilaus was in his eighties and known for his simple ways.

claims.text: Teos raised his war chest by seizing temple wealth and taxing almost every sale.
claims.note: Described in the Greek Oeconomica, once credited to Aristotle. Its tips on raising cash may be exaggerated.

claims.text: Teos died in exile at the Persian court.
claims.note: Greek writers say he fled to Persia. When and how he died is not recorded.

reigns.hook: Nectanebo II has a crown, a Spartan king on his side and a rival claimant marching against him. He is often called the last native pharaoh of Egypt.

reigns.tagline: Egypt's last native pharaoh, or Alexander's secret father?
reigns.previously: Teos is abandoned by his army and flees to Persia. His nephew is king.
paragraphs: Nakhthorheb, the Greeks' Nectanebo II, had to fight for his crown at once. A rival claimant from Mendes raised an army against him, and Agesilaus helped beat him before sailing for home. Then the new Persian king, Artaxerxes III, invaded Egypt, and around 351 BC he was thrown back.

Nectanebo was devout and a busy builder, and temples all over Egypt carry his name. In 343 BC Artaxerxes came again with a far bigger army, and Greek mercenaries fought on both sides. Pelusium fell and the Persians pushed into the Delta. Nectanebo fled south and disappeared from history.

The Greeks wouldn't let him go so easily. A later romance made him a magician who escaped to Macedon and became the father of Alexander the Great. His empty stone sarcophagus turned up in Alexandria, where people came to believe it was Alexander's own. It is now in the British Museum.

claims.text: Nectanebo fled to Macedon, seduced Queen Olympias disguised as the god Ammon, and fathered Alexander the Great.
claims.note: From the Alexander Romance, a Greek fantasy written centuries later. It turned Egypt's last native king into Alexander's father.

claims.text: Nectanebo II was the last native Egyptian pharaoh.
claims.note: Commonly said, and he was the last to rule all of Egypt. Later rebels such as Khababash held parts of it for a while.

claims.text: After fleeing Memphis he went to Upper Egypt or on to Kush.
claims.note: Diodorus says he fled to 'Ethiopia', which may mean Kush. Some think he held out in the south for a while.

reigns.hook: Nectanebo is gone. Artaxerxes III owns Egypt again, and he means to make it pay for sixty years of freedom.

images.caption: Greywacke statue in the Metropolitan Museum: the falcon god Horus towers over a small Nectanebo II, an idealised figure rather than a likeness.
images.alt: Stone statue of a large falcon wearing a double crown, with a small figure of a king standing between its feet

reigns.tagline: Persia's revenge: Egypt pays for sixty years free
reigns.previously: Nectanebo II flees south. Persia owns Egypt once more.
paragraphs: Ochus, son of Artaxerxes II, became Great King in 359 BC as Artaxerxes III, and a pile of dead relatives came with the job. He wanted Egypt back. His first try, around 351 BC, failed. In 343 BC he came again with a far bigger army, Greek mercenaries and his trusted eunuch Bagoas. Pelusium fell, the Delta followed, and Nectanebo II ran.

Then came revenge. Diodorus says Artaxerxes tore down city walls, looted the temples and carried off the sacred books, which Bagoas later sold back to the priests for huge sums. Coins were struck in Egypt with his name and the title pharaoh. In 338 BC Bagoas poisoned him and put his youngest son Arses on the throne.

claims.text: Artaxerxes III killed the sacred Apis bull and had it served up at a feast.
claims.note: Told by Aelian and other writers centuries later, perhaps modelled on the Cambyses story.

claims.text: Silver coins struck in Egypt call Artaxerxes pharaoh in Egyptian demotic script.
claims.note: A small group of Athenian-style tetradrachms carry his name and the title in demotic.

claims.text: The eunuch Bagoas poisoned him.
claims.note: Diodorus says so. Babylonian sources confirm the reigns, but not how they ended.

reigns.hook: Artaxerxes is dead and his young son Arses is king. Bagoas, the eunuch who poisoned the father, holds the real power.

images.caption: Not a portrait: a silver coin struck in Egypt in the name of Artaxerxes III, calling him pharaoh.
images.alt: Photo of an ancient silver coin issued in Egypt under Artaxerxes III

reigns.tagline: A puppet king, poisoned by the man who made him
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by Bagoas
reigns.previously: Bagoas poisons Artaxerxes III and makes his young son king.
paragraphs: Arses, who took the throne name Artaxerxes IV, owed his crown to Bagoas, the eunuch who had poisoned his father. Bagoas had also killed most of Arses's brothers, so there was no one left to rival him. In Egypt, nobody much noticed the change of master.

Somewhere in these years a native rebel named Khababash seems to have held parts of Egypt and called himself pharaoh. He buried an Apis bull at Saqqara. When Arses tried to break free of Bagoas, it is said, the eunuch poisoned him too, along with his children, in 336 BC.

claims.text: Bagoas poisoned Arses and his children when the young king tried to act alone.
claims.note: Diodorus, book 17. Babylonian sources confirm the short reign, not how it ended.

claims.text: The rebel Khababash ruled part of Egypt in these years.
claims.note: An Apis coffin lid dated to his year 2 and the later Satrap Stela prove he existed. His dates are a guess.

reigns.hook: Bagoas needs another king. He picks a royal cousin who will become Darius III. This time Bagoas has chosen the wrong man.

images.alt: Huge stone sarcophagus with a lid, standing in a rock-cut vault of the Serapeum at Saqqara

reigns.tagline: The last Great King to rule Egypt
reigns.previously: Bagoas poisons Arses too, and picks a new king: Darius III.
paragraphs: Darius III was a royal cousin, a great-grandson of Darius II. Bagoas made him king and soon tried to poison him. Darius made Bagoas drink the cup himself. Then the real threat arrived: Alexander of Macedon crossed into Asia in 334 BC. At Issus in 333 BC Darius was beaten and fled, and Egypt's satrap Sabaces died in the fighting.

Egypt was left with a new satrap, Mazaces, and hardly any troops. When Alexander reached Pelusium late in 332 BC, after taking Tyre and Gaza, Mazaces handed the country over without a fight. Alexander marched to Memphis and sacrificed to the Apis bull. In 330 BC Darius, on the run, was stabbed by his own satrap Bessus. The age of the pharaohs was giving way to the Greeks.

claims.text: Darius forced Bagoas to drink the poison he had prepared for him.
claims.note: Diodorus, book 17, writing about 300 years later. A neat ending, but no Persian source tells it.

claims.text: The satrap Mazaces handed Egypt to Alexander at Pelusium without a fight.
claims.note: Arrian, book 3, drawing on Ptolemy and other men who were there. Curtius adds that Mazaces gave up the treasury too.

claims.text: Alexander was formally crowned pharaoh at Memphis.
claims.note: Only the Alexander Romance describes a coronation. Arrian just says he sacrificed to Apis and held games.
